<h2>
<center>MOLECULES</center>
</h2>

<!---------------------------------------------------->
<!-------- SECTION 1 - ELECTRON CONFIGURATION -------->
<!---------------------------------------------------->
<a id="QNE"></a>
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 1. QUANTUM NATURE OF ELECTRONS &thinsp;</span>:** As previously discussed in <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">ChemPrimer2</a></b> electrons have both particle and wave-like properties (i.e. **wave-particle** duality), with the latter being described by the famous **Schrodinger's wave equation** (1926).<b>[@schrodinger_quantisierung_1926; @schrodinger_undulatory_1926]</b> Equally strange is the probabilistic nature (interpretation) of the wave equation. According to **Max Born** (1926)<b>[@born_zur_1926-1; @born_zur_1926]</b> the primary outcome of the wave equation is a probability distribution of the electron within an atom. Central to this probability description are four **quantum numbers** (**Box 1**). Three of these numbers were previously discussed in <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">ChemPrimer2</a></b>, namely: (i) **principal quantum number** ($n$); (ii) <b>angular momentum quantum number</b> ($\ell$); and (iii) <b>azimuthal</b> or <b>magnetic quantum number</b> ($m_{\ell}$). The fourth <b>quantum number</b>, the <b>magnetic spin</b> ($m_{s}$), was confirmed experimentally just over 100 years ago by <b>Otto Stern</b> and <b>Walter Gerlach</b> (i.e. <b><a class="one" href="https://toutestquantique.fr/en/spin/" target="_blank" title="Go to Quantum101">Stern-Gerlach Experiment</a></b> - please consult the University of Colorado's <b><a class="one" href="https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/quantum-measurement/latest/quantum-measurement_all.html" target="_blank" title="Go to PhET">SG Measurement Simulations</a></b>).<b>[ @friedrich_stern_2003; @gerlach_experimentelle_1922-1]</b> At that time <b>Bohr</b> knew that the magnetic moment (i.e. spatial orientation) of an orbiting electron should be quantized.<b>[@bohr_i_1913]</b> However, during the early 1920s many physicists were still using celestial mechanics to solve quantum theoretical calculations of <b>Bohr's</b> atomic model. Even <b>Born</b> himself viewed the idea of quantized space as purely symbolic in nature.<b>[@friedrich_stern_2003]</b> <b>Stern</b> obviously believed that this &ldquo;<i>idea</i>&rdquo; was worth testing experimentally. The initial **Stern-Gerlach Experiment** (**SGE**) involved firing a collimated beam of <u>silver</u> atoms through a non-homogeneous magnetic field (i.e. atoms exposed to a net force) onto a detector (i.e. <u>photographic</u> plates). Although the silver atoms did not escape the affects of gravity (i.e. Maxwell distribution of velocities) there was a clear two-way split in the trajectory of the beam. If the silver atoms obeyed classical mechanics they would precess (i.e. wobble) in response to the magnetic field gradient but remain randomly oriented. As a result magnetic deflections of the beam would cause the atoms to spread out leaving only a broad &ldquo;<i>smeary</i>&rdquo; signal. However the clear two-fold deflection of the silver atoms by the magnetic field gradient supported the concept of space quantization. According to **Wolgang Pauli** (1925) the results of the **SGE** along with other aspects of **Bohr's** atomic model (i.e. energy shells, **n**) suggested that a <u>fourth</u> degree of freedom or **quantum number** was needed to fully describe the <u>quantum state</u> of a particle. He famously referred to this new found degree of freedom as a &ldquo;<i>two-valuedness not describable classically</i>&rdquo;.<b>[@pauli_uber_1925; @pauli_nobel_1946]</b> However its abstract nature makes it unlike the other **quantum numbers**, all of which have real tangible physical meaning (i.e. radial distance, orbital shape and angle). Fortunately that same year **Samuel Goudsmit** and **George Uhlenbeck** (1925) interpreted the electron's fourth degree of freedom as a product of its <u>inner</u> rotational motion (i.e. &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo;).<b>[@uhlenbeck_ersetzung_1925; @uhlenbeck_spinning_1926; @commins_electron_2012]</b> However many, including **Pauli**, were not taken with the idea. After all how can a charged &ldquo;point-like&rdquo; electron, which apparently lacks any internal structure, spin about some imaginary axis? Classically a &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; like property would lead to serious problems since a spherical object the size of an electron would have to be spinning at unimaginable velocities (i.e. greater than the speed of light) in order to attain the required amount of angular momentum. So one has to assume that the electrons behave like tiny magnets with discrete spatial orientations (i.e. $m_{s} = \pm \frac{1}{2}$, &ldquo;<i>spin up</i>&rdquo; or &ldquo;<i>spin down</i>&rdquo;). The significance of **spin angular momentum** will become clearer in the next section when the discussion turns to orbitals since electrons that occupy these quantized spaces are subject to strict constraints as per the **Pauli Exclusion Principle** (i.e. no two electrons within an atom can have the same set of **quantum numbers**).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; It is worth noting that the use of the word &ldquo;orbital&rdquo; in quantum mechanics is often confused with its more familiar use in classical orbital mechanics. This is an important point given that atomic and molecular &ldquo;orbitals&rdquo; are central to the discussion that follows. So an &ldquo;orbital&rdquo; in quantum mechanical parlance has more to do with the underlying mathematical <u>wave function</u> that describes the three-dimensional space occupied by the electron. Physicists often refer to this one electron **wave function** (e.g. $\large \psi_{\normalsize e^-}$) as an **eigenfunction**. It is part of a special **eigenvalue** equation, shown below, that is better known as the **Schrodinger equation**.  


$$\boxed{\, \hat H \cdot \large \psi_{\normalsize e^-} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text E \cdot \large \psi_{\normalsize e^-} \,}$$


Here the <b><a class="one" href="http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/quantum/hamil.html" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">Hamiltonian</a></b>, which in classical mechanics describes the total energy of a system (i.e. $H \; = \; KE \, + \, PE = \; T \, + \, V$), takes the form of an energy <b><a class="one" href="http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/quantum/hamil.html" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">operator</a></b> ($\hat H$). Like other <b><a class="one" href="http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/quantum/qmoper.html#c1" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">quantum mechanical operators</a></b> it describes a measurable parameter of the probabilistic wave function (Recall: quantum mechanics is not deterministic). Here $\hat H$ basically serves as a scalar energy multiplier ($\text E$), which is often referred to as an **eigenvalue**. So an &ldquo;orbital&rdquo; is a volume of space occupied by an electron, described by a probabilistic wave equation, whose discrete energy states can be described using a **Hamiltonian operator**. The specific potential energy ($V$) state of an orbital wave function includes not only the electro-static attraction between electrons and protons, but also the electro-static repulsion between electrons. Nevertheless, both classical and quantum mechanics do share one major problem, namely the inability to provide <u>exact</u> analytical solutions to systems containing multiple moving bodies (i.e. <b><a class="one" href="https://physicshub.github.io/blog/physics-behind-three-body-problem" target="_blank" title="Go to PhysicsHub">three-body problem</a></b>). Fortunately this problem can be largely overcome by using approximation methods (e.g. variational method). However, like the **Kinetic Molecular Theory** (**KMT**) of gases, quantum mechanics generates statistical information about the state of an unseen system (e.g. average speeds and energy). Even though quantum mechanics is one the most successful scientific theories we have, its description of nature is profoundly mysterious for both physicists and non-physicists alike. For this reason alone the quantum reality of molecules is too important and irresistible to ignore.  


<a id="Box1"></a>
<!--------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------ Quantum Numbers Info Box ------------------->
<!--------------------------------------------------------------->

<div style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 5px;">

<div align="center">
<span id="strokeB"><span id="Blue">&thinsp; INFORMATION BOX 1 - QUANTUM NUMBERS &thinsp;</span></span> &nbsp; <b>n</b>, <b>&ell;</b>, <b>m<sub>&ell;</sub></b>, <b>m<sub>s</sub></b>
</div>

<div style="position: relative;">

<b><span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 1. Principal Quantum Number (Shell) &thinsp;</span>:</b> This <b>quantum number</b>, which is symbolized by $n$, is a product of the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">Radial function</a></b> ($\text R(r)$).<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997; @thornton_modern_2013; @Ball_physical_2014]</b> It represents the <b>energy level</b> of an <b>atom</b> and is always a positive integer value (i.e. $n > 0$). Traditionally it is identified using the following letter code:

$$\begin{align*}
n \phantom{1} = & \phantom{1} 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \, ... 
\\
\text{Letter} \phantom{1} = & \phantom{1} \text{K, L, M, N, O}...
\end{align*}
\\$$

Energy levels are often referred to as "*shells*". For example, the lone electron of the [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} **atom** occupies the **K shell** ($n = 1$). Besides having a value greater than zero it is also greater than the value of $\ell$, the so called <b>Orbital angular momentum quantum number</b> (i.e. $n > \ell$).


<b><span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2. Angular Momentum Quantum Number (Sub-shell) &thinsp;</span>:</b> This <b>quantum number</b> ($\ell$) tells us the &ldquo;<i>shape</i>&rdquo; of the orbital, and its value is dependent on $n$. Specifically $\ell$ can be <u>any possible integer value</u> from 0 to $n$ - 1. So if $n$ = 1 than $\ell$ = 0 (1 state). If $n$ = 2 than $\ell$ can be either 0 or 1 (i.e. two possible states). If $n$ = 3 than $\ell$ can be either 0, 1, or 2 (three possible states). Also $\ell$, like the <b>Principal quantum number</b>, is traditionally identified using a letter designation:

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\ell \phantom{1} = & \phantom{1} 0, \phantom{1} 1, \phantom{1} 2, \phantom{1} 3, \phantom{1} 4, \phantom{1} 5 \phantom{1}...
\\
\text{Letter} \phantom{1} = & \phantom{1} \text{s, p, d, f, g, h} \phantom{1}... \\
\end{align*}$$

This letter code was originally used by early investigators, such as <b>Sommerfeld</b>, <b>Born</b> and <b>Hund</b>, to describe the <u>spectral lines</u> of <b>alkali metals</b> (i.e. $\text s$<i>harp</i>, $\text p$<i>rinciple</i>, $\text d$<i>iffuse</i> and $\text f$<i>undamental</i> line series).<b>[@sommerfeld_atomic_1923; @born_vorlesungen_1925; @hund_linienspektren_1927; @jensen_origin_2007]</b> As noted above the values of $\ell$ have to be less than $n$ (i.e. $\ell < n$). It's also customary to denote the <u>quantum state</u> of an <b>electron</b> by using both the $n$ number and $\ell$ letter. For example an <b>electron</b> in the second <b>energy level</b> ($n = 2$) with an $\ell$ value of zero ($\ell = 0$) would be referred to as a <b>2&sscr; electron</b>, while an <b>electron</b> occupying the same <b>energy level</b> but with an $\ell$ value of <u>one</u> would be referred to as a <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} <b>electron</b>. Some quantum states are <u>forbidden</u>. For example, an <b>electron</b> can not occupy a <b>2</b>[&dscr;]{#Turq} <b>quantum state</b>. In this scenario $n = 2$ and $\ell = 2$ which violates the rule: $n \ne \ell$.<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997; @thornton_modern_2013; @Ball_physical_2014]</b>

<b><span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 3. Azimuthal or Magnetic Quantum Number (# Subshells) &thinsp;</span>:</b> This <b>quantum number</b>, symbolized by $m_{\ell}$, describes the spatial <u>orientation</u> of the <b>electron orbital</b>. Since the <b>Azimuthal equation</b> ($g(\phi)$) only deals with one vector component of $\vec L$ (i.e. $L_{\text z}$) the mathematical relationship between $m_{\ell}$ and $L_{\text z}$ is as follows:


$$L_{\text z} \phantom{1} = \phantom{1} m_{\ell} \cdot \hbar$$


The value of $m_{\ell}$ also depends upon $\ell$. Specifically there are 2 $\ell$ + 1 integer values for $m_{\ell}$. So if $\ell$ = 0 than $m_{\ell}$ = 2(0) + 1 = 1 (one possible state $\Rightarrow$ 0), and if $\ell$ = 1 than $m_{\ell}$ = 2(1) + 1 = 3 (three possible states $\Rightarrow$ -1, 0, +1). Overall this relationship can be summarizes as:


$$m_{\ell} \phantom{1} = \phantom{1} -\ell, \phantom{1} (-\ell +1) \phantom{1} .. \phantom{1} 0, \phantom{1} .. \phantom{1} (+\ell -1), \phantom{1} \ell$$


<b><span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 4. Electron Spin Quantum Number (# electrons per orbital) &thinsp;</span>:</b> This quantum number ($m_{s}$) describes an inner or fundamental &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; like property of electrons which is independent of its <b>orbital angular momentum</b> ($\vec L$). Experiments suggest that there are only two possible quantum spin <u>states</u> designated $m_{s} = +\frac{1}{2}$ and $m_{s} = -\frac{1}{2}$. An inner &ldquo;<i>spinning</i>&rdquo; negatively charged electron generates a <u>magnetic field</u>, which makes it behave like a tiny magnet. An electron can &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; in one of two possible directions (i.e. clockwise, or counter-clockwise), which results in a type of spatial quantization. Moreover, this &ldquo;<i>spinning</i>&rdquo; behaviour of a negatively charged electron is a fundamental component of every atom, which means all atoms interact with <u>magnetic fields</u>. In fact researchers discovered that magnetic fields can split the spectral lines of atoms (i.e. <b>Zeeman effect</b>), which is a manifestation of the electron's &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; behaviour. The &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; direction of these tiny <b>quantum magnets</b> in turn determines the direction of its magnetic field and therefore how it interacts with external magnetic fields (i.e. direction of deflection).

<!------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------ END - Quantum Number Info Box ------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------->
</div>
</div>

<a id="AO"></a>
<!--------------------------------------------------->
<!----------- SECTION 2 - ATOMIC ORBITALS ----------->
<!--------------------------------------------------->
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2. ATOMIC ORBITALS &thinsp;</span>:** Previous discussions about the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">Radial wave function</a></b> ($\text R_{n,\ell}$) of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}ydrogen ([[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}) showed that the <b>s</b>pherical ($\ell = 0$) <b>probability distributions</b> ($\text R_{n,\ell}(r, 0, 0)$) of its [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital is solely dependent on the $r$adial component (i.e. $\theta = 0$, $\phi = 0$). Although the $r$adial probability function falls off rapidly with increasing distance it does essentially continue to infinity. Fortunately the spherical shape of <b>&sscr; orbitals</b> accounts for the majority of electronic charge within a [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom (e.g. ~99% probability of finding the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} electron within a spherical radius of 4 atomic units, or approximately $4 \times 10^{-10} \phantom{.} \text{m}$). As a result the boundary surface of the sphere provides a useful representation of any <b>&sscr;-shaped</b> orbital regardless of the energy level. Moreover since there is a single $m_{\ell}$ value when $\ell = 0$ (i.e. $m_{\ell} = 2\ell + 1 = 1$) there can only be one possible orbital state (<b>Table 1</b>). For a much closer look at these and other atomic orbitals please consult the following useful websites: Prof. Mark Winter's (University of Sheffield) <b><a class="one" href="https://winter.group.shef.ac.uk/orbitron/" target="_blank" title="Go to Orbitron">Oribtron</a></b>, and Wolfram's <b><a class="one" href="https://demonstrations.wolfram.com/VisualizingAtomicOrbitals/" target="_blank" title="Go to Wolfram's">Visualizing Atomic Orbitals</a></b>. These visual tools help clarify the <b>Schrodinger equations</b> that generate these <b>atomic orbitals</b>. However, progressively filling up these <b>atomic orbitals</b> for atoms larger than [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} requires some additional rules that are partly explained below.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; The <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbital</b> emerges when $\ell = 1$ (<b>Table 1</b>). According to established quantum rules (i.e. $\ell = 0 \phantom{.} \text{to} \phantom{.} n-1$, $m_{\ell} = 2(\ell) +1$, and $m_{s} = \pm \frac{1}{2}$) these odd dumbbell-shaped <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> will only appear at higher energy levels (i.e. $n = 2 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \ell = 2-1 = 1$). There will also be a maximum of three possible <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbital</b> states ($m_{\ell} = 2(1) +1 = 3$) with each one holding a maximum of 2 electrons that occupy either a &ldquo;<i>spin up</i>&rdquo; ($m_{s} = +\frac{1}{2}$) or &ldquo;<i>spin down</i>&rdquo; quantum state ($m_{s} = -\frac{1}{2}$). The letter subscripts attached to each <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbital</b> indicates its particular three dimensional orientation (i.e. <b>&xscr;</b>, <b>&yscr;</b>, or <b>&zscr;</b> axis). Despite their different spatial orientation these three <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> are identical in size, shape, and energy. As alluded to above the boundary surface of a <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbital</b> takes on an odd two-lobed or dumbbell shape with the nucleus located in the middle. Also similar to <b>&sscr; orbitals</b> the <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> increase in size as the energy level increases.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; The last electron <b>orbital</b> of note is the <span id="Turq">&dscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b>. According to the same quantum rules (i.e. $\ell = 0 \phantom{.} \text{to} \phantom{.} n-1$, $m_{\ell} = 2(\ell) +1$, and $m_{s} = \pm \frac{1}{2}$) <span id="Turq">&dscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> only emerge when $n \ge 3$. At this higher energy level there are <u>three</u> possible $\ell$ states ($\ell = 0, 1, 2$). The first of these states ($\ell = 0$) represents a single <b>3&sscr; orbital</b>, the second of these $\ell$ states generates three <b>3</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> and the last $\ell$ state produces five <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> ($m_{\ell} = 2(2) +1 = 5$). As always a maximum of 2 electrons ($m_{s} = \pm \frac{1}{2}$) can occupy any given orbital regardless of the energy level, which means that five <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> can hold up to 10 electrons. Similar to <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> the five <span id="Turq">&dscr;</span> <b>orbitals</b> each have different spatial orientations (i.e. <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>xy</sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>yz</sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>xz</sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>x<sup>2</sup>-y<sup>2</sup></sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>z<sup>2</sup></sub></span>), but share the same amount of energy. However, there are differences in the overall shape of the different <span id="Turq">&dscr;</span>-<b>orbitals</b>. For example, the <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>xy</sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>yz</sub></span>, <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>xz</sub></span> and <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>x<sup>2</sup>-y<sup>2</sup></sub></span> orbitals have a similar four lobed structures, but the <b>3</b><span id="Turq">&dscr;<sub>z<sup>2</sup></sub></span> orbital has only two symmetric lobes oriented along the z-axis along with a central doughnut or torus shaped lobe. There are of course higher energy levels with other types of atomic <b>orbitals</b>, but they are rarely encountered in biochemical settings since they involve the heavier metal elements (i.e. atomic number greater than 57).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; Although the <u>energy</u> of a one electron [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom is determined solely by its <b>principal quantum number</b> (**n**), heavier elements with multiple electrons behave differently. Specifically multiple negatively charged electrons within different shells and sub-shells interact with one another (i.e. <b>electrostatic energy</b> and <b>angular momentum</b> considerations), which affects the overall stability and energy of the sub-shells (e.g. sub-shell energy levels differentiate and are therefore no longer <u>degenerate</u>). As a consequence additional rules and guidelines were introduced. For example the energy of different sub-shells (i.e. <b>&sscr;</b>, [&pscr;]{#Blue}, [&dscr;]{#Turq}, <b>&fscr;</b>) found in different energy levels (i.e. $n \ge 3$) eventually begin to overlap one another which complicates shell and sub-shell electron assignments. To determine which energy shell or sub-shell &ldquo;<i>truly</i>&rdquo; has the lowest energy the so called <b>Madelung</b> or <b>Janet rule</b> was introduced. It essentially ranks orbital energy using the basic formulas: $n + \ell$ values, and $n$ (in case of identical $n + \ell$ values).<b>[@janet_classificaiton_1928; @janet_concordance_1930; @madelung_mathematischen_1936; @stewart_charles_2010]</b> For example the energy of an atom is lower when the <b>4s</b> sub-shell is filled (i.e. $n + \ell = 4 + 0 = 4$) as apposed to the <b>3</b><span id="Turq"><b>&dscr;</b></span> sub-shell ($n + \ell = 3 + 2 = 5$). This new rule is part of the overall <i>Aufbau</i> principle first proposed by <b>Bohr</b> (German: <i>Aufbau prinzip</i> or &ldquo;<i>building-up principle</i>&rdquo;), which essentially states that the electronic structure of atoms is built by first placing electrons within orbitals that have the lowest energy.<b>[@bohr_bau_1922; @Bohr_AtomicTheory_1922]</b> This is very much consistent with basic thermodynamic principles that have been mentioned in the previous <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer1_atomists/#Max" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC ChemPrimer1">ChemPrimer1</a></b> project.


<a id="EC"></a>
<!----------------------------------------------------->
<!----------- SECTION 2.1 - ATOMIC ORBITALS ----------->
<!----------------------------------------------------->
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2.1 ELECTRON CONFIGURATION &thinsp;</span>:** To understand molecules we need to know how electrons are configured within atomic orbitals. This goal can be achieved using what we know about <b>quantum numbers</b>, as well as some empirical rules (e.g. <b>Madelung rule</b>) and guiding principles (i.e. <i>Aufbau</i>). One of the most convenient approaches is to write down all of the individual <b>quantum numbers</b> using the following notation: ($n, \ell, m_{\ell}, m_{s}$). For example, the notation for the lone electron occupying the ground state of a [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom would be either: ($1, 0, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$) or ($1, 0, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$). Now consider a slightly more complicated atom like [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}arbon (<b><sup>6</sup></b>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}) which has six electrons. The first energy level, which has a single <b>1&sscr;</b> orbital can accommodate up to 2 electrons. So we can register both of them using the simplified orbital notation: ($1, 0, 0, \pm\frac{1}{2}$). The second energy level of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} has 4 electrons. The first two electrons will fill up the <b>2&sscr;</b> orbital since it's the lowest energy sub-shell within the second energy level. We can therefore register both of them using the following simplified notation: ($2, 0, 0, \pm\frac{1}{2}$). The other two electrons will be registered within one of three possible <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> orbitals, since they represent the only other energy sub-shells within the 2<sup>nd</sup> energy level. Here things get a little more interesting since (theoretically) there are a few possible notations. The first scenario would have the two remaining electrons occupying only one of the three <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> orbital such as <b>2</b> <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, \pm\frac{1}{2}$). The second scenario would have each electron occupying separate <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> orbitals. Since all three <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> orbitals have the <u>same</u> energy (i.e. <b>degenerate</b>) we can simply select any two of them (i.e. <span id="Blue"> <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span></span> and  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>y</sub></span>). Here we would have the following possible notations: (i)  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$) and  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>y</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$), or (ii)  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$) and  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$), or (iii)  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$) and  <span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span>: ($2, 1, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$). So obviously there must be some additional rules that can help determine the correct notations.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; The <b>Pauli exclusion principle</b> (<b>PEP</b>) is an important concept that governs how electrons are configured within atomic orbitals. The basic principle states that <u>no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four <b>quantum numbers</b></u>. For example if two electrons in the ground state of an atom have the same $n$, $\ell$, and $m_{\ell}$ values, then they must have different $m_{s}$ values. For example [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>lium</b> ([[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}), has two electrons within the $1\text{s}$ energy shell. Its electron orbital notation would be: ($1, 0, 0, 1, \pm\frac{1}{2}$), and not: ($1, 0, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$) and ($1, 0, 0, -\frac{1}{2}$), or ($1, 0, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$) and ($1, 0, 0, +\frac{1}{2}$). The key point here is that <u>only two electrons with opposite &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; states can occupy the same atomic orbital</u>. The validity of the [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} electron configuration can be easily tested since if the two electrons had parallel &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; states (i.e. both &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; up, or &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; down) the magnetic fields of the electrons (<b>quantum magnets</b>) would reinforce each other resulting in the gas being <b>para-magnetic</b> (i.e. attracted to a magnet). However experiments have shown that [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} has <u>no net magnetic field</u>, which clearly supports the idea that the two electrons have anti-parallel (opposite) &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; values.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; Another important concept to consider when assigning electrons to atomic orbitals is the so called **Hund's rule**.<b>[@hund_zur_1925; @hund_zur_1926; @hund_zur_1927; @hund_zur_1928]</b> It states that the most stable arrangement of electrons within sub-shells is the one with the greatest number of parallel &ldquo;<i>spins</i>&rdquo;. For example if we take a closer look at <b><sup>6</sup></b>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (<b>1s</b><sup>&#8639;&#8642;</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>&#8639;&#8642;</sup><b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sup>&#8639;&#8642;</sup>) there are three possible ways of arranging the <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sup>&#8639;&#8642;</sup> electrons.
<br>

<div align="center">

[A]{#Blk} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [B]{#Blk} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [C]{#Blk}
<br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [&nbsp;]{.ib} &nbsp; [&nbsp;]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑]{.ib} &nbsp; [&nbsp;]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑]{.ib} &nbsp; [↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [&nbsp;]{.ib}
<br>
<b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>y</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>z</sub></span> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>y</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>z</sub></span> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>x</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>y</sub></span> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>z</sub></span>

</div>

According to the <b>PEP</b> all three of the above arrangements (<b>A</b>, <b>B</b>, <b>C</b>) are allowed. However since the stability of the system has to be taken into account the next obvious question is - which arrangement is more stable? According to **Hund’s rule** the most stable arrangement of electrons in any given sub-shell is one that has the greatest number of parallel &ldquo;<i>spins</i>&rdquo; (i.e. arrangement B). Specifically **Hund's rule** uses the term **maximum multiplicity** which is defined as: <b>2&Sscr; + 1</b> (Note: <b>&Sscr;</b> is the total &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; <b>angular momentum</b>, or number of unpaired electrons). Under this rule the <u>lowest</u> energy state is one where <b>&Sscr;</b> is <u>maximized</u> (i.e. maximum number of unpaired electrons with equal <b>spin angular momentum</b> values). For the above [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} example if both <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} electrons have the same $m_s = +\frac{1}{2}$ value then $S = 2(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}) + 1 = 3$, whereas if they have opposite $m_s$ values ($\pm\frac{1}{2}$) then $S = 2(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}) + 1 = 1$. In this case <b>maximum multiplicity</b> is attained if both <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} electrons have the same &ldquo;<i>spins</i>&rdquo; values, which means they must occupy different <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals. Also for equal values of <b>&Sscr;</b> <b>Hund's</b> second rule stipulates that the configuration with highest <b>total angular momentum</b> (<b>&Lscr;</b>) would be energetically more favourable. Collectively <b>Hund's</b> rules address stability issues that can be compromised by electron-electron repulsive <b>electrostatic energy</b>. Presumably increasing the distance between negative charged electrons and factoring in the direction of their motion can <u>reduce</u> the overall repulsive <u>electrostatic energy</u> of the system (i.e. lower energy state). So in the case of <sup>6</sup>[C]{#Blk} we can now write its full electron configuration as:


<div align="center">

[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>:</b> <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sup>2</sup> or <b>[</b><span id="strokeB"><span id="Purple">He</span></span><b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sup>2</sup>
<br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑]{.ib} &nbsp; [&nbsp;]{.ib}
<br>
&nbsp; <b>1&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sub>x</sub> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sub>y</sub> &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sub>z</sub>

</div>


A more concise electron configuration notation for <sup>6</sup>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} is <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;</span><sup>2</sup>. In fact since the electron configuration of [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} is <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup> an alternative way of representing the electron configuration of <sup>6</sup>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} is: [[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}]<b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>2</sup>. This preferred abbreviated notation (i.e. <span id="strokeB"><span id="Purple">He</span></span> &ldquo;<i>core</i>&rdquo;) comes in handy when dealing with much heavier chemical elements.


<a id="Box2"></a>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!--------------- BOX 2 Electron Configuration Rules ---------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------->

<div style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 5px;">

<div align="center">
<span id="strokeB"><span id="Blue">INFORMATION BOX 2 - ELECTRON CONFIGURATION GUIDE</span></span>
</div>

<div style="position: relative;">

<b>1. Electron Numbers:</b> It's important to note that all electron orbitals can hold a maximum of two electrons (i.e. in accordance with the <b>PEP</b>, $m_s = \pm\frac{1}{2}$), whereas the total number of electrons per energy level can be calculated based on the formula: $2n^2$. For example we know that <sup>6</sup><span id="Blk">C</span> has six electrons. Based on the above formula the first and second energy levels can only hold a maximum of 2 (i.e. $2(1)^2 = 2$) and 8 electrons (i.e. $2(2)^2 = 8$), respectively. Thus all six electrons will be found within the first two energy levels. The <i>Aufbau</i> principle (i.e. building up) also tells us that the address of the first 2 electrons will be the first (lowest) energy level, with the four remaining electrons occupying the second shell.
<br>
<b>2. Number of Orbitals per Energy Level:</b> After determining how many electrons there are per energy level (step 1) we now need to decide which orbitals to place them in. Calculating the number and types of orbitals for a given shell can be done as follows: <br>
(i) if $n = 1 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \ell = 0 \phantom{.} \text{to} \phantom{.} n - 1 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \ell = 0$. Thus there is only one <b>&sscr;</b> type orbital found within the first shell. <br>
(ii) the number of <b>&sscr;</b> orbitals within the first shell is one since: $2\ell +1 = 2(0) + 1 = 1$. This lone <b>1&sscr;</b> orbital can hold up to 2 electrons as per the <b>PEP</b>.<br>
(iii) if $n = 2 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \ell = 0 \phantom{.} \text{to} \phantom{.} n - 1 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \ell = 0 \phantom{.} \text{and} \phantom{.} 1$. Thus there is both <b>&sscr;</b> (i.e. $\ell = 0$) and <span id="Blue">&pscr;</span> type orbitals (i.e. $\ell = 1$) within the second shell. Moreover there is a total of 4 orbitals since: $\text{for } \ell = 0 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} 2\ell + 1 = 2(0) + 1 = 1$, and $\text{for } \ell = 1 \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} 2\ell + 1 = 2(1) + 1 = 3$. These four orbitals can accommodate up to 8 electrons. In the case of <b><sup>6</sup></b>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} there are only 4 electrons that need to be assigned to the second energy level or shell. Again we must heed the <i>Aufbau principle</i> and build-up from the lowest energy orbital, which means the lone <b>2&sscr;</b> orbital is filled first. The remaining 2 electrons will now be assigned to one or more <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals. Using <b>Hund's rule</b> (i.e. most stable arrangement of electrons in sub-shells is the one that maximizes parallel &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; states) we know that the last two electrons will be assigned to separate <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals since this maximizes parallel &ldquo;<i>spin</i>&rdquo; states (i.e. $m_s = +\frac{1}{2}$ and $\text{ and } m_s = +\frac{1}{2}$). All three <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals have the same energy so the choice of <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals (i.e. <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue}, <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue}, or <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}) is an arbitrary one.

</div>
</div>


<a id="PTEC"></a>
<!----------------------------------------------------------->
<!----------- SECTION 2.2 - PT & ELECTRON CONFIG  ----------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------->
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2.2 PERIODIC TABLE & ELECTRON CONFIGURATIONS &thinsp;</span>:** Configuring electrons within atomic orbitals according to the rules and guidelines set down by quantum mechanics provides a powerful way of understanding the chemistry of all elements. For example the periodic nature of the chemical and physical properties of elements that inspired the development of the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">Periodic Table</a></b> (<b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b>) is a direct result of the <u>way electrons are arranged</u> within **atomic orbitals**. The quantum mechanical constraints placed on electrons, namely how orbitals are filled and how many orbitals exist within each energy level, controls whether or not an electron will take part in a chemical reaction. This is why quantum mechanics is such a powerful tool when in comes to explaining the chemistry of atoms and molecules.
