<a id="ECF"></a>
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2.2.1 ELECTRON CONFIGURATIONS OF FAMILIES (PT COLUMNS) &thinsp;</span>:** If we take a closer look at the electron configuration of <u>Families</u> or <u>Groups</u> (i.e. columns) of elements within the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b>, such as the **Alkali Metals** (**Group 1**) or **Halogens** (**Group 7A** or **17**), we can begin to see why they share similar chemical properties (**Fig. 1**). For example **lithium** (<sup>3</sup>[[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}) and **sodium** (<sup>11</sup>[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}), two members of the highly reactive **Alkali Metal** family, have the following electron configurations:


<div align="center">
[[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}: <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> or <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup>
<br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑]{.ib}
<br>
<b>1&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2&sscr;</b>
</div>

<div align="center">
[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}: <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>6</sup><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> or <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup>
<br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑]{.ib}
<br>
<b>1&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b><span id="Blue">&pscr;<sub>z</sub></span> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>3&sscr;</b>

</div>

Both of these **Alkali Metals** have a <u>single</u> electron within their <u>outer-most</u> energy level, which is why they occupy the 1<sup>st</sup> column (**Group 1**) of the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b>. The presence of this lone electron is what makes these elements so chemically reactive, and consequently why they never exist (naturally) in pure elemental form. **Halogens** are another very chemically reactive family of elements that make up the **Group 7A** column of the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b>. The electron configuration of two members of this family, namely **fluorine** (<sup>9</sup>[[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}) and **chlorine** (<sup>17</sup>[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}), are shown below.

<div align="center">
[[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}: <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup> or
<b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup> <br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑]{.ib}
<br>
[&nbsp;]{#White}<b>1&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}
</div>

<div align="center">
[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}: <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>6</sup><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup> or <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup>
<br>
[↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑↓]{.ib} &nbsp; [↑]{.ib}
<br>
&nbsp; <b>1&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>2</b>[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>3&sscr;</b> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>3</b>[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>3</b>[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} &nbsp; <b>3</b>[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}
</div>

Above you can see that [[F]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} have <u>seven</u> electrons within their <u>outer-most</u> energy levels, which is why **Halogens** occupy the **Group 7A** column of the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b> (i.e. 17<sup>th</sup> column if you also include the transition metal block). All of the **Halogens** are just one electron &ldquo;<i>shy</i>&rdquo; of a complete **octet** of electrons within their outer-most shell. The **octet** electronic structure (e.g. members of the **Nobel Gas** family) is essentially what all elements are &ldquo;<i>striving for</i>&rdquo; since it ultimately confers energy stability (e.g. **Nobel gasses** such as [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}**lium**, [[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}**on** and [[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}**gon** are all largely chemically inert). The fact that **Alkali Metals** are ideal electron donors for **Halogens** also helps to explain why these naturally abundant elements produce many well known compounds (i.e. salts such as [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}, [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}, [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}[[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}).
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Looking at the electronic configuration of reactants and products in a typical chemical reaction between a **Halogen** and **Alkali Metal** is also telling. For example consider the reaction between [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} (i.e. highly dangerous and volatile solid in elemental form) and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} (i.e. highly reactive and poisonous gas) that produces common table salt (i.e. very stable and relatively safe and edible compound).

<div align="center">
<b><sup>11</sup></b>[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b><sup>11</sup></b>[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>1</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
<br>
<b><sup>17</sup></b>[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup>
&nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>1</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b><sup>17</sup></b>[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>:
<b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>6</sup> or <b><sup>17</sup></b>[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
~~--------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
[[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>&#9783;[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b><sub>(<i>s</i>)</sub> (table salt)
</div>

Showing the electron configuration of two common elements that readily react with one another clearly shows that the number of **valence electrons** ([[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}: outer-most sub-shell electrons) determines their chemical reactivity. Even though the number of [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} is different for [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} (**1**) and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} (**7**), both elements clearly prefer a **Nobel Gas** type electron configuration (**octet rule**). The latter family of elements (e.g. [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}**lium**, [[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}**on**, [[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}**gon**) are well known for their chemically inert nature (i.e. **thermodynamically** stable state). For [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} it is much easier to lose one electron (<b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><sup>+</sup>) than it is to gain 7 more electrons (<b>[</b>[[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><sup>-7</sup>). For [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} it is quite the opposite since it only needs to gain one more electron to attain a **thermodynamically** more stable <b>[</b>[[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> electron configuration, albeit negatively charged. So **thermodynamically** speaking a full outer **valence shell** is energetically more stable than a partially filled one. Moreover because [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} are **thermodynamically** more stable in the form of the <u>reaction product</u>, common table salt, the chemical reaction will also release a considerable amount of energy (mostly heat). How readily two elements or groups of elements (i.e. molecules) react with one another can be calculated by determining the amount of energy needed to drive each step of a chemical reaction. If the overall energy <u>output</u> is greater than the energy <u>input</u> (e.g. [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>&#9783;[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b><sub>(<i>s</i>)</sub>) the reaction is **exothermic** (i.e. heat released) while the opposite type of reaction (energy <u>output</u> < energy <u>input</u>) is termed **endothermic** (i.e. heat absorbed). If we re-visit the **octet rule** (i.e. atoms prefer a **Noble Gas** electron configuration) one could theoretically argue that [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} could also accept seven more electrons and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} could also give up seven electrons to attain a full **valence shell** (i.e. **Noble Gas** electron configuration). However the resulting multi-charge species ([[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<sup>-7</sup>&#9783;[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<sup>+7</sup>) would be highly improbable since atoms are far more **thermodynamically** stable when they have little or no charge (i.e. reduce **electrostatic** energy). **Richard Abegg** (1904) was the first chemist to realize that the difference between the maximum positive and negative valence of most <u>main group</u> elements is usually eight (i.e. **Abegg's rule**).<b>[@abegg_valenz_1904]</b> This revelation was later used by **Gilbert Lewis** (1916) to help formalize his own cubical atomic theory that contains his famous **Lewis** dot diagrams (i.e. dots used to represent [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}).<b>[@lewis_atom_1916]</b> The so called **Abegg's rule** (aka: &ldquo;<i>Abegg’s law of valence and counter-valence</i>&rdquo;) was essentially a precursor to **redox** chemistry (i.e. element can both accept and donate electrons resulting in multiple valence states). Some important examples of **redox** chemistry were highlighted in the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">OPC Soil Ecology</a></b> project when discussing <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">Biogeochemical Cycles</a></b>. So **Abegg’s Rule** essentially describes whether an atom acts as an electron donor or receiver, which determines its valence state. Since **oxidation** reactions are a good example of this principle consider the chemistry of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (**Group 4A** element). When it bonds with four atoms of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} it forms methane gas:

<div align="center">
<b>4</b> <b><sup>1</sup></b>[H]{#Blue}: <b>1&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>4</b>[H]{#Blue}<b><sup>+</sup></b> &nbsp; + &nbsp;<b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
<br>
<b><sup>6</sup></b>[C]{#Blk}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>] 2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>2</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [C]{#Blk}<b><sup>-4</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>] 2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>6</sup> or [C]{#Blk}<b><sup>-4</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
~~--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
[C]{#Blk}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>2</b>[H]{#Blue}<sub>2 (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [C]{#Blk}<b><sup>-4</sup></b>&#9783;([H]{#Blue}<b><sub>4</sub></b>)<b><sup>+4</sup></b><sub>(<i>g</i>)</sub>
</div>


The [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} in methane has a valence state of -4. This is typical of many hydrocarbons since [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} has a slightly stronger <b><a class="one" href="https://ptable.com/#Properties/ElectronAffinity" target="_blank" title="Go to Interactive PT">electron affinity</a></b> ([EA]{#Blk} = 1.263 **eV** or 349 **kJ/mol**, where one [[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}**lectron** **V**olt is approximately 96.5 **kJ/mol**) than that of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} (0.754 **eV**). This is an important property of chemical elements since it greatly influences their chemical behaviour (i.e. ability to accept or donate electrons). By convention [EA]{#Blk} is the <u>negative</u> value of the <u>energy change</u> (<b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b>) that occurs when an electron is accepted by a neutral atom in its gaseous state to form a singly charged negative ion species (i.e. **anion**). For example gaseous [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} is known to have the highest [EA]{#Blk} value of any element within the <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/#property=ElectronConfiguration" target="_blank" title="Go to PT">PT</a></b> (i.e. -<b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> = 349 **kJ/mol** or 3.617 **eV**). This reaction is shown below.

<div align="center">
[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<sup><b>-</b></sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> = -349 kJ/mol
</div>

Another way of measuring an atom's affinity for electrons is to calculate its **ionization energy** ([IE]{#Blk}). This specifically measures the amount of energy a gaseous atom needs to absorb in its ground state to release an electron and become a positive ion species (i.e. **cation**). For [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} this would be represented as:

<div align="center">
[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<sup><b>-</b></sup> &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> = 1251.2 kJ/mol
</div>


The <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> term in the above expressions is known as the <u>Heat</u> or <u>Enthalpy of reaction</u>. It's a **thermodynamic** unit of measurement for the amount of energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction. Typically the <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b>°<sub>rxn</sub> notation is used when reaction conditions are standardized (i.e. 25° C and 1 atm of pressure). One major advantage of this type of calculation is that <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> is a <u>state function</u>, which means you can calculate it by simply subtracting the <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> values from the <u>final</u> and <u>initial</u> states (i.e. <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> = <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b><sub>products</sub> - <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b><sub>reactants</sub>). So if the reaction proceeds through multiple steps one can simply sum up all of the standardized <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> values from each step to calculate the overall <b>Δ</b><b><i>H</i></b>&deg;<sub>rxn</sub> value of the entire chemical system (i.e. **Hess's Law**).<b>[@Hess_1840]</b> When the overall <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> is a negative value the reaction is generally considered favourable since the products contain less energy than the reactants and therefore more stable. Alternatively, if energy is required to convert the reactants into products than the <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b> value will be positive (i.e. **endothermic** reaction). Since thermodynamic calculations are not always easy perhaps a simple analogy may help. Consider a boulder sitting on the edge of a steep cliff or hill. Having the boulder spontaneously fall down the cliff is far more likely than having it spontaneously move up the hill. The latter represents a major energy barrier that requires a considerable amount of input energy to overcome. On the other hand a boulder perched on the edge of a cliff represents an unstable system, which is likely to undergo a rapid correction or change (i.e. cliff gives way). When the rock eventually tumbles to the bottom of the cliff its potential energy will be much lower. Atoms with partially filled electron orbitals also represent energetically unstable systems. Conversely, a singly charged ion species with a filled valence shell is relatively more stable compared to its previous open-shell configuration.  
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Returning to the chemical reaction between [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} one can see that [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} is essentially accepting electrons (i.e. being <u>reduced</u>), albeit not in the same manner as what happens between [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}. Notably the [EA]{#Blk} value of [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} (3.617 **eV**) is 3.069 **eV** greater than that of [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} (0.548 **eV**). By comparison the [EA]{#Blk} value of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (1.263 **eV**) is only 0.509 **eV** greater than that of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} (0.754 **eV**). The difference in the [EA]{#Blk} values of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} is relatively small, which means that the electrons are much more likely to be shared between these two atoms (i.e. nature of **covalent bonds**). On the other hand the much stronger [EA]{#Blk} of [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} when compared to [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} means that the electron donated by the latter element is far more likely to be found closer to the nucleus of [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} resulting in a more clear cut separation of charge (i.e. nature of **ionic bonds**). However if [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} reacts with [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xygen** ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}), which is a typical <u>oxidation reaction</u>, than the electron configuration exercise would yield the following:

<div align="center">
<b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b> [[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>6</sup> or <b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
<br>
<b><sup>6</sup></b>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>] 2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>2</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+4</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
~~-------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub>2 (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>⚏[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+4</sup></b>⚏[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b><sub>(<i>g</i>)</sub>
</div>

Here we can see that the valence state of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} is very different (i.e. +4). This is due to the differences in the [EA]{#Blk} values of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (1.263 **eV**) and [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (1.461 **eV**). In this situation the greater [EA]{#Blk} value of [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} means that the bonding electrons are more likely found closer to the nucleus of [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} than that of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}. However, like the previous chemical reaction of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}, the difference in [EA]{#Blk} values of the two reactants is relatively small (i.e. <b>&Delta;</b>[EA]{#Blk} = 1.461 - 1.263 = 0.198 **eV**). So the bonding character of these electrons is more **covalent** (i.e. sharing) and not **ionic**. Although [EA]{#Blk} is related to the character of a chemical bond, perhaps the more preferred way of characterizing chemical bonds involves a quantity known as <b><a class="one" href="https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/E01990" target="_blank" title="Go to IUPAC Gold Book">electronegativity</a></b> ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}). The actual concept that positive and negative electrical charges may lie at the heart of chemical bonding dates back to the turn of the 19<sup>th</sup> century with some of the early pioneers of chemistry such **Humphrey Davy** (1807), **Amedeo Avogadro** (1809) and **Jöns Berzelius** (1811).<b>[@davy_i_1807; @jensen_electronegativity_2003]</b> For example **Berzelius** devised his own electro-chemical theory based on the chemical affinities of acids and bases. He also proposed a universal scale for <b><a class="one" href="https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/E01990" target="_blank" title="Go to IUPAC Gold Book">electronegativity</a></b>, a term he originally coined. By the early 20<sup>th</sup> century both **Linus Pauling** (1932) and **Robert Mulliken** (1934) created the first quantitative measurements of <b><a class="one" href="https://ptable.com/#Properties/Electronegativity" target="_blank" title="Go to Interactive PT">electronegativity</a></b> ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}).<b>[@pauling_nature_1932; @mulliken_new_1934]</b> For **Mulliken** calculating [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>M</i></sub> involved averaging the [IE]{#Blk} and [EA]{#Blk} values of an element:
<a id="ENeg"></a>


$$\large \chi_{\normalsize _M} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{\text{IE} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \large \text{EA}}{2}$$

Alternatively **Pauling** created a dimension-less quantity (<i>r</i>elative scale) based on <u>bond dissociation energies</u> (i.e. measures strength of a chemical bond using standardized <b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b><b>&deg;</b> values: <b>A</b>—<b>B</b> &rarr; <b>A</b><sup>⋅</sup> + <b>B</b><sup>⋅</sup>). Fortunately the <b><a class="one" href="https://ptable.com/#Properties/Electronegativity" target="_blank" title="Go to Interactive PT">electronegativity</a></b> values of **Mulliken** ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>M</sub></b>) and **Pauling** ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub>) are related mathematically by the following simple expression:

$$\large \chi_{r} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 3.48 \left[ \frac{\text{IE} \; + \; \text{EA}}{2} \; - \; 0.602 \right]$$

**Pauling's** more familiar [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub> values can be easily used to determine the <u>ionic character</u> of a chemical bond by simply calculating the ratio of [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub> values for two bonding atoms:

$${\tag 1}
\\
\large \% \, \text{Ionic} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \left[ \frac{\chi_{r_{_\text{high}}} \normalsize \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \large \chi_{r_{_\text{low}}}}{\chi_{r_{_\text{high}}}} \right] \normalsize \times 100$$

Based on <b>Eqn. 1</b> values ≥50% would signify an **ionic bond**, while values that fall below 50% would be classified as **polar covalent**. Only values close to 0% (i.e. ≤5%) would be classified as a &ldquo;<i>true</i>&rdquo; **covalent** bond (e.g. diatomic molecules like [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>). For example the ionic character of the chemical bond between [[Na]{#gray}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 0.93) and [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.16) is relatively high (~70.6%). By comparison the chemical bond between [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.44) and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 2.2) is polar covalent (~36% ionic). Based on these simple calculations one can begin to understand the chemical behaviour of many compounds. For example, the distinct polar covalent nature of the bond between [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} explains why molecules that contain [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b>ydr</b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b>xyl</b> groups (i.e. <b>R</b>-[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}), such as sugars and alcohols, readily interact with water (i.e. high water solubility). The partial charge separation of **polar covalent bonds** (i.e. dipole moments: <b>&delta;</b><sup>-</sup>‐‐‐<b>&delta;</b><sup>+</sup>) create very distinctive chemical-physical properties (e.g. bulk water has an extensive network of dipole-dipole interactions that produces high surface tension, a unique low density crystalline structure, and high heat capacity).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; Clearly the electron affinity of an atom directly affects the strength of its chemical bonds. For example, common di-atomic molecules like [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<sub>2 (g)</sub> and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2 (g)</sub> share their bonding electrons equally since they are composed of identical atoms. However, in the case of [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}, the lone [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} of [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} is essentially donated to [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} due to the strong ionic character (70.6%) of the bond. Nevertheless most biomolecules are made up of **covalent bonds** that have varying degrees of **bond polarity**. For example, atoms that are held together by <u>non-polar</u> **covalent bonds** share electrons equally, whereas atoms held together by <u>polar</u> **covalent bonds** do not. In the latter case electrons are preferentially attracted to one of the atoms due to their markedly different [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub> values (e.g. <b>R–</b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sup><b>&delta;<sup>-</sup></b></sup><b>—</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sup><b>&delta;<sup>+</sup></b></sup>). It should therefore come as no surprise that elements with low [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub> (i.e. weak attraction for shared electrons in bonds), [IE]{#Blk} (i.e. low energy threshold to remove a valence electron) and [EA]{#Blk} (i.e. release little to no energy when gaining an extra electron) values are good electron donors and also good electrical conductors (e.g. Alkali metals). On the other hand elements with relatively high [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub><i>r</i></sub>, [IE]{#Blk} and [EA]{#Blk} values are good electron acceptors (e.g. oxidants in **redox** reactions) and therefore poor electrical conductors (e.g. non-metals like **Halogens**).  

<a id="ECP"></a>
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 2.2.2 ELECTRON CONFIGURATIONS OF PERIODS (PT ROWS) &thinsp;</span>:** The chemical properties of elements that make up the **Periods** or <u>rows</u> of the <b><a class="one" href="https://ptable.com/#Properties/Electronegativity" target="_blank" title="Go to Interactive PT">PT</a></b> show distinctive trends in their chemical and physical properties. Most of the changes in chemical behaviour are due to the fact that each **Period** represents a different **energy level**. So as you move across a **Period** (i.e. increasing atomic number) more electrons are being added to a given **energy level**, which changes its chemical and physical behaviour. For example, as you move from left-to-right across a **Period** the atomic number (i.e. # **protons**) increases. The additional nuclear charge increases the electrostatic force exerted on the outer electrons and as a result reduces the size of the atomic radius (Note: often measured in **angstroms**, or $\mathring{\text{A}}$, where $1 \, \mathring{\text{A}} \; = \; 1 \times 10^{-10} \, \text{m} \; = \; 0.1 \, \text{nm}$). In addition the atomic radius of a given element also changes when its electron configuration changes, such as when ions are formed. For example, consider [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}.  


<div align="center">
[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>] 3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> (<b>190 pm</b>) &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> (<b>102 pm</b>) &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>1</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
<br>
[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}:<b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup> (<b>79 pm</b>) &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>1</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> (<b>181 pm</b>)
</div>


For **cations** like [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b> the loss of a negatively charged electron decreases the overall repulsive electrostatic forces within a given **shell** ($n = 3$), while simultaneously increasing its effective nuclear charge (i.e. reduced electron &ldquo;<i>shielding</i>&rdquo; effect by inner shell electrons) resulting in a smaller atomic <u>radius</u> (<b>190 pm</b> &rarr; <b>102 pm</b>). On the other hand for **anions** like [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> the additional electron increases its atomic radius (<b>79 pm</b> &rarr; <b>181 pm</b>) due to increased repulsive electrostatic forces and a reduced <u>effective</u> nuclear charge (i.e. increased electron &ldquo;<i>shielding</i>&rdquo; effect). In both situations the volume of space occupied by the electrons is fundamentally altered.
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Another notable change in the elements as you move across a **Period** from left to right is the transition from **metals** (i.e. electron donors) to **non-metals** (i.e. electron acceptors). This transition simply reflects the underlying changes in their electronic structure and associated electron affinities (i.e. <b>IE</b> and <b>EA</b>). Perhaps a more informative approach is to compare the properties of **Period** elements that undergo the same chemical reaction such as [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidation**. For example, various oxides of **Period 3** elements (i.e. [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}, [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}, [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}). The electron configuration of the [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidation** reaction involving [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} can be expressed as:


<div align="center">
<b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> <b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
<br>
<b>4</b> [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>4</b> [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b> [[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
~~-------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
<b>4</b> [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub><b>2</b> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>2</b> [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>⚏[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>⚏[[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b><sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub>
</div>


The strong ionic character (73%) of the chemical bond between [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 0.93) and [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.44) results in a high melting point (1275°C). This ionic property of sodium oxide (aka <b>soda</b>) makes it very useful **flux** reagent in glass making (i.e. it lowers the melting point of silica by disrupting the three-dimensional network of [[Si]{#Tan}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>4</sub></b> molecules). In fact the vast majority of commercial windowpanes and glass containers (bottles and jars) are made of <u>soda-lime glass</u> (i.e. 69-73% [[Si]{#Tan}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>, 12-15% [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and 8-12% [[Ca]{#Khaki}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}).<b>[@gerace_characterization_2024]</b>
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Moving across the **Period** to [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB} (**Group 13** or **3A**) we can now examine its changing electron configuration as it undergoes an [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidation** reaction.


<div align="center">
<b>6</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> <b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>12</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>6</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
<br>
<b>4</b> [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}:<b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>1</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>4</b> [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+3</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>12</b><i>e</i><b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
~~--------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
<b>4</b> [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>3</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub><b>2</b> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>2</b>
([[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+3</sup></b>)<b><sub>2</sub></b>☷([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>)<b><sub>3</sub></b><sub>
(<i>s</i>)</sub>
</div>


The chemical bonds of <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Aluminum-Oxide" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">aluminum oxide</a></b> have a strong ionic character (53%) much like sodium oxide. Moreover, the structure of [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b> and [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b> contains a strong [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xide ion** ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>). For [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b> the extended network of regularly arranged [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xide anions** and trivalent [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB} results in a high melting point (2030°C) and a high boiling point (2977°C). A well known mineral made of [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b> is <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mindat.org/min-1136.html" target="_blank" title="Go to Mindat.org">corundum</a></b>, which has many <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Aluminum-Oxide#section=Uses" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">commercial and industrial applications</a></b> (e.g. hardness: 8.8 on **Mohs' scale** which makes it an ideal abrasive). However <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mindat.org/min-1136.html" target="_blank" title="Go to Mindat.org">corundum</a></b> is especially admired for its rare vitreous gemstones (i.e. [[rubies]{#Red}]{#strokeB}, [[sapphires]{#Pink}]{#strokeB}). The vibrant colours of [[rubies]{#Red}]{#strokeB} and [[sapphires]{#Pink}]{#strokeB} is due to the presence of trace amounts of **metal** impurities (i.e. minor amounts of [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB}, [[Cr]{#Coral}]{#strokeB}, and [[V]{#Rasp}]{#strokeB} substitute for [[Al]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}). Deep red varieties known as [[rubies]{#Red}]{#strokeB} are considered the rarest of all known gemstones. All non-red varieties of this gemstone are known as [[sapphires]{#Pink}]{#strokeB}, which can be [[pink]{#Pink}]{#strokeB}, [[blue]{#SBlue}]{#strokeB}, [[green]{#Gr2}]{#strokeB}, [[yellow]{#Yellow}]{#strokeB}, or [[violet]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}.
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Finally consider the electron configuration of [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}**ulphur** as it undergoes an [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidation** reaction. Here, as in the other two [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidation** reactions described above, the -2 oxidation state of [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} is maintained to allow for comparisons. Even though [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} belong to the same **Family** (**Group 6A**), and thus require only 2 more electrons to fill their respective outer shells, [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} plays the role of <u>electron acceptor</u> (i.e. [[o]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xidant**). This is due to their relative **electro-negativity** values (i.e. [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.44; while [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 2.58). Therefore [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} plays the role of <u>electron donor</u> (i.e. **reductant**). With this in mind consider the following expressions.  


<div align="center">
<b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> <b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> &nbsp; → &nbsp; <b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b>
<br>
<br>
[[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}:<b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+4</sup></b>: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>4</b>[[<i>e</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>
<br>
~~--------------------------------------------------------------------------------~~
<br>
[[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}<sub> (<i>s</i>)</sub> &nbsp; + &nbsp; <b>2</b> [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub><b>2</b> (<i>g</i>)</sub> &nbsp; → &nbsp; [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b>⚏[[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+4</sup></b>⚏[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-2</sup></b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub>
</div>


The chemical bond between [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}**ulphur** ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 2.58) and [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xygen** ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.44) has low ionic character (25%) and therefore classified as **polar covalent**. Having elemental [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} function as an electron donor is characteristic of its multi-valent nature, which was highlighted in the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">OPC Soil Ecology</a></b> project section on <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">Biogeochemical Cycles</a></b>. Although the individual bonds are polar the overall net charge of <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Sulfur-Dioxide" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">Sulphur dioxide</a></b> is zero. Nevertheless the structure of the molecule is slightly bent owing to the repulsive **electrostatic forces** exerted by the lone pair of electrons within the <b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup> orbital of [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}. Its non-linear shape combined with the asymmetrical charge distribution associated with the <u>polar</u> **covalent bonds** (i.e. dipole moment: <b>&delta;</b><sup>-</sup>‐‐‐&nbsp;<b>&delta;</b><sup>+</sup>) results in weak inter-molecular attractions. Physically the end result is a gaseous molecule with a very low melting point (-75.5°C) and low boiling point (-10°C).


<a id="CB"></a>
**<span style="border: 2px solid black;">&thinsp; 3. CHEMICAL BONDS &thinsp;</span>:** One of the early pioneers of electro-chemical theory was **Gilbert Lewis**. He was the first to postulate that a chemical bond is based on the sharing of pairs of electrons.<b>[@lewis_valence_1913; @lewis_atom_1916; @lewis_introductory_1923]</b> In his classic paper entitled &ldquo;<i>The Atom and the Molecule</i>&rdquo; (1916) **Lewis** provides a clear picture of how electrons form chemical bonds using his well known <u>electron dot diagrams</u>.

> “<i>In order to express the idea of chemical union in symbols I would suggest the use of a colon, or two dots arranged in some other manner, to <u>represent the two electrons which act as the connecting links between the two atoms</u>. Thus we may write</i> [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> <i>as</i> [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} <b>:</b> [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} <i>If in certain cases we wish to show that one atom in the molecule is on the average negatively charged we may bring the colon nearer to the negative element....it will be noted that, since in the hydrogen-helium row we have the rule of two in place of the rule of eight, the insertion of one electron into the shell of the hydrogen atom is entirely analogous to the <u>completion of the cube</u> in the case of the halogens....It is evident that the type of union which we have so far pictured, although it <u>involves two electrons held in common by two atoms</u>, nevertheless <u>corresponds to the single bond</u> as it is commonly used in graphical formulae</i>.”<b>[@lewis_atom_1916]</b>

All chemistry students are well acquainted with his <u>electron dot diagrams</u>, particularly as it relates to his electronic theory of acids and bases (i.e. **Lewis** acids and bases being electron donors and acceptors, respectively). In the paper **Lewis** (1916) also elaborated on the nature of polar and non-polar molecules in terms of the ability of an atom to attract electrons.

> “<i>We may very <u>safely assume</u> that the essential difference between the <u>polar</u> and the <u>nonpolar molecule</u> is that, in the former, one or more <u>electrons</u> are held by sufficiently weak constraints so that they may become separated from their former positions in the atom, and in the extreme case pass altogether to another atom, thus producing in the molecule a <u>bipole</u> or multipole of high <u>electrical moment</u>. Thus in an extremely polar molecule, such as that of sodium chloride, it is probable that at least in the great majority of molecules the chloride atom has acquired a unit <u>negative charge</u> and therefore the sodium atom has acquired a unit <u>positive charge</u>, and that the <u>process of ionization</u> consists only in a further <u>separation</u> of these charged parts. If then we consider the nonpolar molecule as one in which the electrons belonging to the individual atom are held by such constraints that they do no move far from their normal positions, while in the polar molecule the electrons, being more mobile, so move as to separate the molecule into positive and negative parts, then all the distinguishing properties of the two types of compounds become necessary consequences of this assumption</i>.”<b>[@lewis_atom_1916]</b>

He also famously coined the term **electrophile** (i.e. electron &ldquo;<i>loving</i>&rdquo;), one of the most common terms used in chemistry, which helps to convey the importance of electron mobility with regards to the physical and chemical properties of molecules. For example **Lewis** (1916) highlights how &ldquo;<i>free</i>&rdquo; or loosely held electrons contribute to the **dielectric** nature of molecules.  

> “<i>When a molecule owing to the displacement of an electron, or electrons, becomes a bipole (or multipole) of high electrical moment, that is, when its charged parts are separated by an appreciable distance, its force of attraction for another molecular bipole will be felt over a considerable intervening distance, and two or more such bipoles will frequently be drawn together ....molecules of a polar substance will therefore not only exhibit an unusually high intermolecular attraction at a distance, but will frequently combine with one another and show the phenomenon known as association ....We come then to the consideration of the electrical properties which distinguish polar from nonpolar substances, or, in accordance with the terminology I formerly used, which distinguishes good <u>electrophiles</u> from poor electrophiles. The first difference is in the <u>dielectric constant</u> ....In polar molecule the constraints which operate against a separation of the charges, being already weak, may be further stretched in the electric field, and what is more important, the biopoles (or multipoles) which already exist in the polar substance may, by rotation, orient themselves in the electric field, thus producing a large displacement current and therefore a high dielectric constant</i>.”<b>[@lewis_atom_1916]</b>

Materials that have low **dielectric** constants, such as glass, do not contain free electrons or polar bonds that can be manipulated by an external electrical field (i.e. good insulators). For example glass, which is essentially <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mindat.org/min-10916.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MinDat.org">silica dioxide</a></b> ([[Si]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>, or simply **silica**), is a good insulator and largely chemically resistant. The lack of chemical reactivity is due to the strong **covalent bonds** between [[Si]{#Silver}]{#strokeB} and the tetrahedral co-ordinated [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atoms (**Note:** the use of the term **silica dioxide** is due to its three dimensional tetrahedral unit structure where each [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atom within a [[Si]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>4</sub></b> unit is shared with a neighbouring unit resulting in an overall element ratio of 1:2). On the other hand molecules with high **dielectric constants** have highly polar bonds that can be manipulated by an external electrical field (i.e. **dielectric polarization**). Today stable **dielectric** materials capable of high-energy densities are in great demand (i.e. **electrostatic energy** storage devices).
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; The <b><a class="one" href="http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Chemical/lewis.html#c2" target="_blank" title="Go to HyperPhysics">Lewis dot diagram</a></b> is one of the most memorable contributions of **Lewis**. According to **Lewis** a single pair of electrons makes up a chemical covalent bond, which is certainly consistent with previous discussions about the **quantum** nature of electron orbitals (i.e. **PEP**). Also chemical bonds are formed by outer shell electrons, otherwise known as **valence electrons** ([[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}). This makes sense if you simply consider an atom's internal or core electronic structure (i.e. non-valence electrons found within the inner shells). The **electrostatic** forces generated by this core structure would obviously limit the region of contact between two neighbouring atoms. Since chemical bonds are all about [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} it makes sense to highlight them using dots that are symmetrically arranged, as per **Lewis'** cubic theory, around an element's symbol. As noted by **Lewis** there is a limit to the number of electrons and hence dots that can be arranged around each element, which corresponds to its place (i.e. **Group** or **Family**) within the <b><a class="one" href="http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/pertab/perlewis.html#c1" target="_blank" title="Go to HyperPhysics">PT</a></b> (Note: with the exception of [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}). This is much less confusing than writing out its detailed electronic configuration. In fact **Lewis** dot diagrams are often added to the **Periodic Table** (**Fig. 1**). For example, there is a dot for each of the four [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}. However, when it comes to heavier elements (e.g. transition metals) a simple **Lewis dot** diagram is not possible because of their complicated, partially filled sub-shells.  


<a id="CBI"></a>
[&thinsp; **3.1 IONIC BONDS & LEWIS STRUCTURES** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** A chemical bond with <u>ionic character</u> (<b>Eqn. 1</b>) involves two atoms (i.e. **metal** and non-metal) with very different **electronegativity values** (i.e. [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b>). This difference in electron affinities between the two atoms is such that the electrons from a **metal** are donated to the non-metal. The resulting separation of charge creates an attractive **electrostatic** force that holds the **anion** and **cation** together. For example, in [[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} (table salt) the **sodium** atom donates its one [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} ([[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>1</sup>) to **chlorine** ([[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>5</sup>), which has seven dots for each of its [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} (**Fig. 2**). Of course atoms making up an ionic compound do not necessarily contain the same charge. For example in **sodium oxide** ([[Na]{#Gray}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}) each **sodium** atom donates one [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} to the divalent [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xygen** atom ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup>), which has six [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} (**Fig. 2**). As a result [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} forms the [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xide anion**. Note that in both of these examples the **anions** have achieved a stable **Noble gas** electron configuration (i.e. **iso-electronic** with either [[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB} or [[Ar]{#Turq}]{#strokeB}).

<a id="CBC"></a>
[&thinsp; **3.2 COVALENT BONDS & LEWIS STRUCTURES** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** When the <u>ionic character</u> of a chemical bond is low (<b>Eqn. 1</b>) its classified as a <u>non-ionic</u> **covalent bond**. However as noted previously there are two types of **covalent bonds**. When the [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> values of the two atoms are the same, or very nearly so (i.e. less than 5% ionic character), than the chemical bond is classified as a &ldquo;<i>true</i>&rdquo; **covalent bond** (e.g. [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>, **Fig. 3**). However if the ionic character of the bond is somewhere between these two extremes (i.e. 5% &lt; [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> &lt; 50%) then it is considered a <u>polar</u> **covalent bond**. For these types of bonds the probability of finding an electron is higher closer to the atom with the highest [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> value, or what **Lewis** would term the more **electrophilic** atom. This type of unequal sharing of electrons produces small dipole moments (<b>&delta;</b><sup>-</sup>‐‐&thinsp;<b>&delta;</b><sup>+</sup>), and if the molecule has a net charge imbalance (e.g. net dipole moment due to asymmetric structure) then these molecules can interact with one another or other like polar molecules. Regardless of the type of **covalent bond** each shared electron pair is depicted by a single straight line. If the two bonding atoms share multiple electron pairs (i.e. <u>double</u> or <u>triple</u> **covalent bonds**) than there may be more than one line connecting the two atoms (e.g. [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub> → <b>⁚</b>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}&#9776;[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b>⁚</b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub>). **Lewis dot diagrams** also depict non-bonding electrons that are referred to as **lone pairs** of electrons (e.g. <b>⁚</b>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}&#9776;[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b>⁚</b><sub> (<i>g</i>)</sub>). These **lone pairs** of electrons can greatly affect the chemical behaviour and shape of molecules (e.g. [H]{#Blue}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}).
<br>

<!-------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------ FIG 3 - Covalent Bonds & ES Dipoles ------------->

<!------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------->


&nbsp; &nbsp; Differences in **electro-negativity** not only help to explain the <u>polar</u> nature of **covalent bonds**, but also the different **oxidation states** of elements that commonly undergo **redox** chemical reactions. For example consider a simple water molecule and the polar nature of its covalent bonds (**Fig. 3**). The **Group 6A** [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atom is more **electrophilic** (i.e. [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.44) than the two [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms (i.e. [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 2.2). As a result there is a shift in the electron density distribution such that the bonding electrons are more likely to be found closer to [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} than [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}. Occasionally one of these polar bonds undergoes ionization giving rise to a [H]{#Blue}**ydr**[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**xyl anion** ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>) and [H]{#Blue}<b><sup>+</sup></b> (**Note:** technically [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b> usually becomes incorporated into a neighbouring water molecule to become a **hydronium** ion: [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>). This type of separation of charge within a water molecule occurs all the time, albeit at low levels (**Note:** water dissociation constant = <b>K<sub><i>w</i></sub></b> = [[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>][[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>] = [<b>10<sup>-7</sup></b> <b>M</b>olar][<b>10<sup>-7</sup></b> <b>M</b>olar] = <b>10<sup>-14</sup></b> <b>M</b><sup>2</sup>, see discussions on **pH** in <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/#Fig4CBS" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">Soil Ecology</a></b> section). So we can assign an **oxidation number** of -2 to [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (electron acceptor) and +1 to [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} (electron donor). The charge of [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} is certainly consistent with its **Group 6A** designation ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}: <b>[</b>[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b> <b>2&sscr;</b><sup>2</sup><b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup>) since it needs 2 more electrons to attain a more stable Noble gas electronic configuration (i.e. **octet** rule). Once all the electrons have been assigned to the atoms it's important to check the <u>formal charge</u> of each atom, which amounts to making sure the number of electrons assigned to an atom (i.e. dots) matches its expected valence state (i.e. **Group** number). A quick way to calculate the formal charges is:  


$$\tag{2}$$

$$\large \text{Formal Charge} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} VE \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \normalsize \bigg)
\\$$


In the above expression [<i>VE</i>]{#Blk} represents the number of [[V]{#Red}]{#strokeB}**alence** [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}**lectrons** in the <u>free</u> atom (i.e. **Group** number), [<i>L</i>]{#Blk} is the number of **electrons** present on the bonded atom as **lone pairs**, and [<i>B</i>]{#Blk} is the number of **bonding electrons** on the atom. So if the atom has more electrons when it's part of a molecule than when it's free (i.e. neutral elemental form), then the atom will have a formal negative charge (i.e. **anion**). Conversely if the molecular electron assignment for an atom results in fewer electrons than its normal neutral elemental form, then the atom will have a formal positive charge (i.e. **cation**). For example the formal charge of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} when part of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> would be:  

$$\tag{2.1}$$


$$\\
\large \text{First Lewis Structure} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \overbrace{:\stackrel{..}{\text{O}}}^0 = \overbrace{\text{C}}^0 = \overbrace{\stackrel{..}{\text{O}}:}^0
\\
\large \text{C Formal Charge} \normalsize \; = \; V \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 4 \, - \, \bigg ( 0 \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot 8 \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\large \text{O Formal Charge} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} V \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 6 \; - \; \bigg( 4 \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0$$

<br>

So the **Lewis Structure** proposed in <b>Eqn. 2.1</b> has no formal charges assigned to any of the bonded atoms. This structure would be preferred since the absence of any formal charges means it's a stable arrangement (i.e. no **electrostatic energy** gradients). A possible alternative **Lewis Structure** is offered below (<b>Eqn. 2.2</b>). Even though each atom has an **octet** of electrons there are formal charges assigned to the [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atom as well as one of the [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atoms, which makes it energetically unstable.


$$\tag{2.2}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \text{Second Lewis} & \large \text{ Structure} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \overbrace{: \stackrel{..}{\text{O}}}^0 = \overbrace{\text{O}}^{+2} = \overbrace{\stackrel{..}{\text{C}}:}^{-2}
\\[5px]
\large \text{C Formal Charge} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} V \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 4 \; - \; \bigg( 4 \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 2
\\
\large 1^{st} \, \text{O Formal Charge} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} V \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 6 \; - \; \bigg( 4 \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\large 2^{nd} \, \text{O Formal Charge} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} V \; - \; \bigg( L \; + \; \frac{1}{2}B \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 6 \; - \; \bigg( 0 \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot 8 \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} + 2
\end{align*}$$

<br>

<a id="Res"></a>
[&thinsp; **3.3 RESONANCE STRUCTURES** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** Drawing **Lewis Structures** with the aid of a few simple rules helps to explain **chemical bonding** for many molecules. However there are many aspects of **chemical bonding** that they can not explain (e.g. varying bond lengths, bond strengths, bond angles and interactions in different chemical environments). For example, unlike the above structures of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> there are many other molecules that have more than one possible stable structure (e.g. simple carboxylates, complex aromatic compounds). These equally probable structures are called **resonance structures**. The concept of **resonance** has been mentioned previously in other project sections (e.g. **Phenolics** and **Free Radical Scavenging** sections of <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Phenolics" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC PNP">PNP</a></b>) since it has a profound affect on biological systems. However the fact that they are equally likely structures once again forces us to confront the quantum reality of molecules. In many ways **resonance structures** represent some sort of **quantum** meta-state (i.e. invoking **superposition**), that we use to minimize the **electrostatic energy gradients** (i.e. established dipole moments) that would otherwise appear if electrons take up fixed positions within any one of the possible structures (i.e. thermodynamically “<i>costly</i>” and therefore unstable). In fact it's possible to view all molecules as **resonance** hybrids of purely **covalent** and **ionic** structures (i.e. **quantum** fluctuations or some sort of molecular &ldquo;<i>breathing</i>&rdquo;). For example consider the relatively simple diatomic molecule [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> (**Fig. 4**).  


<!---------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------ FIG 4 - H2 Resonance Structures ------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig4"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/H2_mol_res.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 4</u>:</b> <span id="strokeB"><span id="Blue">H</span></span><b><sub>2</sub> Resonance Structures.</b> The quantum state with the lowest total energy value and maximum stability is called the <b>normal state</b> ($\psi_{\text o}$). It's possible that $\psi_{\text o}$ is represented by multiple structures that collectively give the total quantum system maximum stability. Only structures that contribute significantly to the overall energy stability of the system should be considered. For the hydrogen molecule ([[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>) above multiple possible quantum states or structures and their associated numerical coefficients can represent the overall system. Fortunately only the <u>coefficient ratios</u> (e.g. <b>b/c</b>) are of interest here since the <u>wave function</u> ($\psi$) is the same for all these structures (i.e. same atomic orbital). So calculating the energy of $\psi$ as a function of the coefficient ratios can determine the energy minimum of the system (i.e. maximum stability). If the value of <b>a/b</b> is very large, then the best <u>wave function</u> for $\psi$ would be $\psi_{\text a}$. Thus the normal state, or $\psi_{\text o}$, would be represented by structure <b>a</b> as apposed to structure <b>b</b>. For example, given the following hypothetical coefficient ratios: <b>b/c</b> = 1, <b>a/b</b> = 0.02, and <b>d/b</b> = 0.02, one can assume that <b>b</b> and <b>c</b> are identical with respect to their energy contributions. Moreover, in this scenario structures <b>a</b> and <b>d</b> contribute very little to the overall energy stability of the normal state (i.e. very unlikely structures). Therefore $\psi_{\text o}$ is best represented by both $\psi_{\text b}$ and $\psi_{\text c}$ (i.e. theoretically consider all possible states including the exchange of electrons, although electrons are essentially indistinguishable from each other). It's important to note that $\psi_{\text o}$ is formed in part by all structures that make significant contributions to the overall stability of the quantum system, and not some sort of hybrid or intermediate structure. The overall quantum state somehow <u>resonates</u> between all of the key stable structures. The main point here is that the <b>total energy</b> of this <u>resonating</u> system is less than the energy associated with each individual structure (e.g. $\text{Energy of } \psi_{\text o} < \text{Energy of } \psi_{\text b} \text{ or } \psi_{\text c}$). The energy minimum ($\psi_{\text o}$) arises from the interactions (i.e. <i>resonance</i>) of the most stable structures (i.e. <b>resonance energy</b>). Incorporating the ionic structures into the overall wave function (i.e. $\psi_{\text a}$ and $\psi_{\text d}$) stems from the de-localized nature of the electron, which can result in partial charge separation. However, as noted previously, such <b>electrostatic energy gradients</b> are energetically &ldquo;<i>costly</i>&rdquo;. Of course the <b>resonance</b> phenomena described above pertains to electrons between two identical nuclei. Even though the concept of a <b>resonance hybrid</b> is a convenient mathematical approximation, all of the experimental data (i.e. bond strength, bond length) strongly supports this resonance model.  


</div>

<!----------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------->

The above structures depict a kind of simple oscillating-like charge (Recall: <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#SHOmodel" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">simple oscillator model</a></b>). However structures with charge separation are thermodynamically &ldquo;<i>costly</i>&rdquo; (i.e. **electrostatic energy gradients**) and therefore unlikely to contribute to the hybrid **resonance** structure. In fact one could safely assume that the two symmetric ionic structures (i.e. $a$ and $d$) would cancel each other out on average, resulting in a &ldquo;<i>true</i>&rdquo; **covalent** bond represented by both $b$ and $c$. Unfortunately this type of scenario would not apply to molecules that contain different elements (e.g. [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}, [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></b>). For example each of the **Lewis Structures** depicted for <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Hydrochloric-Acid" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">hydrochloric acid</a></b> ([[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}) do not contribute equally to the hybrid **resonance** structure. Namely the relatively low energy ionic structure [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>‐‐[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> is far more likely to contribute to the hybrid **resonance** structure than the unstable ionic structure [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>--[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>. Based on the differences in the **electro-negativity** of these elements (i.e. [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 3.16, [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<b><sub><i>r</i></sub></b> = 2.2) it's clear that [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} has a greater affinity for electrons than [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}. In this scenario one would expect a small net **electrostatic** charge imbalance (i.e. dipole moment) to be associated with the molecule, even though the formal charge assigned to each atom (according to the rules) is zero.

&nbsp; &nbsp; In the case of the **nitrate ion** [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></b> (**Fig. 6**) there are three possible **Lewis Structures** each containing two single bonds and one double bond. However, experiments have clearly shown that all three bonds within this **nitrate ion** are <u>equivalent</u> in length (i.e. 124 **pm**) and strength. In fact experiments show that the real bonds are intermediate in value when compared to single (e.g. 140 **pm**) and double bonds (e.g. 120 **pm**). Although the three **Lewis Structures** are equally probable they still do not correctly represent the real bonds of this molecule. The only short term solution is to invoke the **superposition** principle and draw a hybrid **resonance** structure with three equivalent bonds represented by dashed lines (**Fig. 6B**). These dashed lines highlight the dynamic nature of electrons (i.e. **de-localized**). This type of hybrid **resonance structure** is common among compounds that contain alternating single and double bonds (i.e. <u>conjugated</u> double bond system), such as <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Phenolics" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP">Phenolics</a></b>. The increased <u>mobility</u> of electrons (i.e. **de-localized**) within **resonance structures** results in their movement along the length of the entire molecule, which is an important feature of many biomolecules (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Phenolics" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP">Phenolics</a></b>, <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Fig_VitCE" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP">antioxidants</a></b>).
