<a id="CBE"></a>
[&thinsp; **3.4 CHEMICAL BOND ENERGY** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** Another useful way of characterizing chemical bonds is to take a thermodynamic approach. This involves measuring the changes in thermal energy, otherwise known as the **Heat of Enthalpy** change (<b>&Delta;</b><b><i>H</i></b>), associated with chemical reactions using an instrument known as the **calorimeter**. Because **work** and **energy** are essentially the same thing (i.e. same units of measure: **Joule** = 1 Newton&sdot;metre) it's possible to directly quantify the amount of **chemical bond energy** based on the work it performs in a carefully controlled environment (e.g. heat energy flowing into or out of a chemical system can perform work on its surrounding environment, like a change in pressure or volume). So it's possible to view chemical **work** and chemical **energy** as being equivalent. In fact most people understand the connection between the potential energy contained within food **calories** (i.e. 1 **cal** = 4.187 **Joules**) and the ability of cells to metabolize them (i.e. &ldquo;<i>burn</i>&rdquo; them, much in the same way that **calorimeters** work) to generate the necessary **energy** for basic metabolic functions (i.e. **work**).
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; When chemical reactions do take place thermodynamic functions can tell us the amount of heat gained or lost by the surrounding system under <u>standardized</u> conditions (e.g. constant temperature, pressure, or volume). So the heat released or absorbed by a chemical reaction within the confines of a carefully controlled environment (i.e. **calorimeter**, is essentially a closed system with regards to mass) provides a direct measure of the changes in the flow of heat **energy**. Based on thermodynamic principles (i.e. conservation of **energy**) we can define the **internal energy** of our chemical system ([[<i>U</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) as the sum of its <u>kinetic</u> and <u>potential</u> energies.<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997; @thornton_modern_2013; @Ball_physical_2014]</b> The change in the **internal energy** of a chemical system can be expressed mathematically as:


$$\tag{3}
\\
\large \Delta U \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \large w$$


<b>&Delta;</b>[[<i>U</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB} represents the change in the <b>internal energy</b> of our system, [<i>q</i>]{#Blk} represents <u>heat</u>, and [<i>w</i>]{#Blk} represents <u>work</u>. The values generated by this equation can be either negative or positive. By convention if the magnitude of the value is negative that indicates an outward flow with respect to our chemical system (i.e. heat flowing out of molecules into the surrounding). These types of reactions are referred to as <b>exothermic</b> (i.e. heat is <u>released</u> by a chemical reaction). On the other hand if heat flows into the chemical system it is referred to as <b>endothermic</b>. If we use a <b>calorimeter</b> to measure the heat released by a chemical reactions we can simply relate the flow of energy of our system mathematically as:


$$\tag{4}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
- \large q \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} \large q_{\text{cal}}
\\
\large q_{cal} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \text{C}_{cal} \cdot \Delta \text{T} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} - \large q \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} \large \text{C}_{cal} \cdot \Delta \text{T} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{C}_{cal} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{-q}{\Delta \text{T}}
\\[5px]
\large \text{C}_{specific} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{\text{C}_{cal}}{m} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} - \large q \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} \large m \cdot \text{C}_{s} \cdot \Delta \text{T} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{C}_{s} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{-q}{m \cdot \Delta \text{T}}
\\
\end{align*}$$

As shown above the heat <u>gained</u> ([q<sub>cal</sub>]{#Blk}) by the <b>calorimeter</b> is lost ([-q]{#Blk}) by the chemical system (Note: conservation of energy). The value of [q<sub>cal</sub>]{#Blk} can be found by first determining the <b>heat capacity</b> of the <b>calorimeter</b> (i.e. [C<sub>cal</sub>]{#Blk} = <b>calorimeter constant</b>) experimentally prior to carrying out the chemical reaction of interest. Note that [C<sub>cal</sub>]{#Blk} is simply the ratio of the heat released by the reaction to the rise in temperature produced. If the heat capacity is large that means the supply of heat will only produce a <u>small</u> change in temperature. Regardless, if we know the <b>heat capacity</b> of the <b>calorimeter</b> then we can measure the change in temperature and thus calculate how much heat was lost or gained during a chemical reaction. Often times <b>heat capacity</b> is standardized with respect to the sample in terms of either its mass (i.e. [C<sub>specific</sub> = C/m]{#Blk}) or the number of moles (i.e. [C<sub>specific</sub> = C/n]{#Blk}). For example, the <b>specific heat capacity</b> of water at room temperature is 4.18 <b>J</b>&sdot;<b>&deg;C</b><sup>-1</sup>&sdot;<b>gm</b><sup>-1</sup>, which is a relatively high value compared to most other compounds. This is due to the amount of energy required to disrupt the network of attractive <b>electrostatic gradients</b> within liquid water (i.e. inter-molecular network of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} <b>bonds</b>: <b>R-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sup><b>&delta;</b><sup>+</sup></sup>‐‐‐&thinsp;<sup><b>&delta;</b><sup>-</sup></sup>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b>-R</b>) in order to increase its <b>kinetic energy</b> (i.e. raise its temperature). The <b>calorimeter</b> itself can be a rather simple piece of apparatus (e.g. Styrofoam insulated cup with a thermometer), but many labs often use a more expensive piece of equipment known as a &ldquo;<i>bomb</i>&rdquo; <b>calorimeter</b>. This device is made of a sealed metal container immersed in water, which can control the pressure of a chemical reaction.<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997; @thornton_modern_2013; @Ball_physical_2014]</b>

&nbsp; &nbsp; A thermodynamic expression that can measure changes in energy at constant pressure is called <b>Enthalpy</b> (<b>[<i>H</i>]{#Blk}</b>). Its a state function (i.e. internal energy of our isolated chemical system is <u>constant</u>) that can be represented mathematically as:


$$\tag{5}$$


$$\begin{align*}
\large \text{At constant} \phantom{.} P \normalsize \phantom{..} & \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \Delta U \normalsize \; + \; \large P \, \Delta V
\\[10px]
\large \text{Input } Eqn. \phantom{.} 3 \normalsize \phantom{..} & \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q \normalsize \; + \; \large w \normalsize \; + \; \large P \, \Delta V
\end{align*}
\\$$


$$\tag{6}$$


$$\large w \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \large P_{external} \, \Delta V
\\$$


$$\tag{7}
\\
\large \text{Combine Eqn.} \, 5 \; \text{and} \; 6 \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q \normalsize \; - \; \large P_{external} \, \Delta V \normalsize \; + \; \large P \, \Delta V
\\[5px]
\large \text{Constant Pressure} \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q
\\[10px]
\large \Delta H_{(equil.)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large H_{(final \phantom{.} state)} \normalsize \; - \; \large H_{(initial \phantom{.} state)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q$$


In <b>Eqn. 5</b> the values <b>&Delta;[[<i>U</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}</b> and [&Delta;<i>V</i>]{#Blk} represent the change in <b>internal energy</b> and <b>volume</b>, respectively. The <b>work</b> ([<i>w</i>]{#Blk}) term from <b>Eqn. 3</b> represents the change in expansion or volume of the chemical system under constant pressure (i.e. [<i>w</i> = -P<sub>(external)</sub> &Delta;<i>V</i>]{#Blk}). The value is negative from the perspective of the chemical system since energy is flowing outward into the surrounding environment (e.g. water bath in <b>calorimeter</b>). The classic example is the work generated by a changing volume of gas within a piston cylinder (e.g. combustion process). As the gas expands the piston is pushed outward against the atmosphere under constant pressure (i.e. atmospheric pressure) resulting in <b>expansion work</b>. Liquids and solids also expand in the same way, but on a smaller scale. Overall you can see that the change in <b>enthalpy</b> of a chemical system under constant pressure (i.e. <b>expansion work</b> taken into account) is simply equal to the <b>heat energy</b> released or absorbed during the reaction. Also if there is no <b>expansion work</b> during a chemical reaction ([<i>V</i>]{#Blk} constant) then the <b>internal energy</b> ([[<i>U</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) of the chemical system would simply be equal to [<i>q</i>]{#Blk} (i.e. heat transfer).  


$$\tag{8}
\\
\large \Delta U \normalsize \phantom{.} (\text{constant } V, \phantom{.} w \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0) \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta U \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q \normalsize \; + \; \large w \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q$$


If we combine <b>Eqn. 4</b> and <b>Eqn. 8</b> we can come up with the following mathematical relationship:


$$\tag{9}
\large q \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \Delta U \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{C}_{V} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{q}{\Delta T} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{\Delta U}{\Delta T}$$


And if we combine <b>Eqn. 4</b> and <b>Eqn. 7</b> we can show the following mathematical relationship:


$$\tag{10}
\large q \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{C}_{p} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{q_p}{\Delta T} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta T}$$


So we can define the <b>heat capacity</b> ([<i>C</i>]{#Blk}) of a substance under constant volume ([<i>C</i>]{#Blk}<b><sub>V</sub></b>) or pressure ([<i>C</i>]{#Blk}<b><sub>P</sub></b>) as the change in the <b>internal energy</b> (<b>&Delta;[[<i>U</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}</b>) or <b>Enthalpy</b> (<b>&Delta;[[<i>H</i>]{#Red}]{#strokeB}</b>) per unit change in temperature, respectively. The fact that [<i>C</i>]{#Blk}<b><sub>V</sub></b> and [<i>C</i>]{#Blk}<b><sub>P</sub></b> values of solids are very similar is largely due to the fact that they generally produce little or no <b>expansion work</b> when heated. This can also be said for liquids, but obviously not for gases.  


$$\tag{11}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \text{Given:} \phantom{..} q_{cal} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} - \large q \normalsize \phantom{....} \text{and} \phantom{....} \large \Delta H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H_{(rxn.)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} & \large H_{(products)} \normalsize \; - \; \large H_{(reactants)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large q
\\[5px]
\text{When} \; q \; \text{is negative} \normalsize & \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \Delta H \normalsize \, \lt \, \large 0 \normalsize \phantom{..} \text{(Exothermic reaction)}
\\[5px]
\text{When} \; q \; \text{is positive} \normalsize & \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \Delta H \normalsize \, \gt \, \large 0 \normalsize \phantom{..} \text{(Endothermic reaction)}
\end{align*}$$


Since <b>&Delta;<i>H</i></b> is a <u>state function</u> (i.e. defines the equilibrium state of a system) any change in the <b>Enthalpy</b> of a chemical system depends only on its <u>initial</u> and <u>final</u> states (e.g. reactant and products).<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997; @thornton_modern_2013; @Ball_physical_2014]</b> So there is no limit to the number of intermediate steps you can choose to get to the final state. This would be analogous to a person standing at the top of a mountain trying to reach the bottom. At the top the person has more potential energy by virtue of their elevation (Recall: <b>PE = mgh</b>, where <b>h</b> is height). This difference in the <b>PE</b> is fixed and does not change regardless of the number of steps, or the actual route the person takes to reach the bottom. Differences in <b>PE</b> will always remain the same. Chemical reactions are very similar, with the <b>PE</b> of a molecule being defined by the number and strength of its chemical bonds either as a reactant or product. The actual number of chemical steps or reactions a molecule undergoes to transform from one form (i.e. reactant) into another (i.e. product) does not really matter since the energy difference between these two forms is fixed. Therefore it's possible to visualize a reaction by breaking it up into multiple reaction steps where the standard <b>Enthalpy of formation</b> ([&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk}) is known for each step (i.e. <b>Hess's Law</b>).<b>[@Hess_1840]</b> These standardized [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} values represent the formation of 1 mole of a compound from its component elements. For example the most stable form of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} at room temperature is <u>graphite</u>, which can react with [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> to produce [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>:  


$$\tag{12}$$


$$\\
\large elements \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large compounds \normalsize \phantom{....} \large H^\text{o}_{\phantom{.} (rx.)} \normalsize \; = \; \large \Delta H^\text{o}_{f}
\\[10px]
\large \text{C}_{ \, (s, \, \text{gr} \, )} \normalsize \; + \; \large \text{O}_{2 {\,(g)}} \normalsize \phantom{..} \longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{CO}_{2 {\, (g)}} \normalsize \phantom{....} \large \Delta H^\text{o}_{f} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} -393.51 \, \text{kJ}$$



Like standardized <b>&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub></b> values (i.e. 1 <b>atm.</b> of pressure, 1 Molar), each initial pure substance must be in its <u>standard state</u> (i.e most <u>stable</u> form, at 1 <b>atm</b> and a specified &deg;C). These standard states serve as reference points for all chemical reactions (<b>&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub></b> = 0). For example, since graphite (not diamond) is the most stable state of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} under standard conditions then:  


$$\tag{13}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
& \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; (\text{C}, \, graphite) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0 \phantom{....} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \phantom{.} (\text{O}_{2 \, (g)}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0 \phantom{....} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \phantom{.} (\text{H}_{2, \, (g)}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\[5px]
& \phantom{............} \large \text{C}_{\normalsize (s, \phantom{.} graphite)} \normalsize \phantom{..}
\longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{C}_{\normalsize (s, \, diamond)} \normalsize \phantom{....} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; = \; 1.9 \, \text{kJ}
\\
& \phantom{......} \large \text{H}_{\normalsize 2 \phantom{.} (g)} \normalsize \; + \; \frac{1}{2} \large \text{O}_{\normalsize 2 \phantom{.} (g)} \normalsize \phantom{..} \longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text{H}_{\normalsize 2}\text{O}_{\normalsize (\ell)} \normalsize \phantom{....} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; = \; - 285.8 \, \text{kJ}
\end{align*}$$


The relatively large negative [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} value for liquid water means that the forward chemical reaction is thermodynamically very favourable. However even favourable reactions need an small kick start in order to take place, what chemists call <b>activation energy</b> (e.g. spark, UV light, effective collision). This is due to the fact that chemical bonds usually need to be broken in order to release chemical energy that can be used to fuel new bond formation (i.e. product). Nevertheless, it should be noted that there are barrier-less exothermic reactions (e.g. some free-radical chemistry, acid-base neutralization reactions).<b>[@denny_barrierless_1999]</b> **Reactants** that do require bond-breaking events usually form one short-lived <b>transition states</b> during their transformation into **product**. However, with the appropriate set of [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} values it's relatively easy to calculate [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>rxn.</sub>]{#Blk}. So for the following hypothetical chemical reaction:<br>


$$\tag{14}$$


$$\\
a \, \text{A} \; + \; b \, \text{B} \phantom{..} \longrightarrow \phantom{..} c \, \text{C}
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_{rxn.} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \Big( c \cdot \Delta H^{\text o}_f \; (\text C) \Big) \; - \; \Big( a \cdot \Delta H^{\text o}_f \; (\text A) \; + \; b \cdot \Delta H^{\text o}_f \; (\text B) \Big)$$


Note that in the above expression the small letters (a, b, c) are coefficients that account for the stoichiometry of the **reactants** and **products** (i.e. balanced equation = conservation of mass). A more general formula is presented below. So once we know all of the [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} values of the molecules involved in the reaction we can apply the formula to calculate [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>rxn.</sub>]{#Blk}. Often times a chemical reaction can not be carried out in one step, which is why a given reaction is broken down into a series of balanced reactions (i.e. **Hess' Law**).<b>[@Hess_1840]</b> The number of steps can vary since all that matters is the initial and final state functions ([&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f(reactants)</sub>]{#Blk} and [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f(products)</sub>]{#Blk}).  


<a id="HL"></a>
$$\tag{15}$$


$$\\
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_{\, \text{rxn.}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\sum n \cdot \Delta H^{\text o}_f \, (products)}^{\text{sum products}} \; - \; \overbrace{\sum n \cdot \Delta H^{\text o}_f \, (reactants)}^{\text{sum reactants}}
\\$$


For example, consider the following common biochemical reaction (i.e. oxidation of glucose):


$$\tag{16}
\large \text{C}_6 \text{H}_{12} \text{O}_{6 \; (s)} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \large 6 \; \text{O}_{2 \; (g)} \normalsize \phantom{..} \longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large 6 \, \text{CO}_{2 \; (g)} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \large 6 \; \text{H}_{2} \text{O}_{\phantom{.} (\ell)}$$


$$\tag{17}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; (\text{C}_6 \text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6 \; (s)}) \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} - 1273.3 \; \text{kJ} \phantom{......} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \phantom{.} (\text{O}_{2 \; (g)}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; (\text{CO}_{2 \; (g)}) \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} - 393.5 \; \text{kJ} \phantom{.......} \large \Delta H^{\text o}_f \normalsize \; (\text{H}_2 \text{O}_{\; (g)}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 285.8 \; \text{kJ}
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_{\text{rxn.}} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} \Big( 6( - 393.5) \normalsize \; + \; 6( - 285.8) \Big) \; - \; \Big( 1 ( - 1273.3)  \; + \; 6(0) \Big)
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H^{\text o}_{\text{rxn.}} \normalsize \phantom{.} & = \phantom{.} \Big( - 4075.8 \; + \; 1273.3 \Big) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 2802.6 \; \text{kJ}
\end{align*}$$


Plugging in the [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} values for the **products** and **reactants** into the [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>rxn.</sub>]{#Blk} formula (**Eqn. 15**) gives us a value of -2802.6 kJ per mole of glucose. The large negative value of [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>rxn.</sub>]{#Blk} indicates that it's an <b>exothermic reaction</b> (i.e. a lot of chemical energy contained in one mole of glucose). We could also reverse the reaction and determine how much energy is required to make a mole of glucose using carbon dioxide and water (i.e. [[photosynthesis]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}). Not surprisingly the answer would be +2802.6 <b>kJ</b>.

<br>

&nbsp; &nbsp; It's also possible to take a look at the energy required to break or make a specific chemical bond, otherwise known as **Bond Enthalpy** ([&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>B</sub>]{#Blk}). Since [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>B</sub>]{#Blk} represents the <u>average</u> energy required to break one mole of a specific type of bond (i.e. gas phase), it therefore provides information about the stability of particular molecules (i.e. how susceptible it is to chemical attack). Applying **Hess' Law** we can quantify the difference in the standard molar **Enthalpy** values of a molecule and its fragments:


$$\tag{18}
\large \Delta H_{\text{B}} \; \normalsize (\text{A-B}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \Big( \large H^{\text o}_m \normalsize (\text A)_{\, (gas)} \; + \; \large H^{\text o}_m \normalsize (\text B)_{\,(gas)} \Big) \normalsize \; - \; \Big( \large H^{\text o}_m \normalsize (\text{A-B)}_{\, (gas)} \Big)$$


As mentioned previously <u>breaking</u> bonds requires energy ([&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup>]{#Blk} &gt; 0), while making or forming bonds releases energy ([&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup>]{#Blk} &lt; 0). Although different molecules can have slightly different bond energies for a specific type of chemical bond, <u>average</u> bond energies generally provide good approximations of how favourable a specific bond making and breaking event is for a given molecule. For example, below are the average bond energies for several different types of chemical bonds found in many molecules.  


$$\begin{align*}
\\
\large \Delta H^{\circ}_{\normalsize (\text{HO}-\text{H})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 502 \; \text{kJ} & \phantom{......} \large \Delta H^{\circ}_{\normalsize (\text{C}-\text{C})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 346 \, \text{kJ}
\\[5px]
\large \Delta H^{\circ}_{\normalsize (\text{C}=\text{C})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 602 \; \text{kJ} & \phantom{......} \large \Delta H^{\circ}_{\normalsize (\text{C} \equiv \text{C})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 835 \; \text{kJ}
\end{align*}
\\$$


As alluded to above [&Delta;<i>H</i><sub>rxn.</sub>]{#Blk} can be approximated using the specific <b>bond energy</b> values. For example based on the [&Delta;<i>H</i><sup>o</sup><sub>f</sub>]{#Blk} (1 atm, 25 &deg;C) data catalogued at the <b><a class="one" href="https://data.nist.gov/od/id/mds2-2124" target="_blank" title="Go to NIST">National Institute of Standards</a></b><b>[@wagman_nbs_1982]</b> the <u>average</u> bond energy of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>–</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} would be:

<br>

$$\\
\Delta H^{\circ}_f \phantom{..} \text{CH}_4 \,_{(g)} \; = \; - 74.81 \; \text{kJ} \phantom{.....} \Delta H^{\circ}_f \phantom{..} \text C_{\, (g)} \; = \; 716.68 \, \text{kJ} \phantom{.....} \Delta H^{\circ}_f \phantom{..} \text H_{\, (g)} \; = \; 217.965 \, \text{kJ}
\\[10px]
\text C_{\, (g)} \; + \; 4 \, \text H_{\, (g)} \phantom{..} \rightarrow \phantom{..} \text{CH}_4 \,_{(g)}
\\[5px]
\Delta H^{\circ}_{(\text C - \text H)} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\Delta H^{\circ}_f \; (\text{CH}_4)_{\, (g)} \; - \; \Big[ \Delta H^{\circ}_f \; \text{C}_{\, (g)} \; + \; 4 \big( \Delta H^{\circ}_f \; \text H_{\, (g)} \big) \Big]}{\large 4} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 415.838 \, \text{kJ}
\\$$

<br>

Based on the above calculations it is clear to see that there is a significant amount of energy contained within each [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>–</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} bond (i.e. 416 kJ/mol). In fact there is a version of **Hess' Law** where you can use the chemical bond energies to calculate the amount of energy released or absorbed by a chemical reaction. For example, the combustion of methane would release the following amount of energy.  

$$\\
\text{Average Bond Energies (kJ/mol)}
\\
\begin{align*}
\text C – \text H \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} & 416 \phantom{.....} \text O = \text O \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 498
\\
\text C = \text O \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} & 799 \phantom{......} \; \text O – \text H \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 463
\end{align*}
\\$$

$$\\
\text{According to Hess' Law}
\\[10px]
\Delta H_{rxn}^\circ \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sum \text{Bonds}_{\small \text{broken}} - \sum \text{Bonds}_{\small \text{formed}}
\\[10px]
\text{CH}_4 \; + \; 2 \, \text O_2 \phantom{.} \longrightarrow \phantom{.} \text{CO}_2 \; + \; 2 \, \text H_2 \text O
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
4 \, \text{C–H  bonds (methane)} \; \Longrightarrow & \; 4 \times 416 = 1,664 \text{ kJ}
\\
2 \, \text{O=O bonds } (2 \, \text O_2) \; \Longrightarrow & \; 2 \times 498 = 996 \text{ kJ}
\\[5px]
2 \, \text{C=O bonds } (\text{CO}_2) \; \Longrightarrow & \; 2 \times 799 = 1,598 \text{ kJ}\
\\
4 \, \text{O–H bonds } (2 \, \text H_2 \text O) \; \Longrightarrow & \; 4 \times 463 = 1,852 \text{ kJ}
\\
\end{align*}
\\
\Delta H_{rxn}^\circ \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{2,660 \, \text{kJ/mol}}^{\text{Broken Bonds}} \; - \; \overbrace{3,450 \, \text{kJ/mol}}^{\text{Formed Bonds}} \phantom{..} \approx \; - 790 \, \text{kJ/mol}
\\$$


<a id="CBMG"></a>
[&thinsp; **4. CHEMICAL BONDS & MOLECULAR GEOMETRY** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** The physical and chemical properties of molecules is largely a product of its <u>valence electrons</u> ([[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) and its overall three dimensional shape or geometry. For example water is a bent molecule due to the repulsive electrostatic forces exerted by its **lone pairs** of electrons (**Fig. 3**). When the dipole moments (i.e. **electrostatic gradients**) associated with the two [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**–**[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} bonds are superimposed onto its asymmetric geometry a <u>net dipole</u> moment emerges (i.e. polar molecule). This in turn promotes <u>inter-molecular</u> interactions that affect its physical and chemical behaviour (e.g. melting point, boiling point, density, reactivity). Focusing on the **electrostatic** forces associated with the outer [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} is a relatively simple but effective approach to modelling the structure of small molecules. The **Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion** (**VSEPR**) model is a logical extension of **Lewis Structures** since the **electrostatic** forces are not fully accounted for by a simple **Lewis** dot diagram.<b>[@gillespie_inorganic_1957; @gillespie_valence-shell_1963; @gillespie_teaching_2004]</b> **VSEPR** uses an **AX<sub><i>n</i></sub>E<sub><i>m</i></sub>** classification system where **A** is the central atom surrounded by <i>n</i> bonded atoms (**X**) and potentially <i>m</i> **lone pairs** of electrons (**E**). The total number of bonding or lone electron pairs (**n** + **m**) is referred to as the <b><u>steric number</u></b> (e.g. **AX<sub>2</sub>E<sub>2</sub>** = 4). The simple empirical based approach of **VSEPR** is what makes it such an effective teaching tool. It assumes that <u>valence shell electrons</u>, be they **bonding** or **lone pairs**, determines the shape of molecules via their repulsive **electrostatic** interactions. So minimizing the overall repulsive **electrostatic** energy should optimize the distances separating neighbouring [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} &ldquo;<i>clouds</i>&rdquo; or **domains**. The resulting shape or geometry, codified by **AX<sub><i>n</i></sub>E<sub><i>m</i></sub>**, is subject to some modifications due to the behaviour of the two <u>different types</u> of **electron domains**. Notably the **electrostatic repulsion** of **lone pairs** is <u>slightly stronger</u> than **bonding pairs** owing to their more de-localized nature, while the repulsion exerted by **bonding pairs** is stronger for multi-bonded atoms (i.e. triple &gt; double &gt; single bonds). Based on these assumptions the relative positions of the electron **domains** surrounding the central atom can be optimized.  


<a id="Vesp"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.1 VALENCE SHELL ELECTRON PAIR REPULSION (VSEPR)** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** Predicting the geometry of molecules based on the number and types of electron **domains** (i.e. [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}, and **lone pairs**) surrounding its central atom, using a **Lewis Structure** is quite an effective technique. The general assumption is that both **bonding** and **lone** pairs of electrons within the outer-most shell repel each other resulting in optimal separation distances. This, in turn, helps to fix the geometry of the surrounding bonded atoms. While the **bonding domain** occupies a fairly defined space (i.e. restricted to inter-nuclear region), the **lone-pair domain** is slightly more <u>de-localized</u>, which means it has a slightly larger <u>angular spread</u> about the central atom. This results in greater **repulsive electrostatic** interactions with neighbouring [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} **domains**.<b>[@gillespie_teaching_2004]</b> This model largely ignores differences in bond length (i.e. single, double and triple bonds treated the same) when assigning molecular geometries. Overall there are two main groups, namely those without **lone pairs** of electrons (e.g. **AX<sub>n</sub>**) and those with **lone pairs** (e.g. **AX<sub>n</sub>E<sub>n</sub>**). Although there are many molecules with non-bonding **electron domains** its important to keep in mind that the shape of the molecule is ultimately dictated by the position of the bonded atoms. The figure below describes some of the most common **VSEPR** based molecular geometries (Note: other shapes have been omitted for brevity).

<br>

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


**(i) AX<sub>2</sub>:** These linear molecules are the simplest molecular geometries. The two **bonding pairs** of electrons are positioned on opposite sides of the central atom. A good example of this type of geometry is [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>, which has two double bonded oxygen atoms. The high electron densities associated with the double bonds ensures optimal separation (i.e. 180&deg; angle).
<br>
**(ii) AX<sub>3</sub>:** Molecules with three bonding pairs of electrons are arranged in a trigonal-planar fashion. The most stable positions coincide with the vertices of an equilateral triangle with a predicted 120&deg; angle of separation. So all four atoms occupy the same imaginary plane (i.e. flat molecule). A good example of this type of **VSEPR** geometry is the carbonate ion ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub><sup>-2</sup></b>), which plays an important role in cellular physiology and **biogeochemical cycles** (i.e. <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/#Fig4CBS" target="_blank" title="Go to Soil Ecosystem">carbonate</a></b> chemistry).
<br>
**(iii) AX<sub>4</sub>:** This is one of the more familiar **VSEPR** groups since it includes tetra-valent elements like [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (i.e. organic chemistry) and [[Si]{#Silver}]{#strokeB} (i.e. geochemistry). These types of molecules have four bonding pairs of electrons (e.g. methane, [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>4</sub></b>) that have bond angles of 109.5&deg;. For methane the four [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms occupy positions corresponding to the vertices of an imaginary tetrahedron (i.e. polygon with four equilateral triangular faces).
<br>
**(iv) AX<sub>5</sub>:** This trigonal bi-pyramid molecular structure (i.e. fusion of two three sided pyramids) is one of the more uncommon **VSEPR** shapes found in nature. Although there are few if any biomolecules with this type of covalent geometry, there are examples of metal co-ordinated complexes that take on a trigonal-bipyramidal geometry. One specific example is a metallo-enzyme known as **carbonic anhydrases**.<b>[@supuran_carbonic_2003]</b>

<!------------ FIG 8 - VSEPR AX5 ------------->

<a id="Fig8"></a>

<div align="center">

![](images/VSEPR_CA_mech.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 8</u>:</b> <b>Carbonic Anhydrase Active Site Geometry.</b>  

</div>

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->

Normally the active site of this enzyme (**Fig. 8**) co-ordinates the binding of a [[Zn]{#Almond}]{#strokeB}**<sup>+2</sup>** cation using **electrostatic** interactions provided by a water group (**lone pair** of electrons in [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}) and three histidine residues (**lone pairs** of electrons belonging to [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} within each **histidine** side chain). However this normal <u>tetrahedral geometry</u> is disrupted when a **sulfonamide** <u>inhibitor</u> is introduced to the active site (**Fig. 9**). In its de-protonated state the soluble **sulfonamide** moiety replaces the water group and co-ordinates [[Zn]{#Almond}]{#strokeB}**(II)** binding using two **lone pairs** of electrons belonging to [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} (i.e. bi-dentate binding mode). The introduction of an additional binding site to co-ordinate metal binding distorts the normal tetrahedral geometry in favour of a <u>trigonal-bipyramidal</u> geometry.<b>[@wischeler_bidentate_2010]</b> 


<!-------------------------------------------->
<!------------ FIG 9 - VSEPR AX6 ------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig9"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/VSEPR_CA_inhibitors.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>
<b><u>Figure 9</u>:</b> <b>Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors.</b>  

</div>

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


A more classical example of this geometry is **phosphorus penta-chloride** ([[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}**<sub>5</sub>**). This inorganic molecule has a central [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} atom which shares 5 bonding pairs of electrons with 5 [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} atoms. The surrounding [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} atoms occupy positions corresponding to the vertices of an imaginary trigonal bi-pyramid. Two atoms lie directly above and below the shared triangular base (i.e. 180&deg; angle of separation), while the three equatorial atoms are separated by a bond angle of 120&deg;.  
**(v) AX<sub>6</sub>:** Biomolecules with six bonding pairs of electrons are exceptionally rare species. These electron domains are positioned around a central atom as if they occupy the vertices of an imaginary octahedral polygon. The chemistry of biomolecules (i.e. [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} chemistry) is generally governed by the <u>octet rule</u>. Only elements found in the third period of the [[PT]{#Dred}]{#strokeB} (e.g. [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}, [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}) have available [&dscr;]{#Turq} orbitals that can accommodate more than eight electrons and form six bonds. However most of these are inorganic molecules (e.g. [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}[[F]{#Mag}]{#strokeB}<sub>6</sub>). Nevertheless there are a number of vital biomolecules that form transition metal co-ordinated complexes that take on an octahedral shape (i.e. <b>AX<syb>6</sub></b>). One example is the <b><a class="one" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l2_3ZMQUKC0" target="_blank" title="Siderophore video">siderophore</a></b> <b><a class="one" href="https://virtual-museum.soils.wisc.edu/display/ferrichrome/" target="_blank" title="Go to Virtual Museum of Minerals & Molecules">Ferrichrome</a></b> (**Fig. 10**).<b>[@zalkin_crystal_1964; @winkelmann_ecology_2007]</b> This compound is produced by fungi to sequester extracellular sources of vital <b>iron</b> ([[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB}).  

<a id="Fig10"></a>
<figure id="FRight350">
![](images/VSEPR_Ferrichrome.jpg){width=335px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 10</u>: Ferrichrome Siderophore.</b>
</figcaption>
</figure>

<a id="Fig11"></a>
<figure id="FRight450">
![](images/VSEPR_Heme_Myoglobin.jpg){width=400px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 11: Heme (Protoporphyrin [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB} complex)</b>
</figcaption>
</figure>

&nbsp;&nbsp; Many other higher organisms also produce [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB} sequestering molecules to carry out important biochemical processes (e.g. carrier proteins, enzymes that fight infection). Although the amounts of [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB} and other transition metals (e.g. [[Co]{#Coral}]{#strokeB}, [[Mn]{#Mag}]{#strokeB}) present within living cells are very small, these cations catalyze reactions by virtue of their multi-valent nature (i.e. <b>redox</b> chemistry).<b>[@montesdeoca_metal_2026]</b> They serve as important electron carriers within mitochondria (e.g. cytochrome c), as well as key catalysts in numerous biochemical reactions (e.g. catalases, peroxidases). Some of the more notable biomolecules that use [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB} are **cytochromes** and **haemoglobins** ([[Hb]{#Dred}]{#strokeB}). Both employ a <u>planar</u> tetra-dentate **porphyrin** ring (i.e. <u>four</u> **lone pairs** of electrons from four [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} atoms) as a prosthetic group to co-ordinate [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB}**<sup>+2</sup>**/[[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB}**<sup>+3</sup>** binding. **Haemoglobins** use **porphyrins** and the side chains of centrally located amino acid residues to facilitate the binding of [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB}. The former has four [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} that border a central hole that accommodates an iron cation (**Fig. 11**). Another more common name for the [[Fe]{#Rust}]{#strokeB} **porphyrin** complex is **heme**. However, perhaps the most abundant octahedral shaped molecules in nature are the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/#Fig5SPhy" target="_blank" title="Go to Soil Ecology">alumina hydroxide</a></b> groups found in clay minerals.<b>[@Thair_Clays_2008; @bergaya_clays_2011]</b> The octahedral geometry of these inorganic metal hydroxides are held together by ionic bonds. The angles of separation between the central and peripheral atoms is 90&deg; for the equatorial positioned atoms (square base) and 180&deg; for the axial oriented atoms that occupy the &ldquo;<i>peaks</i>&rdquo; of the two imaginary four sided pyramids.  
**(vi) AX<sub>2</sub>E:** This is the first of a series of molecular geometries involving non-bonding valence shell electrons. One of the assumptions of the **VSEPR** model is that all bonding electron pairs (i.e. single, double, triple) are treated as simple single bonds. For example, sulphur dioxide ([[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}**<sub>2</sub>**) has two double bonded oxygen atoms as well as one **lone pair** of electrons surrounding the central sulphur atom. One may assume that the planar arrangement of the three electron **domains** (i.e. two bonding and one **lone pair**) results in a 120&deg; angle of separation between the two [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atoms. However the **lone pair** electron **domain** exerts a strong repulsive force on the two neighbouring [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atoms resulting in an angle of separation of <u>less than</u> 120&deg; (i.e. slightly bent boomerang-like shape).<br>
**(vii) AX<sub>3</sub>E:** This is the second molecular geometry involving non-bonding [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}. The presence of the four **electron domains** suggests a tetrahedral type of arrangement for the peripheral atoms. However the presence of slightly more repulsive **lone pair** results in a trigonal pyramidal arrangement for the bonded atoms. A good example of this molecular geometry is ammonia ([[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}**<sub>3</sub>**). Again the **lone pair** exerts a strong repulsive **electrostatic** force on the neighbouring bonding **electron domains**. The overall trigonal pyramidal shape of [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}**<sub>3</sub>** has the central [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} atom occupying the peak of an imaginary pyramid, while the three [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms occupy the vertices of the pyramid's triangular base. The repulsive **electrostatic** forces of the **lone pair** of electrons reduces the bond angles separating the three [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms to ~107&deg; instead of 109.5&deg;.
<br>
**(viii) AX<sub>2</sub>E<sub>2</sub>:** The four **electron domains** are arranged in a tetrahedral-like fashion around the central atom. The water molecule ([[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}**<sub>2</sub>**[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}) is the simple example of this type of molecular geometry. The central [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} atom has two single bonded [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms that are separated from each other by an angle of 104.5&deg;. This reduced bond angle is due to the strong repulsive **electrostatic** forces exerted by two **lone pairs**. As a consequence the shape of a water molecule is noticeably asymmetric, which results in a net dipole moment (i.e. polar molecule).
<br>
&nbsp; &nbsp; Overall **VSEPR** provides a relatively simple and effective way to model non-metallic molecular geometries that have one central atom. However, most biomolecules have multiple bonding &ldquo;<i>centres</i>&rdquo;. This introduces problems since the theory itself can not solve such complex multi-body systems. Nevertheless [VSEPR]{#Blk} can serve as a guide even though it is limited to one central atom at a time. Certainly larger structural patterns do emerge when computational tools are used to model molecules (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://jp-minerals.org/vesta/en/" target="_blank" title="Go to VESTA">VESTA</a></b>), such as the extended polygon-like geometries of <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/prairie_soil_ecosystem/#Fig5SPhy" target="_blank" title="Go to OPC Soil Ecology">clay minerals</a></b>.  


<a id="VBT"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.2 VALENCE BOND THEORY (VBT)** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** [VBT]{#Blk}, unlike [VSEPR]{#Blk}, assumes that **valence electrons** ([[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) occupy different types of atomic orbitals ([AO]{#Blk}) with different bonding properties (e.g. energies, lengths). It addresses these issues by introducing new concepts, specifically <u>resonance energy</u> and <u>hybridization</u> of [AO]{#Blk} to explain chemical bonding behaviour in a very localized and intuitive manner.<b>[@heitler_wechselwirkung_1927; @pauling_nature_1931-1; @slater_directed_1931; @pauling_nature_1960]</b> For example based on the electronic configuration of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} ([[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}] **2&sscr;<sup>2</sup>2**[&pscr;]{#Blue}**<sup>2</sup>**) we know that it can form a maximum of four covalent bonds (i.e. **tetravalent**). These four [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} are clearly assigned to two different types of atomic orbitals (i.e. [&sscr;]{#Blk} and [&pscr;]{#Blue}) that vary in shape, length and orientation. Therefore one might suspect that a molecule like methane ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}**<sub>4</sub>**) must form different types of covalent bonds based on the different types of atomic orbitals. However experiments clearly show that all four covalent bonds in methane are essentially identical in bond length, strength and separation angle. As a result [VBT]{#Blk} proposes that four identical hybrid orbitals, called [sp3]{#SBlue} orbitals, are generated via the fusion of one [&sscr;]{#Blk} and three [&pscr;]{#Blue} type [AO]{#Blk}. As detailed below [VBT]{#Blk} also allows for fewer [AO]{#Blk} to undergo hybridization in order to explain multi-bond types (i.e. double and triple bonds).  

[I. Hybrid]{#Blk} [sp3]{#SBlue} [Orbitals:]{#Blk} Given that all life is largely based on carbon chemistry it should therefore come as no surprise that virtually all large organic molecules are built using [sp3]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals. Methane ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>), being the simplest of all organic molecules, is a good example of this type of hybridization. The normal [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} configuration of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} ([[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}] **2&sscr;<sup>2</sup>2**[&pscr;]{#Blue}**<sup>2</sup>**) is:

According to the [VB]{#Blk} theory the energy required to cause orbital hybridization is more than compensated for by the energy released when [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}**-**[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} bonds are formed (Recall: bond formation is an exothermic process, **Eqn. 18**). Since the four [sp3]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals have identical bond strength and bond separation angles (i.e. 109.5&deg;) the resulting molecular geometry has each covalent bond directed toward the corners of an imaginary regular <u>tetrahedron</u>. The same [sp3]{#SBlue} geometry is also found in many inorganic molecules like ammonia ([[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>3</sub>) and water ([[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>[[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}). Both of these molecules have lone pairs of electrons occupying the hybrid orbital system. Their presence generates additional repulsive electrostatic forces that distort covalent bond angles. Specifically the normal 109.5&deg; bond angles seen in methane are reduced to 107.3&deg; and 104.5&deg; for ammonia and water respectively. The electronic configuration of native [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} ([[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}]**2&sscr;<sup>2</sup>2**[&pscr;]{#Blue}**<sup>3</sup>**) and [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB} ([[[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}]**2&sscr;<sup>2</sup>**[&pscr;]{#Blue}**<sup>4</sup>**) and their respective hybrid orbitals used to bond with [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} are shown below.

[II. Hybrid]{#Blk} [sp2]{#SBlue} [Orbitals:]{#Blk} Unsaturated organic molecules that have a planar geometry (e.g. benzene) are built using [sp2]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals. Ethylene ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>) is the simplest example of this type of molecule. Although carbon has four valence electrons not all of them (under this scenario) take part in the hybridization process. As shown below the [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals combine with the [2&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital while the [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital remains unchanged during the hybridization process. For each carbon two of the three [sp2]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals form bonds with the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbitals of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms, while the remaining [sp2]{#SBlue} hybrid orbital of each [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atom overlap with one another to form an additional covalent bond. The four [sp2]{#SBlue}-[&sscr;]{#Blue} and lone [sp2]{#SBlue}-[sp2]{#SBlue} covalent bonds are generated by end-to-end orbital overlap directly between the atoms, which is termed a [sigma bond]{#Blk} (i.e. $\large \sigma$). The remaining [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital of each carbon atom also combine with one another, in a sideways manner, to form a new type of chemical bond known as a $\large \pi$ bond. The electron density that defines this type of covalent bond is concentrated above and below the imaginary plane of the $\large \sigma$-bonding framework. So the resulting orbital overlap is, as mentioned above, accommodated in a <u>sideways</u> fashion. The overall configuration of the $\large \sigma$ and $\large \pi$ bonds is somewhat analogous to a &ldquo;<i>hotdog-and-bun</i>&rdquo;, with the $\sigma$ bond serving as the &ldquo;<i>hotdog</i>&rdquo; and the $\large \pi$ bond acting as the &ldquo;<i>bun</i>&rdquo; (refer to: **Fig. 21**).

[III. Hybrid]{#Blk} [sp]{#SBlue} [Orbitals]{#Blk}: Linear molecules that contain carbon-carbon triple bonds have [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals. Acetylene ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>) is the simplest organic molecule that has this type of hybrid bonding orbital. As shown below the [2&sscr;]{#Blk} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals of carbon undergo hybridization, while its [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals remain unhybridized. The two [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals form two different types of $\large \sigma$ bonds, one overlapping end-to-end with a neighbouring [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbitals of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}, and the other overlapping end-to-end with with the [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbital of the adjacent carbon atom. The remaining [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals of each carbon overlap with one another, respectively, to form two $\large \pi$ bonds. The two [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals lie on opposite sides of each carbon atom resulting in a bond angle of 180&deg;.

[IV. Hybrid]{#Blk} [sp3d]{#SBlue} [and]{#Blk} [sp3d2]{#SBlue} [Orbitals]{#Blk}: Most elements associated with organic molecules are found within the first three periods of the [[PT]{#Dred}]{#strokeB} (**Fig. 1**). These common elements generally follow the **octet rule**. However, some of the heavier elements (i.e. 3<sup>rd</sup> period and beyond) can make use of [&dscr;]{#Turq} type orbitals during the hybridization process. One example of this is **phosphorus penta-chloride** ([[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}**<sub>5</sub>**). The electron configuration of [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} (i.e. <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;<sup>2</sup></b><b>3[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>3</sup></b>) has <u>five</u> [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}, as would be expected of a **Group V** element of the [[PT]{#Dred}]{#strokeB} (**Fig. 1**). The **Lewis** structure of [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}**<sub>5</sub>** shows five covalent bonds (i.e. 10 electron pairs). Clearly the lone <b>3&sscr;</b> and three <b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals are not enough to account for such a molecular structure (i.e. **AX<sub>5</sub>** trigonal bi-pyramid). The only other available orbitals within the 3<sup>rd</sup> energy level are [&dscr;]{#Turq} type orbitals. The fact that the <b>3</b>[&dscr;]{#Turq} orbitals are relatively close in energy to the <b>3&sscr;</b> and <b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals allows for the promotion of one <b>3&sscr;</b> electron to a <b>3</b>[&dscr;]{#Turq} orbitals. Here the **octet rule** fails us since there are five bonding electron pairs. As shown below the [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB} atom is [sp3d]{#SBlue} hybridized in [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}**<sub>5</sub>**.

[[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}[[F]{#Mag}]{#strokeB}**<sub>6</sub>** is another example of a hybridization scheme involving [&dscr;]{#Turq} type orbitals. [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}, unlike [[P]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}, is a member of the **Group VI** family of elements (**Fig. 1**). Its electron configuration (i.e. <b>[</b>[[Ne]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB}<b>]</b><b>3&sscr;<sup>2</sup></b><b>3[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sup>4</sup></b>) has <u>six</u> [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}. The **Lewis** structure of [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}[[F]{#Mag}]{#strokeB}**<sub>6</sub>** (i.e. **AX<sub>6</sub>** octahedral) shows six covalent bonds (i.e. 12 electron pairs), which also violates the **octet rule**. This unique electron configuration can not be accounted for by combining only <b>3&sscr;</b> and <b>3</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals. Here, like in the previous example, <b>3</b>[&dscr;]{#Turq} type orbitals are employed. However, unlike the previous example, more than one <b>3</b>[&dscr;]{#Turq} type orbital is used in the hybridization process. As shown below the [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB} atom is [sp3d2]{#SBlue} hybridized in the [[S]{#Gold}]{#strokeB}[[F]{#Mag}]{#strokeB}**<sub>6</sub>** molecule.

<a id="VBThyb"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.2.1 VBT & HYBRIDIZATION** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** **Walter Heitler** and **Fritz London** (1927), along with **Linus Pauling** (1931) and **John Slater** (1931) pioneered the use of quantum mechanics to model covalent bonds.<b>[@heitler_wechselwirkung_1927; @pauling_nature_1931-1; @slater_directed_1931]</b> For **Pauling** (1931) the identical covalent bonds of carbon is due to <u>resonance hybridization</u> of the four atomic orbitals ([AO]{#Blk}). Even though the [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} of carbon are found in different sub-shells (i.e. [&sscr;]{#Blk} and [&pscr;]{#Blue}) they have to be assimilated somehow to account for the experimental evidence. **Heitler** and **London** (1927) provided the first important quantum model of valence bonds based on the assumption that covalent bonds are the product of electron orbital <u>overlap</u>. Since an electron orbital is defined by its <u>wave function</u> it therefore follows that the strength of a bond is dependent on the degree of <u>overlap</u> between atomic wave functions (i.e. constructive interference).<b>[@pauling_nature_1931-1]</b>  
&nbsp; &nbsp; According to **Pauling** hybrid orbitals provide atoms with greater &ldquo;<i>reach</i>&rdquo;, which helps facilitate orbital overlap. Greater orbital overlap means more energy exchange between atoms, which increases the strength and stability of the chemical bond.<b>[@pauling_nature_1931-1; @pauling_nature_1960]</b> **Pauling** used this hybridization concept to describe the simultaneous covalent and ionic character of chemical bonds.  

> “<i>With the aid of the quantum mechanics there is formulated a set of rules regarding electron-pair bonds, dealing particularly with the strength of bonds in relation to the nature of the single-electron <u>eigenfunctions</u> involved. It is shown that one single-electron eigenfuntion on each of two atoms determines essentially the nature of the electron-pair bond formed between them; this effect is accentuated by the phenomenon of concentration of the bond eigenfunctions....From <b>s</b> and <b>p</b> eigenfunctions the best bond eigenfunctions which can be made are four equivalent tetrahedral eigenfunction, giving bonds directed toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron.</i>.”<b>[@pauling_nature_1931-1]</b>


Wave functions that describe stable chemical structures involve statistical calculations of possible quantum states (e.g. $\psi_{\text o} = a \phantom{.}\psi_1 + b \phantom{.} \psi_2$). The <u>ratio</u> of the <u>numerical</u> scalar factors (i.e. coefficients) associated with each wave function (e.g. [a/b]{#Blk}) can provide information about the contribution of each quantum state to the overall chemical structure.<b>[@pauling_nature_1931-1; @pauling_nature_1960]</b> For example, if the scalar <u>ratio</u> [a/b]{#Blk} is large then $\psi_1$ will contribute significantly to the overall structure. Conversely if [a/b]{#Blk} is very small then $\psi_2$ will make the most significant contribution to the molecular structure. However, if the value of [a/b]{#Blk} is close to unity then both quantum states described by $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$ contribute equally to the chemical structure. In the latter scenario the &ldquo;true&rdquo; chemical structure is said to be a <u>resonance hybrid</u> of these two quantum states.<b>[@pauling_nature_1931-1; @pauling_nature_1960]</b> This quantum behaviour can be modelled mathematically by defining the wave function of the system as:  


$$\tag{19}
\\
\large \psi_{_\text{o}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.}  a \, \large \psi_{_\text{I}} \normalsize \; + \; b \, \large \psi_{_\text{II}} \normalsize \; + \; c \, \large \psi_{_\text{III}} \normalsize \phantom{..} ..... \, c_n \large \psi_n$$


**Werner Heisenberg** (1926) was the first to suggest that a chemical element <b>resonates</b> between different quantum states.<b>[@heisenberg_uber_1926]</b> His use of a virtual <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#SHOmodel" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">harmonic oscillator</a></b> to approximate an <b>anharmonic</b> system (i.e. deviates from a simple harmonic oscillator) is an important concept in quantum mechanics. For example the [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> molecule is made up of 2 protons and 2 electrons. For convenience we can arbitrarily label the individual atoms **A** and **B**, and the individual electrons **a** and **b**. If the distance separating the two nuclei is relatively large then there is a slight attraction between the two neutral atoms (repulsive energy is negligible). However, when the inter-nuclear distance is small the repulsive **electrostatic** energy becomes dominant. Neither of these scenarios are favourable bonding states. However if we consider all <u>possible</u> quantum states then atom **A** could be coupled to electron **b**, while atom **B** could be coupled to electron **a**. Other possible configurations would include both electrons coupled to a single atom (i.e. structure 3 and 4). These different quantum states can be represented as follows:


$$\tag{20}$$


$$\begin{align*}
\large \text{Quantum State I:} \normalsize &
\phantom{...} \text{structure 1} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} H^+_A \cdot e^-_a \phantom{.......} H^+_B \cdot e^-_b
\\[5px]
\large \text{Quantum State II:} \normalsize &
\phantom{...} \text{structure 2} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} H^+_A \cdot e^-_b \phantom{.......} H^+_B \cdot e^-_a
\\[5px]
\large \text{Quantum State III:} \normalsize &
\phantom{...} \text{structure 3} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} H^+_A \cdot e^-_a \cdot e^-_b \phantom{...} H^+_B
\\[5px]
\large \text{Quantum State IV:} \normalsize &
\phantom{...} \text{structure 4} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} H^+_A \phantom{...........} H^+_B \cdot e^-_a \cdot e^-_b
\end{align*}$$


The contribution of each quantum state to the overall structure is directly related to their energy states (i.e. stability of each quantum state). If the electrostatic interactions are favourable such that they overcome the repulsive proton-proton forces then an energy minimum emerges that represents a <u>bound state</u> (i.e. stable chemical bond). This stable state is characterized by an optimal separation distance between the two bonding hydrogen atoms. If the atoms move toward each other the repulsive **electrostatic** energy rises exponentially. Conversely if the two atoms move away from each other than the attractive **electrostatic** energy slowly increases. So we can view the covalent bond of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}**<sub>2</sub>** as being a hybrid **resonance** structure where the electrons <u>oscillates</u> between the two nuclei, which is somewhat analogous to a <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#SHOmodel" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">simple harmonic oscillator</a></b>. The resulting overlap between the hybrid orbitals (i.e. <u>constructive interference</u> operating) creates a stable chemical bond.  

<a id="VBTen"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.2.2 VBT & Electronegativity** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** The concept of **electronegativity** can be mathematically represented in the form of two **eigenfunctions**. One defines the chemical bond between identical atoms (i.e. homo-diatomic molecule) and the other the chemical bond between two different atoms (i.e. hetero-diatomic molecule). The differences in these two chemical bonds can be largely attributed to their varying **electro-negative** character. For convenience we can arbitrarily designate our two diatomic molecules as **A–A** and **A–B**. Mathematically this can be represented as:


$$\tag{21}$$


$$\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
\text{Homo-diatomic} \phantom{.} & \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(\text{AA})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large a \, \psi_{(\text A -\text A)} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \large b \, \psi_{(\text A^+ - \text A^-)} \normalsize \; + \; \large b \, \psi_{(\text A^{-} - \text A^+ )}
\\[5px]
\text{Hetero-diatomic} \phantom{.} & \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(\text{AB})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large c \, \psi_{(\text A - \text B)} \normalsize \; + \; \large d \, \psi_{(\text A^+ - \text B^-)} \normalsize \; + \; \large e \, \psi_{(\text A^{-} - \text B^+)}
\end{align*}$$


The **eigenvalue** ratio **b/a**, which determines the contribution of the ionic structure(s), is very small for a purely covalent bonded homo-diatomic molecule **A–A**. However **A–B** has two different atoms with potentially very different **electro-negative** values. Here the <b>eigenvalue</b> ratio **d/c** and **e/c** will be very different when compared to **b/a**. The contribution made by ionic <b>resonance energy</b> (e.g. $\psi_{\text A^+ - \text B^-}$) combined with the energy of the normal covalent bonded state ($\psi_{\text A - \text B}$) is likely intermediate in value between **A–A** and **B–B**. According to this scenario the <u>arithmetic</u> mean of the $Energy \, (\text A - \text A)$ and $Energy \, (\text B - \text B)$ should approximate the normal covalent bond $Energy \, (\text A - \text B)$.<b>[@pauling_additivity_1932; @pauling_nature_1960]</b> As a consequence **Pauling** devised an <i><u>additivity</u></i> concept where the actual bond energy of $Energy \, (\text A - \text B)$ would always be greater than or equal to the <u>arithmetic</u> mean of the corresponding symmetrical bond energies.


$$\tag{22}$$

$$\\
\large \Delta \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} Energy \, (\text A - \text B) \; - \; \frac{1}{2} \Big( Energy \, (\text A - \text A) \; + \; Energy \, (\text B - \text B) \Big)
\\[5px]
\large Ionic \; Resonance \; Energy \; \normalsize (\text A - \text B) \normalsize \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta \, \ge \, 0
\\$$


However **Pauling** noted that not all molecules obey the <u>additivity</u> rule.<b>[@pauling_nature_1960]</b> For example **alkali metals** form not only common salts, but also **hydrides** and homo-diatomic molecules (e.g. [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}**–**[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}, [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}**–**[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}, [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}**–**[[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}). The covalent bonds holding together the homo-diatomic **alkali metals** are very weak, and the **metal hydrides** have ionic character (e.g. [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}**–**[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}). Since the [&Delta;]{#Blk20} values for some of these metal hydrides are negative an alternative <u>geometric mean</u> postulate was devised where the <u>geometric mean</u> (i.e. square root of the product) is used instead of the <u>arithmetic mean</u> for the [ionic resonance energy]{#Blk} calculations.  


$$\tag{23}$$

$$\\
\large \Delta' \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} Energy (\text{A} - \text{B}) \; - \; \sqrt{\Big[ \, Energy(\text{A} - \text{A}) \; \Big] \Big[ \; Energy(\text{B} - \text{B}) \, \Big]}
\\[5px]
\large Ionic \; Resonance \; Energy \; \normalsize \text{(A} - \text{B)} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \Delta' \normalsize \, \ge \, 0
\\$$

So according to the *<u>geometric mean</u>* rule the [ionic resonance energy]{#Blk} of an asymmetrical covalent bond, like the one found in [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB}**–**[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}, can be defined by [&Delta;&prime;]{#Blk20}. In fact **Pauling** stated that [&Delta;&prime;]{#Blk20} is likely a more satisfactory measure of covalent bond energy between different atoms. He also refined his calculations of <b>electronegativity</b> ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}) by taking the square root value of [&Delta;&prime;]{#Blk20} expressed in units of 30 kcal/mole (Note: previously used 1 eV units = 23 kcal/mol).  


$$\tag{24}$$
$$\\
\big| \large \chi_{_A} \normalsize \; - \; \large \chi_{_B} \normalsize \big| \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \sqrt{\frac{\Delta'}{30}}
\\[10px]
\large \Delta' \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large 30 \normalsize \cdot \big| \large \chi_{_A} \normalsize \; - \; \large \chi_{_B} \normalsize \big|^{2}
\\$$


By combining the two equations above the covalent bond energy between two different atoms [Energy(A-B)]{#Blk} can be now be represented as the <u>difference</u> in the [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB} values of two atoms (**Eqn. 25**). Because the new formula is based on <u>differences</u> in [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB} values that means if you assign a reference value to a particular element (i.e. standard) then individual [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB} values for all the other chemical elements can be calculated. Based on this logic **Pauling** assigned [[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}**luorine**, the most **electro-negative** element within the Periodic Table, a [[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}<sub>[[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB}</sub> value of 4.<b>[@pauling_nature_1960]</b>  


$$\tag{25}$$


$$\\
\\[15px]
\large \Delta' \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} Energy \, (\text{A} - \text{B}) \; - \; \sqrt{ \Big[ \, Energy(\text{A} - \text{A}) \, \Big] \Big[ \, Energy(\text{B} - \text{B}) \, \Big] } \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 30 \cdot \big| \chi_{_A} \; - \; \chi_{_B} \big|^{2}
\\[10px]
Energy (\text{A} - \text{B}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{ \, \Big[ Energy(\text{A} - \text{A}) \, \Big] \Big[ \; Energy(\text{B} - \text{B}) \, \Big]} \; + \; 30 \normalsize \cdot \big| \chi_{_A} \; - \; \chi_{_B} \big|^{2}
\\$$


<a id="VBTsp"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.2.3 VBT - <span id="Blk26">&sigma;</span> & <span id="Blk26">&pi;</span> Bonds** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** As discussed above orbital overlap is a measure of the amount of shared electron density between atoms that determines the strength of a covalent bond. Although the radial distance of an orbital is central to this concept, so too is the <u>direction</u> in which the bonding orbital is concentrated. This spatial information is described by the molecule's <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#SHfunc" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">Spherical harmonic</a></b> function ([Y<sub>&lscr;,m<sub>&lscr;</sub></sub>(&theta;, &straightphi;)]{#Blk}). For example an electron in a [&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital has an equal probability of being found at any point along its radially defined surface. However electrons occupying [&pscr;]{#Blue} type orbitals are more highly concentrated along one of three **Cartesian** axes (i.e. [&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue}, [&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue}, [&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}). This spatial bias affects the extent of orbital overlap between two atoms. In fact because the radial part of [&sscr;]{#Blk} and [&pscr;]{#Blue} type orbitals are so similar any differences in their bond strength can be largely attributed to the directional characteristics of the hybrid orbitals (e.g. [sp3]{#SBlue} hybrid orbital = 25% [&sscr;]{#Blk}+ 75% [&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital). Differences in their spatial geometry results in different bond energies: (i) [&sscr;]{#Blk}-[&pscr;]{#Blue} based bonds are ~1.73 times greater than a [&sscr;]{#Blk}-[&sscr;]{#Blk} based bond; (ii) [&pscr;]{#Blue}-[&pscr;]{#Blue} bond energy is ~3 times greater than that of [&sscr;]{#Blk}-[&sscr;]{#Blk} based bonds. Clearly the relative bond strength is enhanced by the hybridization process since the electron density of hybrid orbitals are often concentrated within the inter-nuclear bonding region (e.g. 75% [&pscr;]{#Blue} type character of [sp3]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals means more electron density within the inter-nuclear region where $\large \sigma$-bonding takes place).
