<a id="MOT"></a>
[&thinsp; **4.3 MOLECULAR ORBITAL THEORY (MOT)** &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}**:** [MOT]{#Blk} was pioneered by many important scientists, including (among others) **Fredrich Hund** (1926),<b>[@hund_zur_1926; @hund_linienspektren_1927; @hund_zur_1928]</b>, **Robert S. Mulliken** (1926),<b>[@mulliken_electronic_1926; @mulliken_electronic_1927; @mulliken_assignment_1928; @mulliken_electronic_1932]</b> and **J.E. Leonnard-Jones** (1929).<b>[@lennard-jones_electronic_1929; @lennard-jones_molecular_1949]</b> [MOT]{#Blk} uses wave functions to describe electrons in relation to the entire molecule (i.e. electronic structure and reactivity). Unlike [VBT]{#Blk} it does not restrict valence electrons ([[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) to the inter-nuclear space between atoms, as typified by **Lewis** structures, but rather takes into account the delocalized nature of electrons. This key feature of [MOT]{#Blk} was previously touched upon when describing biomolecules with conjugated double bond systems like <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Phenolics" target="_blank" title="Go to Plant Natural Products">phenolics</a></b>. The most powerful explanatory tool of [MOT]{#Blk} is perhaps [MO]{#Blk} diagrams, which shows [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} being placed within <u>pro-bonding</u> and <u>anti-bonding</u> [MO]{#Blk} in accordance with **Bohr's** *Aufbau Principle*. [MO]{#Blk} are the result of the linear combination of atomic orbitals ([LCAO]{#Blk}). For example, the [MO]{#Blk} diagram of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> (**Fig. 13**), a relatively simple homo-nuclear diatomic molecule, shows two [1&sscr;]{#Blk} atomic orbitals ([AO]{#Blk}) giving rise to two [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. <u>bonding</u> and <u>anti-bonding</u>). The bonding [MO]{#Blk} is the product of <u>constructive interference</u> (i.e. wave functions are in-phase), while the <u>anti-bonding</u> [MO]{#Blk} is a product of <u>destructive interference</u> (i.e. wave functions are out-of-phase). A simple mathematically representation of [MO]{#Blk} are shown below.  


$$\tag{26}
\\
\large \text{Molecular Orbital} \normalsize \phantom{.} \Rightarrow \phantom{.} \psi_{\pm} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \text s_{\text A} \; \pm \; 1 \text s_{\text B}
\\[10px]
\large \text{Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals} \; \text{(LCAO)}
\\[10 px]
\overbrace{\large \psi_{+} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{c}_1 \Big( \text{1s}_{\text A} \; + \; \text{1s}_{\text B} \Big)}^{Bonding} \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} \overbrace{\large \psi_{-} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{c}_2 \Big( \text{1s}_{\text A} \; - \; \text{1s}_{\text B} \Big)}^{Anti-Bonding}$$


Constructive interference of the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} wave functions (i.e. in-phase) produces a $\large \sigma$ (&ldquo;sigma&rdquo;) bond, while destructive interference of the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} wave functions (i.e. out-of-phase) produces a $\large \sigma^*$ (&ldquo;sigma star&rdquo;) anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} (<b>Fig. 13</b>). The <u>electron density distribution</u> of these two types of [MO]{#Blk} are symmetrically arranged along a line connecting the two nuclei. Specifically the $\large \sigma$ bonding orbital is concentrated between the two atoms, while the $\large \sigma^*$ anti-bonding orbital forms a <u>node</u> (i.e. electron density is zero) in the same inter-nuclear region. An <u>exact</u> mathematically solution of the <u>electron density distribution</u> of a [MO]{#Blk} is possible, but only for the simplest quantum systems (i.e. [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b><sup>+</sup>). Nevertheless [MOT]{#Blk} can explain some properties of molecules that [VBT]{#Blk} can not, such as the para-magnetism of molecular oxygen. As mentioned previously in <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#MaxBorn" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">ChemPrimer2</a></b> <b>Max Born</b> (1926) provided a statistical interpretation of <b>Schrodinger's</b> (1926) wave equation that calculates the probability of observing a particular experimental outcome. Specifically <b>Born</b> produced an <u>expectation value</u> using the absolute value of the square of the magnitude of the underlying wave function. This value is proportional to the <b>probability density</b> of finding a particle within a given region of space.<b>[@born_zur_1926-1; @born_zur_1926; @pais_max_1982]</b> Such a relationship can be expressed mathematically as:  


$$\tag{27}$$


$$\\
\text{Probability (P):} \phantom{..} \text{P}(x \in [a, b]) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} pdf \cdot dx
\\
\Big( \text{Probability Density function:} \; pdf, \phantom{.} \text{Complex Conjugate wave function:} \; \large \psi^*_{\normalsize \text{(x,t)}} \normalsize \Big)
\\[5px]
pdf \cdot dx \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int^b_a \Big| \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{(x,t)}} \normalsize \Big|^2 \, dx \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \large \psi^*_{\normalsize \text{(x,t)}} \normalsize \, \large \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\normalsize \text{(x,t)}} \normalsize \, dx \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
x \in [a, b] \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} x \; \text{is an element of a region defined by} \; a \; \text{and} \; b$$


As shown above (**Eqn. 27**) the probability of finding the electron in a given region of space ($dx$) is calculated by taking the definite integral of $\big|\psi_{\text{(x,t)}} \big|^2$. This squared quantity (i.e. product of the wave function and its complex conjugate) produces a <b>probability density function</b>. When this function is integrated over <u>all possible space</u> the solution is 1 (i.e. 100% probability of finding the electron somewhere). When these functions are <u>normalized</u> the magnitude of the coefficients (<b>Eqn. 28</b>) provide a measure of the <u>contribution</u> that each [AO]{#Blk} makes to the [MO]{#Blk}. For homo-nuclear molecules (e.g. [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>) the magnitude of the coefficients are the same. However, in hetero-nuclear molecules (e.g. [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}[[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB}) the magnitude and/or sign of the coefficient of each wave function are different since the [AO]{#Blk} they describe are not the same.  


$$\tag{28}
\\
\large \text{Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals} \; \text{(LCAO):}
\\[10px]
\overbrace{\large \psi_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text a_1 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_1 \, \text{2p}_z}^{Bonding} \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} \overbrace{\large \psi_2 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text a_1 \, \text{2s} \; - \; \text b_1 \, \text{2p}_z}^{Anti-Bonding}$$


If we take the square of $\psi_1$ and expand it we get the following expression:  


$$\tag{29}
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 1}^2 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \big( \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \, \text{2p}_z \big)^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \big(\text{a}_1 \, \text{2s} \big)^2 \; + \; \big( \text{b}_1 \, \text{2p}_z \big)^2 \; + \; 2 \text{a}_1 \text{b}_1 \big( \text{2s} \, \text{2p}_z \big)$$


This combination of atomic orbitals (**Eqn. 29**) produces an additional term:


$$\tag{29.1}
\\
2 \text{a}_1 \text{b}_1 \big( \text{2s} \phantom{.} \text{2p}_z \big)$$


If both coefficients are positive then this term will increase the **electron density** within the inter-nuclear region (i.e. <u>constructive</u> interference). However, if $\text{b}_1$ is negative due to the phase of the <b>2</b>[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital, then this term becomes <u>negative</u> resulting in the loss of **electron density** between the two nuclei (i.e. <u>destructive</u> interference). When destructive interference is optimal a **node** will appear between the two nuclei (i.e. zero electron density). As a consequence the Coulombic repulsion exerted by the two positively charged nuclei will increase since there are no inter-nuclear electrons to stabilize their bonding positions. Ultimately this unstable state will push the two atoms apart (i.e. anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk}).  


<a id="Fig13"></a>
<!---------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------ FIG 13 - MOT H2 Energy Diagram  ------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------------->
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/H2_MO_diagram.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 13</u>: MO Diagram of <span id="strokeB"><span id="Blue">H</span></span><sub>2</sub>.</b> The energy diagram (left side) for the di-hydrogen molecule (<span id="strokeB"><span id="Blue">H</span></span><b><sub>2</sub></b>) shows the <b>m</b>olecular <b>o</b>rbitals ([MO]{#Blk}) in the middle and the <b>a</b>tomic <b>o</b>rbitals ([1&sscr;]{#Blk} [AO]{#Blk}) on either side. In accordance with the <b><i>Aufbau</i> principle</b> electrons are placed in the lowest energy [MO]{#Blk}, which constitutes a sigma ($\large \sigma$) bonding orbital. Since the bonding [MO]{#Blk} is <u>lower</u> in energy than each of the two [AO]{#Blk} of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} it therefore follows that the molecule is more <u>stable</u> than two separate [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms. The <b>B</b>ond <b>O</b>rder (<b>BO</b> = [# bonding electrons - # anti-bonding electrons]/2 = (2-0)/2 = 1) of the molecule is equal to <u>one</u> (i.e. single bond). The spherical electron density diagrams on the right correspond to the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} energy level (Note: spherical shape of the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital has a single uniform phase since there are no <u>internal</u> <b>radial nodes</b>, a characteristic not shared by [2&sscr;]{#Blk} or higher orbitals. However it can be arbitrarily assigned a positive or negative value to identify overall <u>phase</u> differences). The sign of the <u>wave function</u> ($\large \psi_{1 \text s}$) results in either the addition or subtraction of electron density within the inter-nuclear region. When the coefficients of two orbital wave functions have the same sign (i.e. overall positive value) the electrons density between the two atoms increases (shaded area), which attracts the two positively charged nuclei resulting in a more stable <u>energy</u> state. The positions of the bonded hydrogen nuclei is reminiscent of an <u>ellipse</u> (Note: <b>envelop</b> outline) with the two nuclei forming the two <u>foci</u>. Conversely electrons within an anti-bonding <b>MO</b> are pushed outward, which pulls the nuclei apart resulting in a region of zero electron density between the nuclei called a <b>node</b>. A change in the sign of an orbital wave function is represented by differences in <u>shading</u>. Should the atoms move closer together the repulsive electrostatic forces produced by the positively charged nuclei would increase resulting in an unstable state. The <b>MO</b> created by <b>LCAO</b> includes a <u>bonding</u> <b>MO</b> ($\large \sigma$) and an <u>anti-bonding</u> <b>MO</b> ($\large \sigma^{\normalsize *}$). Experiments have shown that it takes ~436 kJ (25 <sup>o</sup>C) to break apart one mole of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> (<b>Note:</b> see <b><a class="one" href="https://cccbdb.nist.gov/ea2x.asp" target="_blank" title="Go to NIST">NIST</a></b> for standardized experimental energies of molecules).  

</div>
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


Other diatomic molecules, like oxygen ([[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub>2 (<i>g</i>)</sub>) and nitrogen ([[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<sub>2 (<i>g</i>)</sub>), have [MO]{#Blk} diagrams that reveal specific [b]{#Blk}ond [o]{#Blk}rders ([BO]{#Blk}) and [b]{#Blk}ond [e]{#Red}nergies ([B]{#Blk}[E]{#Red}). However the energy levels of the [MO]{#Blk} vary slightly as you move across the 2<sup>nd</sup> row or period of the [[PT]{#Dred}]{#strokeB}. Notably the order of the energy levels is different for [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and [[F]{#Violet}]{#strokeB} when compared to the lighter elements of this period (i.e. [[Li]{#Silver}]{#strokeB} through [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}). As illustrated below (**Fig. 14**) there is a noticeable change in the order of the $\large \sigma$ and $\large \pi$ bonding orbitals for the 2[&pscr;]{#Blue} atomic orbitals. Moreover these [MO]{#Blk} energy diagrams help to explain why these two diatomic molecules respond differently to magnetic fields that [VBT]{#Blk} and <b>Lewis</b> structures fail to explain. Specifically the <u>unpaired</u> electrons within the anti-bonding $\large \sigma^*$ [MO]{#Blk} align with the magnetic field making [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> <b>paramagnetic</b> (i.e. weakly attracted to the magnetic field). In the case of [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> all of its [MO]{#Blk} have electron pairs with opposite spin, which results in no net magnetic moment. This makes [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> <b>diamagnetic</b> (i.e. weakly repelled by magnetic fields). The distinctive paramagnetic property of [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> is not explained by its <b>Lewis</b> structure, which actually shows two lone pairs of electrons (<b>Fig. 14</b>).  


<a id="Fig14"></a>
<!--------------------------------------------------->
<!--- FIG 14 - MOT homonuclear Diatomic Molecules --->
<!--------------------------------------------------->
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/MO_diagram_2nd_row_PT.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 14</u>: MO Energy Diagrams of Homo-nuclear Diatomic Molecules.</b> Covalent bonds (i.e. single, double or triple) are identified by their [B]{#Blk}onding [O]{#Blk}rder ([BO]{#Blk} = [# [B]{#Blk}onding electrons in [MO]{#Blk} - # non-[B]{#Blk}onding electrons in [MO]{#Blk}]/2). The relatively un-reactive nature of [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> gas (i.e. ~78% of the air we breath) is due to the relatively large amount of <u>energy</u> needed to break the triple bond holding the [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} atoms together (i.e. [B]{#Blk}[E]{#Red} ~ 945 kJ/mole). The [B]{#Blk}[E]{#Red} and <u>bond length</u> changes as the [BO]{#Blk} increases (i.e. more electrons shared between two atoms). Unlike [VBT]{#Blk} or <b>Lewis</b> bonding models, [MOT]{#Blk} predicts the presence of two <u>unpaired</u> electrons in molecular oxygen, which in turn explains why [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> is attracted by a magnetic field (i.e. <b>paramagnetic</b>). This unique property of [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> represents an important energy barrier (i.e. &ldquo;spin&rdquo; barrier). For example, when [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> reacts with a typical <b>diamagnetic</b> molecule (i.e. [MO]{#Blk} contain paired electrons), it has to change the spin state of one of its unpaired electrons. This activation step requires a considerable amount of energy, which forces oxygen to react <u>very slowly</u> (i.e. slow oxidizer). This is a &ldquo;blessing&rdquo; for all organic life forms since without this &ldquo;spin&rdquo; barrier oxygen would be highly reactive and therefore very poisonous to all life. In fact life as we know it would have likely not evolved, since an uninhibited oxygen would rapidly oxidize (i.e. &ldquo;burn&rdquo;) organic matter. In fact normal aerobic cellular metabolism does create toxic reactive intermediates of reduced oxygen, such as superoxide radical (<sup>&bull;</sup>[[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<sup>-</sup><b><sub>2</sub></b>) and hydroxyl radical (<sup>&bull;</sup>[[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}). As discussed previously in the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Fig_Oxygen" target="_blank" title="Go to Plant Natural Products">PNP project</a></b> these reactive oxygen species are neutralized by a variety of cellular anti-oxidant defences (e.g. vitamin C and E, superoxide dismutases and catalases). Nevertheless cellular enzymes have evolved ways of carefully harnessing the reactive power of oxygen using appropriate metal catalysts (i.e. metal oxides are tightly bound complexes).  


</div>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


Drawing [MO]{#Blk} diagrams for more complex hetero-nuclear molecules, such as methane, is more challenging since the energy and symmetry of the [AO]{#Blk} are not always compatible (**Fig. 15**). 


<a id="Fig15"></a>
<!--------------------------------------------------->
<!--- FIG 15 - MOT homonuclear Diatomic Molecules --->
<!--------------------------------------------------->
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/MO_diagrams_HomoHetero.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 15</u>: MO Energy Diagram of Homo- and Hetero-nuclear Molecules.</b> The strength of the interaction or &ldquo;mixing&rdquo; of atomic orbitals ([AO]{#Blk}), which determines the stability of the molecular orbital ([MO]{#Blk}), is measured by the stabilization (<b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>) and destabilization (<b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b>) energies of the <u>bonding</u> (e.g. <b>&sigma;<sub>s</sub></b>) or <u>anti-bonding</u> (e.g. <b>&sigma;<sub>s</sub></b>) [MO]{#Blk}, respectively. The greater the overlap or &ldquo;mixing&rdquo; of [AO]{#Blk} (i.e. overlap integral) the larger the <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b> and <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> values. For hetero-atomic molecules (**B**) the bonding [MO]{#Blk} is located closer to the lower energy [AO]{#Blk} (i.e. atom [[B]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}), while the anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} is closest to the higher energy [AO]{#Blk} (i.e. atom [[A]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}). Of course the electron density within the inter-nuclear region must be in phase (i.e. constructive interference) in order to allow for bonding to take place. Another important factor that determines whether the interaction between [AO]{#Blk} is successful or not is the size of the energy gap between the two [AO]{#Blk}. The smaller the energy gap the greater the interaction between [AO]{#Blk}. When the molecule has two spin-paired valence electrons occupying the lowest energy bonding orbitals (e.g. [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>) each electron will be stabilized by <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b> (i.e. total 2<b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>). Since there are no electrons within the anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> = 0) the two atoms will be more stable together as a molecule. However, if these two atoms have more than two valence electrons then the extra electrons will have to occupy the anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk}. The resulting de-stabilizing energy (i.e. <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> > 0) will cancel out the stabilizing energy if <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>-</sup></b> > <b>&Delta;</b>[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sup>+</sup></b>. This is the reason why [[He]{#Purple}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> atoms do not exist under normal conditions.  

</div>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


Changes in the energy levels of &ldquo;mixed&rdquo; orbitals can be difficult to plot for most poly-atomic molecules. Fortunately **Pauling's** <u>hybridization</u> concept is very useful in describing local bonding orbitals within small molecules including delocalized conjugated bonding systems. This &ldquo;mixing&rdquo; of [AO]{#Blk} (i.e. **LCAO** technique) to make hybrid orbitals is a convenient and flexible way of approximating [MO]{#Blk}. This technique is not only very useful at describing bonding concepts (e.g. bonding and anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk}) and molecular structure, but also provides a practical way of calculating the contribution of specific [AO]{#Blk} to the overall [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. normalization coefficients). For example most, if not all, organic molecules contain one or more so called [sp3]{#SBlue} atomic orbitals. These model hybrid orbitals of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} are made by "mixing" one part [2&sscr;]{#Blk} with three parts [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue}. The [sp3]{#SBlue} orbital often interacts with the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} to produce a $\large \sigma$ bonding and $\large \sigma^{\normalsize *}$ anti-bonding molecular orbital. The four $\large \sigma$ hybrid orbitals assume a tetrahedral like geometry, with each one &ldquo;pointing&rdquo; to a separate corner (i.e. vertex) of this regular polygon (**Fig. 19**). The following sections pictures [MO]{#Blk} from an [AO]{#Blk} hybridization point of view.

<!------------- Fig. 16 Vector Diagram --------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig16"></a>

<figure id="FRight400">
![](images/BeH2_sp_vector_diagram.jpg){width=360px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 16: Vector Diagram for [[sp]{#SBlue}]{#strikeB} hybrid orbitals</b>
</figcaption>
</figure>

<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>

<a id="LCAOsp"></a>

**[I. LCAO &]{#Blk} [sp]{#SBlue} [Orbitals]{#Blk}:** <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/139073" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">Beryllium hydride</a></b> ([[Be]{#EmGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>) is a good example of a hetero-nuclear poly-atomic molecule with [sp]{#SBlue} molecular orbitals. This alkaline earth metal hydride is unique because [[Be]{#EmGr}]{#strokeB} forms covalent bonds with hydrogen. Heavier **Group 2A** metals (**Fig. 1**) typically form ionic bonds with hydrogen (e.g. [[Ca]{#Almond}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>). The geometry of free [[Be]{#EmGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub> is linear ([VSEPR]{#Blk}: **AX<sub>2</sub>** group) with two [sp]{#SBlue} orbitals taking positions on opposite sides of the central metal atom (**Fig. 16**). The bonding orbitals of this compound can be represented by the following mathematical expression involving the linear combination of [2&sscr;]{#Blk} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} atomic orbitals.  

<br>

$$\tag{30}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_{\normalsize \text{BeH}_2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \overbrace{\text a_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{Be} \, (\text{2s})} \normalsize \; + \; \text b_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{Be} \, (\text{2p}_z)}}^{\text{LCAO}} \normalsize \; + \; \text c_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{H} \, (\text{1s})} \normalsize \; + \; \text c_2 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{H} \, (\text{1s})}
\\[5px]
& sp \phantom{.} \text{orbitals:} \; \left[
\begin{array}{l}
\large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{2p}_z
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 2 (\text{sp})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \text{2s} \normalsize \; + \; \text{b}_2 \text{2p}_z
\end{array}
\right.
\end{align*}$$


The value of the coefficients can be normalized for the two [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals in **Eqn. 30** given a few logical assumptions. Firstly, since the two hybrid orbitals are on opposite sides of the central [[Be]{#EmGr}]{#strokeB} atom and directed in opposite directions, it is safe to assume that they do not overlap with one another (i.e. **non-degenerate** states). This obviously makes sense since each one is an independent or distinct quantum state (i.e. separate sets of [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}). One important consequence of this is that non-overlapping orbitals can be mathematically evaluated in the following manner:  


$$\tag{31}$$


$$\\
\text{Orthogonal Conditions:} \phantom{..} \large \psi_1 \normalsize \, \ne \, \large \psi_2
\\
\text{(No orbital overlap)}
\\
\text{Note: formal use of spherical co-ordinates}
\\
\int^{\infty}_0 \int^{\pi}_0 \int^{2 \pi}_0 \large \psi^{*}_1 \normalsize \, \large \psi^{\phantom{.}}_2 \normalsize \, r^2 \, \text{sin} \theta \, dr \, d \theta \, d \phi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\text{For convenience let:} \phantom{.} \iiint \; = \; \int^{\infty}_{0} \int^{\pi}_{0} \int^{2\pi}_{0} \phantom{.} \text{and} \phantom{..} r^2 \, \text{sin} \theta \, dr \, d \theta \, d \phi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} d \text v$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
& \text{Recall: for a normalized wave function} \phantom{.} \iiint \large \psi^{*} \psi^{\phantom{.}} \normalsize d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
& \iiint \big( \text{a}_1 \text{2s}^{*} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{2p}_z^{*} \big) \big(\text{a}_2 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_2 \text{2p}_z \big) \, d \text{v} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
& 0 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_2 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^{*} \text{2s} \, d \text{v}}^{1} \; + \; \text{a}_1 \text{b}_2 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^{*} \text{2p}_z \, d \text{v}}^{0} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{a}_2 \iiint \overbrace{ \text{2p}_z^{*} \text{2s} \, d \text{v}}^{0}
\\
& \phantom{.....} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_1 \text{b}_2 \iiint \overbrace{ \text{2p}_z^{*} \text{2p}_z \, d \text{v}}^{1}
\\[5px]
& 0 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_2 \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{b}_2
\\[5px]
& ^{\dagger}\text{Given:} \phantom{..} | \text{a}_1 | \; = \; | \text{a}_2 | \phantom{.}, \phantom{.} | \text{b}_1 | \; = \; | \text{b}_2 | \phantom{....} ^{\dagger}\text{(Note: see Fig. 18)}
\\
& \text{and b}_2 \; = \; \text{neg. value} \phantom{..} \text{(Note: see Fig. 16)}
\\[5px]
& \text{Therefore:} \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_2 \; - \; \text{b}_1 \text{b}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{b}_1 \text{b}_2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} |a| \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} |b|
\end{align*}$$


The negative value of [b<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk} reflects the negative direction of the $\psi_2$ [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sub>z</sub><sup></sup> orbital relative to the $\psi_1$ [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue}<sub>z</sub> orbital (**Fig. 16**). Using normalization arguments (Note: see **Fig. 18**) we can quantify the coefficients in the following manner.  


$$\tag{32}$$
<br>

$$\\
\text{Normalization conditions:} \phantom{.} \int^{\infty}_{0} \int^{\pi}_{0} \int^{2\pi}_{0} \large \psi_1^* \psi^{\phantom{.}}_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} r^2 \text{sin} \theta \phantom{.} dr \phantom{.} d \theta \phantom{.} d \phi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\text{For convenience let:} \phantom{.} \iiint \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int^{\infty}_{0} \int^{\pi}_{0} \int^{2\pi}_{0} \phantom{.} \text{and} \phantom{..} r^2 \text{sin} \theta \phantom{.} dr \phantom{.} d \theta \phantom{.} d \phi \; = \; d \text{v}
\\
\iiint \big(\text{a}_1 \text{2s}^* \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{2p}_z^* \big) \big(\text{a}_1 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{2p}_z \big) \phantom{.} d \text{v} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\begin{align*}
1 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_1 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \text{2s} \phantom{.} d \text{v}}^{1} \; + \; \text{a}_1 \text{b}_1 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} d \text{v}}^{0} \; + \; \text{b}_1\text{a}_1 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \text{2s} \phantom{.} d \text{v}}^{0}
\\
& + \phantom{.} \text{b}_1\text{b}_1 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} d \text{v}}^{1} 
\\
1 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{a}_1 \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{b}_1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{a}_1^2 \; + \; \text{b}_1^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
& \text{Given:} \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{b}_1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} 2 \text{a}_1^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{b}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\\
& \text{All together:} \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{b}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} \text{b}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{align*}$$


The final set of normalized [sp]{#SBlue} hybrid orbital wave functions is shown below:   


$$\tag{33}
\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_{1 (\text{sp})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2s} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2p}_z
\\[5px]
\large \psi_{2 (\text{sp})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_2 \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2s} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2p}_z
\\[10px]
\text{Overall:} \phantom{..} \large \psi_{(\text{sp})} \normalsize \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \bigg(\text{2s} \; \pm \; \text{2p}_z \bigg)
\end{align*}$$

![](images/Borane_sp2_vector_diagram.jpg){width=360px}

<a id="LCAOsp2"></a>
**[II. LCAO &]{#Blk} [sp2]{#SBlue} [Orbitals]{#Blk}:** **Borane**, also known as <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/6331" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">Boron trihydride</a></b> ([[B]{#Silver2}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>3</sub>), is a good example of a hetero-nuclear poly-atomic molecule with [sp2]{#SBlue} hybrid orbitals. Its distinctive planar geometry and bond angles (i.e. 120&deg;) makes it relatively easy to determine the values of the coefficients for each [sp2]{#SBlue} orbital wave function. Firstly, because all three hybrid orbitals lie in a two dimensional plane, arbitrarily denoted [&xscr;-&zscr;]{#Blk}, there is no [&yscr;-axis]{#Blk} component to any of the hybrid orbitals. Also because the vector representing our first [sp2]{#SBlue} orbital can be arbitrarily assigned to the positive [&zscr;]{#Blk}-axis: $(x,y,z) = (0,0,+)$, it will therefore have no &xscr;-axis component. This simplifies the [sp2]{#SBlue} orbital wave equations as shown below.  

$$\tag{34}$$

$$\\
\large \psi_{\text{BH}_3} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\text a_1 \, \large \psi_{\text{B}_{2 \text s}} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text b_1 \, \large \psi_{\text{B}_{2 \text p_z}} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text c_1 \, \large \psi_{\text{B}_{2 \text p_x}}}^{\text{LCAO}} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} 3(\text d_1 \, \large \psi_{\text{H}_{1 \text s}})
\\[10px]
\normalsize \text{sp2} \phantom{.} \text{orbitals: }
\left[
\begin{array}{l}
\large \psi_{1 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{c}_1 \text{2p}_z
\\
\large \psi_{2 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_2 \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_2 \text{2p}_x
\\
\large \psi_{3 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_3 \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_3 \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_3 \text{2p}_x
\end{array}
\right.
\\$$

<!---------------------------------------------------->
<!--------------- Fig 18 Normalized 1s --------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig18"></a>

<figure id="FRight400">
![](images/Normalization_matrix.jpg){width=360px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 18: Normalized 1&sscr; Orbital Wave Functions</b>
</figcaption>
</figure>
<!---------------------------------------------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------->


The key feature of <u>normalized</u> orbital wave functions (**Fig. 18**) is that the sum of the squares of the coefficients for a given set of atomic orbitals (e.g. [2&sscr;]{#Blk}) is equal to unity (e.g. $\text{a}_1^2 + \text{a}_2^2 + \text{a}_3^2 = 1$). Similarly the sum of the squares of the coefficients for a <u>single</u> normalized wave function is also equal to unity (e.g. $\text{a}_1^2 + \text{b}_1^2 + \text{c}_1^2 = 1$). In the case of the single [2&sscr;]{#Blk} atomic orbital, which is shared equally between the three [sp2]{#SBlue} orbitals, we can safely assume that each [a]{#Blk} coefficient must be of equal value.  

<br>

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\text{Given:} & \phantom{..} | \text{a}_1| \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} | \text{a}_2| \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} | \text{a}_3| \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} \text{a}_1^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_2^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_3^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\[5px]
\text{Therefore:} & \phantom{..} 3\text{a}_1^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_3 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{align*}$$


Since $\psi_{1 (\text{sp2})}$ has only two coefficients the equations can be further simplified as shown below.  


$$\begin{align*}
\text{Given:} &
\phantom{..} \text{a}_1^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_1^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{..} \text{a}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} 
\\[5px]
\text{Therefore:} &
\phantom{..} \frac{1}{3} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_1^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{b}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
\end{align*}$$


Given that our initial hybrid orbital $\psi_{1 (\text{sp2})}$ is pointed in the positive direction (**Fig. 17**), we can therefore assign a positive value to [b<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk}. Moreover, given the notable symmetry of the [sp2]{#SBlue} orbitals we can also assign negative values of equal magnitude to the [b]{#Blk} coefficients for $\psi_{2 (\text{sp2})} \phantom{.} (+,0,$ [&mdash;]{#Blk} $)$ and $\psi_{3 (\text{sp2})} \phantom{.} (-,0,$ [&mdash;]{#Blk} $)$. Also, since the sum of squares of the coefficients for the set of [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue}<b><sub>z</sub></b> orbitals must also be equal to unity, the value of [b<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk} and [b<sub>3</sub>]{#Blk} can be easily calculated.  


$$\begin{align*}
\text{Given:} \phantom{..} | \text{b}_2 | \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} | \text{b}_3 | \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} \frac{2}{3} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_2^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_3^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\text{Therefore:} \phantom{..} 2\text{b}_2^2 \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; \frac{2}{3} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{b}_2^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{6}
\\
\text{Overall:} \phantom{..} \text{b}_2 \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \text{b}_3 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}
\\
\end{align*}$$


With the above information it's also possible to quickly calculate the values of the remaining [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue}<b><sub>x</sub></b> orbital coefficients.  


$$\begin{align*}
\text{Given:} \phantom{..} \text{c}_1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0, \phantom{.} | \text{c}_2 | \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} | \text{c}_3| \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{..} \text{c}_1^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{c}_2^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{c}_3^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\[5px]
\text{Therefore:} \phantom{..} 2\text{c}_2^2 \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \text{c}_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\\[5px]
\text{Overall:} \phantom{..} \text{c}_2 \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{..} \text{c}_3 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{align*}$$


Plugging in all of the normalization coefficients to **Eqn. 34** produces the following set of [sp2]{#SBlue} wave functions.  


$$\tag{34.2}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{2s} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text{2p}_z
\\[5px]
\large \psi_{\normalsize 2 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{2s} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2p}_x
\\[5px]
\large \psi_{\normalsize 3 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} &
= \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{2s} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{2p}_x
\\
\end{align*}$$


One way to confirm the values of these coefficients is to make use of a <u>vector</u> diagram (**Fig. 17**). Looking at this figure one can see that the magnitude (i.e. scalar quantity) of each [sp2]{#SBlue} orbital vector is represented by its length, which is made up of smaller component vectors. For example $\vec{\text B}$ vector, which represents $\psi_{2 (\text{sp2})}$, is made by adding two smaller vectors that correspond to [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}. Since these three vectors constitute a right angle triangle trigonometry can be used to solve for the unknown angle $\alpha$. However another geometric approach using vectors is to use the **Dot Product** formula (**Eqn. 35**), which measures the angle between two vectors.  


$$\tag{35}$$


$$\\
\text{Dot Product:} \phantom{..} \vec{\text A} \cdot \vec{\text B} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} | \text{a} | \times | \text{b} | \times \cos (\theta) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_x \text{b}_x \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_y \text{b}_y \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_z \text{b}_z
\\[10px]
\cos \theta \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\text{a}_x \text{b}_x \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_y \text{b}_y \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_z \text{b}_z}{ |\text{a} | \times | \text{b} |} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\Big(\text{a}_x \text{b}_x \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_y \text{b}_y \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_z \text{b}_z \Big)}{\Big( \sqrt{\text{a}_x^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_y^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{a}_z^2} \, \Big) \Big( \sqrt{\text{b}_x^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_y^2 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text{b}_z^2} \, \Big)}
\\$$


Plugging the coefficients of $\psi_{1 (\text{sp2})}$ and $\psi_{2 (\text{sp2})}$ into **Eqn. 35** produces the expected bond $\measuredangle$ of 120&deg;. The same calculation can be carried out for the other two bond $\measuredangle$ (i.e. between $\psi_{2 (\text{sp2})}$ and $\psi_{3 (\text{sp2})}$, or $\psi_{1 (\text{sp2})}$ and $\psi_{3 (\text{sp2})}$). Fortunately, using a simple symmetry argument it's easy to see that all three bond angles for the [sp2]{#SBlue} must be equal to 120&deg;.  


$$\tag{35.1}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\cos (\theta) \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{\bigg( 0 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \bigg) \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \bigg( 0 \bigg) \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \bigg( \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \bigg) \bigg( - \sqrt{\frac{1}{6}} \bigg)}{ \Bigg( \sqrt{0 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} 0 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}^2} \Bigg) \Bigg(\sqrt{ \bigg( - \sqrt{\frac{1}{6}} \bigg)^2 \phantom{.} + 0 \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}^2} \Bigg)}
\\[5px]
\cos (\theta) \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}}}{\Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \Bigg)} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{9}{4}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{2}
\\[5px]
\theta \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \cos^{-1} \Bigg( -\frac{1}{2} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 120^{\circ}
\end{align*}$$


As mentioned above the bond $\measuredangle$ between $\psi_{1 (\text{sp2})}$ and $\psi_{2 (\text{sp2})}$ can be measured using simple trigonometry (i.e. $\tan$ function). Since the normalization coefficients $\text{b}_2$ and $\text{c}_2$ represent the magnitude of the component vectors of $\vec{\text B}$, which forms a right angle triangle, then the $\tan$ function can be used to calculate the missing part of the bond angle (i.e. $\measuredangle \alpha$).  


$$\tag{35.2}$$


$$\\
\text{tan} (\alpha) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{opposite}{adjacent} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{ - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.57735
\\[10px]
\alpha \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} tan^{-1}( - 0.57735) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 30^{\circ}
\\[10px]
\text{Bond} \; \measuredangle \; \text{between} \; \large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp2})} \normalsize \; \text{and} \; \large \psi_{2 (\normalsize \text{sp2})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{90}^{\circ} \; + \; \text{30}^{\circ} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{120}^{\normalsize}$$

<a id="Fig19"></a>

<figure id="FRight400">

![](images/CH4_sp3_vector_diagram.jpg){width=385px}

<figcaption>
<b>Figure 19: Vector Diagram for [[sp3]{#SBlue}]{#strikeB} orbitals</b>
</figcaption>

<!---------------------------------------------------->

<!---------------------------------------------------->

<a id="LCAOsp3"></a>

**[III. LCAO &]{#Blk} [sp3]{#SBlue} [Orbitals]{#Blk}:** <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Methane" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">Methane</a></b> ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>3</sub>) is the simplest example of a molecule containing [sp3]{#SBlue} molecular orbitals. The lone [2&sscr;]{#Blk} and three [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals of [C]{#Blk} that are mixed to form four orbitals (**Eqn. 36**) have similar energy levels, but distinctive shapes and spatial orientations. The well known tetrahedral geometry of methane is a product of its 109.5&deg; bond angles that provide maximum separation of the electron domains.    

<br>
<br>
<br>

$$\tag{36}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
& \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{CH}_4} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\text a_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{C}_{2 \text s}} \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \text b_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{C}_{2 \text p_z}} \normalsize \; + \; \text c_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{C}_{2 \text p_x}} \normalsize \; + \; \text d_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{C}_{2 \text p_y}}}^{\text{LCAO}} \normalsize \; + \; 4(\text e_1 \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{H}_{\text{1s}}})
\\[10px]
& \text{sp3} \phantom{.} \text{orbitals:} \; 
\left[
\begin{array}{l}
\large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_1 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_1 \, \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_1 \, \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text{d}_1 \, \text{2p}_y
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 2 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_2 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_2 \, \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_2 \, \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text{d}_2 \, \text{2p}_y
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 3 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_3 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_3 \, \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_3 \, \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text{d}_3 \, \text{2p}_y
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 4 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{a}_4 \, \text{2s} \; + \; \text{b}_4 \, \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text{c}_4 \, \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text{d}_4 \, \text{2p}_y
\end{array}
\right.
\end{align*}
\\$$


As shown in **Eqn. 36** we can combine the first four terms on the right side of the equation to produce four equivalent [sp3]{#SBlue} orbitals. Because each lobe of a [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital points in opposite direction along a given Cartesian axis, the resulting orbital will end up concentrating its electron densities in one direction (i.e. towards one of the four vertices of an imaginary triangular pyramid). Moreover, since the four [sp3]{#SBlue} orbitals are <u>equivalent</u> the corresponding coefficient for the lone [2&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital is the same for each molecular orbital (i.e. $\text a_1 = \text a_2 = \text a_3 = \text a_4$). Also since the [2&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital is normalized and shared equally between these four orbitals then the sum of squares of this set of coefficients must be equal to unity (**Fig. 18**). As a result each $\text a$-type coefficient must be equal to $1 / \sqrt 4$ (i.e. $(1 / \sqrt 4)^2 + (1 / \sqrt 4)^2 + (1 / \sqrt 4)^2 + (1 / \sqrt 4)^2 = 1$). For convenience we can assign the first [sp3]{#SBlue} orbital as pointing upward toward the &ldquo;peak&rdquo; of our imaginary tetrahedron along the &zscr;-axis. This means this vector has no &xscr; or &yscr; components (i.e. [c<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk} = 0, and [d<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk} = 0), which simplifies the orbital wave function.  


$$\tag{37}
\\
\begin{align*}
\text{Let} \; \large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize &
\phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \text{z-axis oriented orbital}
\\[5px]
\text{Given: } & \phantom{.} \text c_1 \; = \; 0 \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{..} \text d_1 \; = \; 0
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize 1 (\text{sp3})} \normalsize &
\; = \; \frac{1}{2} 2 \text s \; + \; \text b_1 \, 2 \text p_z
\end{align*}$$


In addition, we can apply the same normality test to $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ (**Fig. 18**) to solve for [b<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk}. Since the sum of squares of a set of coefficients for a single normalized wave function equals unity (i.e. $a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2 + d_1^2 = 1$), it therefore follows that the contribution of [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} to the [sp3]{#SBlue} orbital is $\sqrt{3/4}$.  


$$\tag{38}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\int \large \psi^*_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, d \text v \; = &
\; \int \bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s}^* \; + \; \text b_1 \, \text{2p}^*_z \bigg) \bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_1 \, \text{2p}_z \bigg) \, d \text v \; = \; 1
\\
1 \; = &
\; \frac{1}{4} \int \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \, \text{2s} \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{\text{b}_1}{2} \int \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \, \text{2p}_z \, d \text v}^{0} \; + \; \frac{\text{b}_1}{2} \int \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \, \text{2s} \, d \text v}^{0}
\\
& + \; \text b_1^2 \int \overbrace{\text{2p}_z^* \, \text{2p}_z \, d \text v}^{1}
\\
1 \; = &
\; \frac{1}{4} \; + \; \text b_1^2
\\
\text b_1 \; = &
\; \pm \sqrt{1 \; - \; \frac{1}{4}} \; = \; \large \pm \frac{\sqrt 3}{2}
\\
\end{align*}$$


Plugging the positive value of [b<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk} into **Eqn. 37** (Note position of orbital vector, **Fig. 19**) produces:  


$$\tag{39}
\\
\large \psi_1{_{\normalsize (\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z$$


Having the $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ orbital pointed directly upwards along the positive [z]{#Blk} axis means that the vectors representing the other three [sp3]{#SBlue} orbitals must be pointed directly at the vertices located at the base of our imaginary pyramid (**Fig. 19**). These vectors have &xscr; and &yscr; components that optimize their separation (i.e. reduce the electrostatic repulsion between neighbouring **electron domains**), which means there are multiple coefficient calculations per wave function.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; The second vector representing $\psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ lies in the &xscr;-&yscr; plane, separated from the first vector by a bond angle of ~109.5&deg;. Although $\psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ (**Eqn. 39.1**) has an additional vector component, the fact that it does not overlap with $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ means that their electron densities are independent of each other (i.e. use <u>orthogonal</u> test).  


$$\tag{39.1}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z
\\
\large \psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_2 \, \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_2 \, \text{2p}_x
\end{align*}$$


$$\tag{40}$$

$$\\
\int^{\infty}_0 \int^{\pi}_0 \int^{2\pi}_0 \large \psi^*_1{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize\, \large \psi^{\,}_2{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, r^2 \, \text{sin} \, \theta \, dr \, d \theta \, d \phi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\[5px]
\large \text{Let:} \phantom{.} \normalsize \iiint \; = \; \int^{\infty}_{0} \int^{\pi}_{0} \int^{2\pi}_{0} \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{...} r^2 \, \text{sin} \, \theta \, dr \, d \theta \, d \phi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} d \text v
\\[5px]
\iiint \large \psi^*_1{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \, \psi^{\,}_2{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\$$


Applying the &ldquo;orthogonality&rdquo; test (i.e. no shared electron density between two orbital wave functions = <u>empty</u> distribution function) in this way can quick find the solution to an unknown coefficients provided the calculus eliminates other unknown coefficients.  


$$\tag{40.1}$$

<br>

$$\begin{align*}
\iiint \large \psi^*_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize d \text v \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \iiint \Bigg( \frac{1}{2} 2 \text s^* \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} 2 \text p^*_z \Bigg) \Bigg( \frac{1}{2} 2 \text s \; + \; \text b_2 2 \text p_z \; + \; \text c_2 2 \text p_x \Bigg) d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text s^* \; 2 \text s \; d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{\text b_2}{2} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text s^* \; 2 \text p_z \; d \text v}^{0} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \frac{\text c_2}{2} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text s^* \; 2 \text p_x \; d \text v}^{0}
\\
& + \phantom{.} \frac{\sqrt 3}{4} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text p^*_z \; 2 \text s \; d \text v}^{0} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3 \, \text b_2}{2} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text p^*_z \; 2 \text p_z \;  d \text v}^{1}
\\
& + \phantom{.} \frac{\sqrt 3 \, \text c_2}{2} \iiint \overbrace{2 \text p^*_z \; 2 \text p_x \; d \text v}^{0}
\\
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text b_2
\\
\text b_2 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} - \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt 3} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3}
\\
\end{align*}$$


The negative value for [b<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk} (**Eqn. 40.1**) makes sense since the vector representing this function is pointed in the negative direction (**Fig. 19**). Obviously the next task is to calculate the [c<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk} coefficient (**Fig. 40.2**).  


$$\tag{40.2}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z
\\[5px]
\large \psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_2 \text{2p}_x
\end{align*}$$


Solving for [c<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk} can be done using the normality test on $\psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ as was done previously for $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ (**Eqn. 38**).  


$$\tag{41}$$

$$\begin{align*}
\\
\text{(Note: for brevity } & \text{null orthogonal integral products are not shown)}
\\
\int \large \psi^*_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \; \psi^{\,}_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \; d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} &
\int \Bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s}^* \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}^*_z \; + \; \text c_2 \text{2p}^*_x \Bigg) \Bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_2 \text{2p}_x \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\[5px]
\int \large \psi^*_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \; \psi^{\,}_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \; d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} &
\frac{1}{4} \int \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \; \text{2s} \; d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \int \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \; \text{2p}_z \; d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \text c_2^2 \int \overbrace{2 \text p^*_x \; 2 \text p_x \; d \text v}^{1} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\int \large \psi^*_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \; \psi^{\phantom{.}}_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \; d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} &
\frac{1}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \; + \; \text c_2^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \text c_2^2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{2}{3} \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \text c_2 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
\end{align*}$$


Completing the <u>normalization</u> process for two of the four hybrid orbital wave functions leaves us with the following wave functions:  


$$\tag{42}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_1{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z
\\
\large \psi_2{\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text{2p}_x  
\end{align*}
\\$$


Having the complete set of normalization coefficients for both $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ and $\psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ it's now possible to formally calculate the bond angle between these two hybrid orbitals (**Fig. 19**). Once again we can use the formula for the **Dot Product** of two vectors (**Eqn. 35**).  


$$\tag{43}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\cos (\theta) {\normalsize _{(\text{sp3})}} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{\Big( 0 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \, \Big) \; + \; \Big( 0 \Big) \; + \; \Big( \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \Big) \Big( - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \Big)}{\Big( \sqrt{ \, \frac{2}{3} \; + \; 0 \; + \; \frac{1}{12}} \, \Big) \Big(\sqrt{\, 0 \; + \; 0 \; + \; \frac{3}{4}} \, \Big)}
\\
\cos (\theta) \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{ - \frac{1}{4}}{\Bigg( \frac{3}{2 \sqrt 3} \cdot \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \Bigg)} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{4} \; \times \; \frac{4}{3} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{3}
\\
\theta \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \cos^{-1} \Big( - \frac{1}{3} \Big) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 109.47^{\circ} \; \approx \; 109.5^{\circ}
\end{align*}$$


The remaining two hybrid orbital wave functions, $\psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ and $\psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ (**Eqn. 44**), have additional coefficients to solve due to the additional [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue} orbital component.  


$$\tag{44}$$

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z
\\[5px]
\large \psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; + \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text{2p}_x
\\[5px]
\large \psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_3 \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_3 \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text d_3 \text{2p}_y
\\[5px]
\large \psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_4 \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_4 \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text d_4 \text{2p}_y
\end{align*}
\\$$


Fortunately, multiple <u>normality</u> (**Eqn. 32**) and <u>orthogonal</u> tests (**Eqn. 31**) can be applied to these four <u>orthogonal</u> orbitals to calculate the remaining coefficients. For example, applying the orthogonal test to $\psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ and $\psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ generates a value for [b<sub>3</sub>]{#Blk}.  


$$\tag{45}$$

<br>

$$\\
\begin{align*}
\iiint \large \psi^*_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \, \psi^{\,}_3{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, d \text v \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s}^* \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}^*_z \bigg) \bigg(\frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \text b_3 \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_3 \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text d_3 \text{2p}_y \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\text{(Note: for brev} & \text{ity null orthogonal integral products are not shown)}
\\
0 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \, \text{2s} \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text b_3  \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \, \text{2p}_z \, d \text v}^{1} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \normalsize \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text b_3
\\
\text b_3 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} - \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt 3} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3}
\end{align*}
\\$$


Applying the <u>orthogonality</u> test to $\psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ and $\psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ quickly solves for $\text c_3$ (**Eqn. 46**).  


$$\tag{46}$$


$$\\ \;
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
\iiint \large \psi^*_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \, \psi_3^{\,}{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, d \text v \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \bigg( \frac{1}{2} \text{2s}^* \; - \; \frac{1}{2\sqrt3} \text{2p}^*_z \; + \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text{2p}^*_x \bigg) \bigg(\frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2\sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; + \; \text c_3 \, \text{2p}_x
\\[5px]
+ & \; \text d_3 \text{2p}_y \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\[5px]
\text{(Note: for brev} & \text{ity null orthogonal integral products are not shown)}
\\
0 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \, \text{2s} \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \, \text{2p}_z \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text c_3 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_x \, \text{2p}_x \, d \text v}^{1}
\\[5px]
0 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \; + \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text c_3 \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \text c_3 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{3} \times \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{1}{\sqrt 6}
\end{align*}
\\$$


The remaining coefficient for $\psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ can now be easily solved by applying the normalization test on the wave function itself.  


$$\tag{47}$$


$$\\
\;
\\
\begin{align*}
\iiint \large \psi^*_3{_{(\text{sp3})}} \, \psi^{\,}_3{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \, d \text v \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \Bigg(\frac{1}{2} \text{2s}^* \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}^*_z \; - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 6} \text{2p}^*_x \; + \; \text d_3 \, \text{2p}^*_y \Bigg) \Bigg(\frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z 
\\
& - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 6} \text{2p}_x \; + \; \text d_3 \, \text{2p}_y \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\[5px]
\text{(Note: for brevity } & \text{the null orthogonal integral products are not shown below)}
\\
1 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2s}^* \, \text{2s} \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_z \, \text{2p}_z \, d \text v}^{1} \; + \; \frac{1}{6} \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_x \, \text{2p}_x \, d \text v}^{1}
\\[5px]
& + \; \text d_3^2 \iiint \overbrace{\text{2p}^*_y \, \text{2p}_y \, d \text v}^{1}
\\[5px]
1 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{4} \; + \; \frac{1}{12} \; + \; \frac{1}{6} \; + \; \text d_3^2
\\[5px]
\text d_3 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \pm \sqrt{1 \; - \; \frac{6}{12}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}
\end{align*}$$


The final set of coefficients for $\psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ can now be quickly calculated based on the previously mentioned normality conditions of the orbital coefficients (e.g. $\text{b}_1^2 + \text{b}_2^2 + \text{b}_3^2 + \text{b}_4^2 = 1$). Also based on the Cartesian co-ordinates of the orbital vectors (**Fig. 19**) the proper sign of each coefficient can be determined. For example the magnitude and sign of the [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} component of $\psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ is:  


$$\tag{48}$$


$$\\
\Bigg( \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \Bigg)^2 \; + \; \Bigg( - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \Bigg)^2 \; + \; \Bigg( - \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \Bigg)^2 \; + \; \text b^2_4 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\begin{align*}
\text b^2_4 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 1 \; - \; \frac{3}{4} \; - \; \frac{1}{12} \; - \; \frac{1}{12} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{12}
\\[5px]
\text b_4 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \pm \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}
\\
\end{align*}$$


Applying the same normality conditions to the remaining sets of atomic orbitals for $\psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}}$ completes the coefficient normalization process (**Eqn. 49**).  


$$\tag{49}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_1{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; + \; \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \text{2p}_z
\\[5px]
\large \psi_2{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; + \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \text{2p}_x
\\[5px]
\large \psi_3{_{(\text{sp3})}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 6} \text{2p}_x \; - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 2} \text{2p}_y
\\[5px]
\large \psi_4{_{(\text{sp3})}} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{1}{2} \text{2s} \; - \; \frac{1}{2 \sqrt 3} \text{2p}_z \; - \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 6} \text{2p}_x \; + \; \frac{1}{\sqrt 2} \text{2p}_y
\end{align*}
\\$$

<!------------ FIG 20 - MOT CH4 Energy Diagram  ------------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig20"></a>

<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/MO_diagram_CH4_bond.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>
<b><u>Figure 20</u>: Molecular Orbital (MO) Diagram of Methane.</b> According to [VBT]{#Blk} methane ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>) is formed by combining four [sp3]{#SBlue} mixed atomic orbitals of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} with four [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbitals provided by four [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atoms. This combination of atomic orbitals lacks the symmetry seen in molecular [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} (**Fig. 13**). Differences in orbital shape (symmetry), orientation (i.e. direction) and energy largely determine the extent of orbital overlap or &ldquo;mixing&rdquo;. Unlike [VBT]{#Blk} the concept of [AO]{#Blk} hybridization is not used in [MOT]{#Blk}. Instead [MOT]{#Blk} relies on the concept of orbital &ldquo;mixing&rdquo; (i.e. with similar energies and symmetry) when combining [AO]{#Blk} in a linear fashion (**Eqn. 28**). As shown above methane ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>) is formed by simply combining the eight [AO]{#Blk} of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} and [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (i.e. four [1&sscr;]{#Blk}, one [2&sscr;]{#Blk} and three [&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals) to produce four bonding and four anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} (**Note:** the orbital number is always conserved: # [MO]{#Blk} = # [AO]{#Blk}). Orbitals with similar symmetries and orientations can combine even if they belong to different energy levels (i.e. [1&sscr;]{#Blk} and [2&sscr;]{#Blk} orbitals). Although [&sscr;]{#Blk} and [&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals have different shapes certain orientations of the latter orbital can produce productive interactions. The [AO]{#Blk} holding the eight [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} are all fairly close in energy (Note: ionization energy values) suggesting that significant interactions are possible. The mini-cubic diagrams of the [MO]{#Blk} shows the orientation and phase of the [AO]{#Blk} that lead to constructive interference and bond formation (**Note:** phase alignment of [&sscr;]{#Blk}-[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital interactions). Unlike $\large \sigma$ bonds (i.e. located along inter-nuclear axis) involving only spherical orbitals (i.e. [1&sscr;]{#Blk} and [2&sscr;]{#Blk}), $\large \sigma$ bonds involving [1&sscr;]{#Blk} and [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals have distinctive [[nodal planes]{#Hpink}]{#strokeB} along the inter-nuclear axis. The tetravalent nature of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} is represented by the four [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbitals taking up positions at the corners of the tetrahedron. As always the [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB} are assigned to the lowest possible energy [MO]{#Blk} states first in accordance with the <i>[Aufbau Principle]{#Blk}</i>. The labels attached to the [MO]{#Blk} simply reflect their respective $\large \sigma$ symmetries. Normally [MO]{#Blk} naming is based on <b>group theory</b> (symmetry) concepts. Specifically methane belongs to the <b><a class="one" href="https://www.chemtube3d.com/methane-tetrahedral-symmetry-td/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemTube3D">T<sub>d</sub> point group</a></b>, which exhibits <b>a<sub>1</sub></b> and <b>t<sub>2</sub></b> type symmetries (i.e. <b><a class="one" href="https://www.chemtube3d.com/methane-tetrahedral-symmetry-td/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemTube3D"><b>t</b>etrahedral group</a></b> with six [d]{#Blk}ihedral mirror planes). The former is a single degenerate symmetric bonding orbital arising from [&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital interactions, while <b>t<sub>2</sub></b> represents a triply degenerate set of [&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital interactions. The first [[I]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}onization [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}nergy values ([[I]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}) for atomic [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} (i.e. energy required to release the first [[VE]{#Red}]{#strokeB}), as well as the [[I]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB} for the two different types of $\large \sigma$ [MO]{#Blk} are also shown for reference purposes. Applying <b><a class="one" href="https://www.pnnl.gov/explainer-articles/photoelectron-spectroscopy" target="_blank" title="Go to PNNL">Photo-electron spectroscopy</a></b> (<b>PES</b>) to methane reveals two distinct ionization peaks.<b>[@baker_electronic_1968; @hamrin_ionization_1968]</b> Both peaks are relatively broad due to multiple quantized <b><a class="one" href="https://www.chem.purdue.edu/jmol/vibs/ch4.html" target="_blank" title="Go to Purdue U. Chemistry">vibrational states</a></b>. Integrating the two <b>PES</b> peaks reveals an intensity ratio of nearly 3:1, which is consistent with the orbital makeup of methane. Confirmation of the <b>T<sub>d</sub></b> point group by <b>PES</b> (i.e. two distinct sets of degenerate orbitals) is at odds with the [VBT]{#Blk}, since the latter predicts 4 identical degenerate [sp3]{#SBlue} hybrid atomic orbitals for methane. However the four [sp3]{#SBlue}-[1&sscr;]{#Blk} [MO]{#Blk} may simply represent an &ldquo;idealized&rdquo; form of orbital &ldquo;mixing&rdquo;.

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->

<br>

<a id="LCAOpi1"></a>

**[IV - 1. LCAO & Conjugated]{#Blk} <span id="Blk26">&pi;</span> [Bond Systems]{#Blk}:** The simplest organic molecule containing a double bond is **ethylene**, also known as **ethene** ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>). It is one of many organic molecules that contain one or more double (**alkenes**) and/or triple bonds (**alkynes**), a condition referred to as <u>unsaturated</u> (i.e. tetra-valence state not maximized for carbon). **Alkenes** and **alkynes** are chemically more reactive than their saturated counterparts, often undergoing addition reactions to become <u>saturated</u> (i.e. [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}:[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} ratio = 1:4). In the case of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>2</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub> each [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atom forms three $\large \sigma$ bonds via [sp2]{#SBlue} hybridization (<b>Fig. 19</b>), while the two remaining <u>unhybridized</u> [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals form a $\large \pi$ bond through their sideways overlap both above and below the plane of the central [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atoms.  

<a id="Fig21"></a>		
<!------------------------------------------------>
<!------------ FIG 21 - MOT Ethylene ------------->
<!------------------------------------------------>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/Ethylene_MO_diagram.jpg){width=600px}
</figure>
</div>
<b><u>Figure 21</u>: Conjugated Double Bond System of Ethylene.</b>
</div>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


<!-------------------------------------------------->
<!------------ FIG 22 - Matrix Algebra ------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig22"></a>
<figure id="FRight350">
![](images/Matrix_Algebra.jpg){width=335px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 22</u>: Matrix Algebra - Dot Product.</b>
</figcaption>
</figure>  
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


$\large \pi$ bonds are a product of the interaction or &ldquo;mixing&rdquo; of neighbouring [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals. As a result $\large \pi$-electrons are thought to move between the successive [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atoms either above or below the planar network of $\large \sigma$ bonds, otherwise known as the $\large \sigma$ <b>framework</b>. According to **Erich Hückel** (1930) the [MO]{#Blk} of a conjugated $\large \pi$-bond system can be treated independently of the $\large \sigma$ <b>framework</b>.<b>[@huckel_quantentheoretische_1931; @huckel_quanstentheoretische_1931; @huckel_quantentheoretische_1932; @coulson_huckel_1978]</b> For **ethylene** this means the designated [MO]{#Blk} wave function ($\psi_{\pi}$) describing its delocalized $\large \pi$-electrons can be expressed using the familiar <b>LCAO</b> method, where the <b>n<sup>th</sup></b> number of coefficient-weighted atomic orbitals are summed.  


$$\tag{50}$$


$$\\
\text{Let:} \; \large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \; = \; \text{MO wave function}, \; \large \phi \normalsize \; = \; 2p_z \, \text{wave funtion}, \; c_n \; = \; \text{coefficient}
\\
\large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} c_1 \large \phi_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} c_2 \large \phi_2
\\[15px]
\text{Algebraic Matrix Form:}
\\
\text A \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} [c_1, c_2], \phantom{...} \text B \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \left[\begin{array}
\\
\large \phi_1
\\
\large \phi_2
\end{array}
\right]
\\
\large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text{A} \times \text{B} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\large [c_1, c_2]
\left[\begin{array}
\\
\large \phi_1
\\
\large \phi_2
\end{array}
\right]}^{\large \text{Dot Product}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} c_1 \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; + \; c_2 \large \phi_2
\\$$


<b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/matrix-introduction.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">Algebraic matrices</a></b>, like the one shown above, are routinely used to represent these types of orbital energy equations since the math that governs them (e.g. <b><a class="" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/matrix-multiplying.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">Dot Product</a></b>) is extremely convenient when dealing with complex wave functions.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; **Huckel** [MO]{#Blk} **theory** is a very useful way of understanding de-localized $\large \pi$-bond systems for a number of reasons. Firstly, the entire $\large \pi$-bond system can be treated separately from the $\large \sigma$-framework. Secondly, the de-localized electrons are thought to move &ldquo;<i>freely</i>&rdquo; within the conjugated $\large \pi$-bond system all under the influence of an electrostatic potential field. These <u>bound</u> or &ldquo;trapped&rdquo; $\large \pi$-electrons can be conveniently described using a sinusoidal wave function (**Recall:** [P]{#Red}otential [E]{#Red}nergy <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#InfSqW" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">Infinite Square Well</a></b> or electron in a box concept). The length of the trapped **sine wave** corresponds to the length of the molecule's &ldquo;<i>energy well</i>&rdquo; as defined by the $\large \pi$-electron system, and where the sine wave meets the ends of the &ldquo;<i>well</i>&rdquo; a designated node appears (i.e. where wave function has zero electron density). The smallest possible wave length that fits the potential energy &ldquo;<i>well</i>&rdquo; would be a standard half-cycle ($\large \pi \normalsize \; \text{radians} = 180^{\circ}$). This low energy state would represent the bonding [MO]{#Blk}, whereas one complete wave cycle ($2 \large \pi \normalsize \; \text{radians} = 360^{\circ}$) would represent the next highest energy level, which in this case represents an anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} (**Fig. 21**).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; **Huckel's** [MO]{#Blk} theory describes flat or planar molecules (i.e. [sp2]{#SBlue}) with conjugated non-hybridized [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbitals that are perpendicular to the underlying $\large \sigma$ framework. Molecules with multiple conjugated double bonds, such as **1,3-butadiene** (**Fig. 23**), allow $\large \pi$-electrons to move &ldquo;<i>freely</i>&rdquo; (i.e. de-localized) between multiple [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals. For **1,3-butadiene** this means the wave function representing the low energy bonding [MO]{#Blk} spans the entire length of the molecule (i.e. four contiguous [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals). Given the inverse relationship between wave length ($\lambda$) and energy (i.e. $\text E = h \nu$, where $\nu = 1/\lambda$ and $h$ is <b>Plank's</b> constant) the bonding $\large \pi$-electrons represented by a long wave length function would have the lowest energy. For organic molecules like <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Fig_Ret" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP - Retinoid Cycle">carotenoids</a></b> that have extensive conjugated $\large \pi$ bond systems (i.e. >8 alternating double bonds), this means they can absorb photons with relatively long wavelengths (i.e. visible spectrum). As a result many of these types of molecules are quite colourful. These pigmented biomolecules are often put to good use, such as in the case of [[chlorophyll]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} (photosynthesis) and [[retinoids]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (i.e. vision systems). According to [MO]{#Blk} theory the ability of molecules to absorb low energy photons is due to a relatively narrow energy gap between the highest occupied [MO]{#Blk} ([HOMO]{#Blk}) and the lowest unoccupied [MO]{#Blk} ([LUMO]{#Blk}). This so called <b>Frontier Orbital Gap</b> helps to explain many important properties of molecules (e.g. chemical reactivity, electrical conductivity, optical properties). For example relatively stable molecules have a large <b>Frontier Orbital Gap</b> since they only interact with high energy photons (e.g. UV, X-rays). And when an electron successfully interacts with a photon it can enter an &ldquo;<i>excited</i>&rdquo; state (i.e. pictured as &ldquo;<i>jumping</i>&rdquo; up into high energy [MO]{#Blk}). Normally such encounters are very short-lived and the &ldquo;<i>excited</i>&rdquo; electron quickly loses its extra energy often in the form of an emitted photon.  
&nbsp; &nbsp; Going forward it's important to keep in mind that **Huckel's** [MOT]{#Blk} is semi-empirical in nature since the actual values of the base <b>Coulombic</b> ($\alpha$) and <b>Resonance</b> ($\beta$) energy integrals are actually experimental inputs. In fact the $\beta$ energy values, as seen in the [MO]{#Blk} energy diagrams, are expressed as an increase or decrease in the base $\alpha$ value. The relative values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ change for each type of poly-atomic molecule, since different elements have their own characteristic electron affinity or <b><a class="one" href="https://ptable.com/#Properties/Electronegativity" target="_blank" title="Go to Interactive PT">electronegativity</a></b> ([[&Chi;]{#Crim}]{#strokeB}). Although computational methods (e.g. **D**ensity **F**unctional **T**heory, or **DFT**) have largely replaced semi-empirical methods, **Huckel's** [MOT]{#Blk} is still very useful because of its conceptual clarity when explaining $\large \pi$-electron systems.
