$$\\
\large \pi \normalsize \; e^- \; \text{Density}
\\
\Big[ \large \text{Note: } n \normalsize \, = \, \text{#}e^- , \phantom{.} \large \text c \normalsize \, = \, \text{coefficient}, \phantom{.} \large k^{th} \; \normalsize \text{MO}, \phantom{.} \large j^{th} \normalsize \text{atom}, \; \large Q_j \normalsize \, = \, e^- \text{ charge/atom} \Big]
\\
\large D_{j} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \sum_{k \, = \, 1}^{N} \normalsize n_k \; c_{k \, j}^2 \phantom{.....} \large Q_j \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; \large D_{j}
\\[30px]
\text{1,3-butadiene} \; (4 \phantom{.} \large \pi \normalsize e^-)
\\
\begin{align*}
\large D_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.372 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.6018 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_2}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{......} \large Q_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; 1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\large D_2 \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.6018 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.372 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_2}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{......} \large Q_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; 1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\large D_3 \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.6018 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \Big( - 0.372 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_2}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{......} \large Q_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; 1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\large D_4 \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \Big( 0.372 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \Big( - 0.6018 \Big)^2}^{ k \; = \; \large \psi_{\pi_2}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \phantom{......} \large Q_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1 \; - \; 1 \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\\
\end{align*}$$


Similar to the previously described **Allyl radical** &ldquo;<i>species</i>&rdquo; the $\large \pi$-electron density of the lowest energy bonding [MO]{#Blk} of <b>1,3-butadiene</b> is spread evenly across the whole molecule. This <u>uniform</u> $\large \pi$-electron density (i.e. no localized charge) increases the stability of the molecule.  


$$\\
\large \text{Bond Order (BO)}
\\
\Big[ \text{Note:} \phantom{..} n \; = \; \text{#}e^- , \phantom{..} \text c \; = \; \text{coefficient} , \phantom{..} k^{th} \, \text{MO} , \phantom{..} \text{bonded atoms} \; = \; a \; - \; b \Big]
\\
\large \text{BO}_{(a-b)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \sum_{k \, = \, 1}^{N} \normalsize n_k^{\phantom{\,}} \; c_{(k \, a)} \; c_{(k \, b)}
\\$$


$$\\
\large \text{BO: 1,3-butadiene}
\\
\begin{align*}
\large \text{BO}_{\normalsize (\text C_1 - \text C_2)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \big( 0.372 \big) \big( 0.6018 \big)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \big( 0.6018 \big) \big( 0.372 \big)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_2}} \normalsize \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.8955
\\
\large \text{BO}_{\normalsize (\text C_2 - \text C_3)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \big( 0.6018 \big) \big( 0.6018 \big)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \big( 0.372 \big) \big( - 0.372 \big)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_2}} \normalsize \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.4476
\\
\large \text{BO}_{\normalsize (\text C_3 - \text C_4)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \big( 0.6018 \big) \big( 0.372 \big)}^{ \large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_1}} \normalsize \; + \; \overbrace{ (2) \big( -0.372 \big) \big( 0.6018 \big)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_2}} \normalsize \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.8955
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\large \text{BO: Ethylene}
\\
\large \text{BO}_{(\text C_1 - \text C_2)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{ (2) \bigg( \frac{1}{\sqrt 2} \bigg) \bigg( \frac{1}{\sqrt 2} \bigg)}^{\large k \; = \; \psi_{\pi_{\normalsize 1}}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\$$


The **Bond Order** of both [[C<sub>1</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[C<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[C<sub>3</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[C<sub>4</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} (Note: &sigma; bond order not included) is slightly weaker (~90% $\large \pi$-bond character) than the **Bond Order** of the lone $\large \pi$ bond of <b>ethylene</b> (100% $\large \pi$-bond character). Perhaps more interesting is the middle [[C<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[C<sub>3</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} covalent bond, which is depicted in its **Lewis** structure as a simple $\large \sigma$-bond. However, according to **Huckel's** [MO]{#Blk} calculations this covalent bond has a significant amount of $\large \pi$-bond character (i.e. **45%**). Fortunately these calculations are consistent with the experimental evidence that shows the length of the middle [[C<sub>2</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[C<sub>3</sub>]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} bond (i.e. 1.454 &Aring;) to be smaller than a typical single bond (i.e. 1.54 &Aring;) and larger than a typical double bond (i.e. 1.338 &Aring;).  

<br>

$$\\
\large \text{Coulson Formula} - \text{Huckle MO Energy} \; (\text E_{\pi})
\\
\large \text{Linear Planar Polyenes}
\\[5px]
k^{th} \; = \, \large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \, \text{MO index} , \phantom{..} \alpha \, = \, \text{Coulomb Integral} \; \large \pi \normalsize e^- \\ \beta \, = \, \text{Resonance Integral} , \phantom{..} N \, = \, \# \, \text{C atoms} , \phantom{..} a^{\dagger} \, = \, \text{atomic position} \\ \text C_{k \, a^{\dagger}} \, = \, \text{Coefficient for} \; a^{\dagger} \; \text{AO in the} \; k^{th} \; \text{MO} 
\\[10px]
\text E_{\pi_k} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta \; cos \Bigg( \frac{k \; \large \pi}{ N \, + \, 1} \Bigg)
\\[5px]
\text C_{k \, a^{\dagger}} \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{N \, + \, 1}} \; sin \Bigg( \frac{k \; a^{\dagger} \, \large \pi}{N \, + \, 1} \Bigg) \phantom{....} \text{where: } a^{\dagger} = 1, \, 2, \, 3, \, ...N
\\$$


<br>


<b>Coulson</b> (1939)<b>[@coulson_electronic_1939]</b> also produced a formula for calculating the [MO]{#Blk} energies and [AO]{#Blk} weighting factors (i.e. **coefficients**) for <u>linear</u> **polyene** chains. For example, when used on **1,3-butadiene** it quickly produces the expected [MO]{#Blk} energies and coefficients as previous calculated.  


$$\\
\large \text{Coulson Energy Formula: 1,3-butadiene}
\\[5px]
\Big[ \text{Note:} \; ^{\dagger} \large \pi \normalsize \; \text{radians} \; = \; 180^{\circ} , \; N \; = \; 4 \Big]
\\[5px]
\text{MO Energy} \; \Big( \large \psi_{\pi_n} \normalsize \Big) 
\\
\begin{align*}
\large \text E_{\pi_1} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; cos \Bigg( \frac{1 \, \large \pi}{ 4 \, + \, 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta
\; \overbrace{ cos \Bigg( \frac{ \large \pi }{5} \Bigg)}^{\large ^{\dagger} cos(36^{\circ})} 
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \big( 0.8090 \big)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 1.618 \, \beta
\\
\large \text E_{\pi_2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; cos \Bigg( \frac{2 \, \large \pi}{4 \, + \, 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta
\; \overbrace{ cos \Bigg( \frac{ 2 \large \pi }{5} \Bigg)}^{\large ^{\dagger} cos(72^{\circ})} 
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \big( 0.3090 \big)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 0.618 \, \beta
\\
\large \text E_{\pi_3} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; cos \Bigg( \frac{3 \, \large \pi}{4 \, + \, 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta
\; \overbrace{ cos \Bigg( \frac{ 3 \large \pi }{5} \Bigg)}^{\large ^{\dagger} cos(108^{\circ})} 
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \big( - 0.3090 \big)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \alpha \; - \; 0.618 \, \beta
\\
\large \text E_{\pi_4} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; cos \Bigg( \frac{4 \, \large \pi}{4 \, + \, 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \;  2 \, \beta \; \overbrace{ cos \Bigg( \frac{ 4 \large \pi }{5} \Bigg)}^{\large ^{\large \dagger} cos(144^{\circ})} 
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \big( - 0.8090 \big)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \alpha \; - \; 1.618 \, \beta
\\
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\large \text{Coulson Coefficient} \normalsize \; \Big( \text C_{k \, a^{\dagger}} \Big) \; \large \text{Formula: 1,3-butadiene}
\\
\begin{align*}
\text C_{1 , \, 1} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{4 + 1} } \; sin \, \Bigg( \frac{1 \cdot 1 \cdot \large \pi }{4 + 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \overbrace{sin \, \Bigg( \frac{ \large \pi }{5}}^{\large sin(36^{\circ})} \Bigg)
\\
= & \phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} \; \big( 0.5878 \big) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.371748 \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.372
\\
\text C_{1 , \, 2} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{4 \; + \; 1} } \; sin \, \Bigg( \frac{ 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \large \pi}{4 \; + \; 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \overbrace{sin \, \Bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi}{5}}^{\large sin(72^{\circ})} \Bigg)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \big( 0.9511 \big) \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.6015
\\
\text C_{1 , \, 3} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{4 \; + \; 1} } \; sin \, \Bigg( \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot \large \pi}{4 \; + \; 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \overbrace{sin \, \Bigg( \frac{3 \large \pi}{5}}^{\large sin(108^{\circ})} \Bigg)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \big( 0.9511 \big) \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.6015
\\
\text C_{1 , \, 4} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{4 \; + \; 1} } \; sin \, \Bigg( \frac{1 \cdot 4 \cdot \large \pi}{4 \; + \; 1} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \overbrace{sin \, \Bigg( \frac{4 \large \pi}{5}}^{\large sin(144^{\circ})} \Bigg)
\\
= & \phantom{..} \sqrt{ \frac{2}{5} } \; \big( 0.5878 \big) \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} 0.372
\\
\end{align*}$$


**Frost** and **Musulin** (1953) <b>[@frost_mnemonic_1953]</b> also developed a very useful graphical tool to construct [MO]{#Blk} energy diagrams for cyclic planar carbon chains (**Fig. 28**). Known as the **Frost Circle** or **Polygon** method it predicts $\large \pi$ [MO]{#Blk} energy levels for cyclic [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital arrays using an appropriately sided regular polygon (e.g. 4 [C]{#Blk} = square, 6 [C]{#Blk} = hexagon). Once the <u>polygon</u> is oriented correctly with one corner pointing directly downwards a <u>circle</u> is then circumscribed around it (Note: radius is $2 \beta$). Each [MO]{#Blk} energy level corresponds to a point on the circle that intersects a corner of the polygon, and a horizontal line passing through the centre of the circle represents the [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital energy level (i.e. $\alpha$ value). Any energy level lying directly on the $\alpha$ line corresponds to a <u>non-bonding</u> [MO]{#Blk}, while any energy level lying above or below the line is designated an anti-bonding or bonding [MO]{#Blk}, respectively. The lowest energy [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. $\alpha + 2 \beta$) at the bottom of the circle corresponds to in-phase [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals. For even numbered carbon chains there will be one anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} occupying the highest energy level (i.e. top vertex), whereas odd numbered carbon chains will have one or more pairs of anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} that share the same energy level (i.e. <b>degenerate</b> [MO]{#Blk}). This means that most [MO]{#Blk} come in <u>degenerate pairs</u>, with the notable exception of the lowest energy bonding [MO]{#Blk} and the highest energy anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} for even numbered cyclic carbon chains. An unfortunate product of <b>degenerate</b> energy states is that they are often derived as <u>complex</u> wave functions, which means the infamous imaginary number <b>&iscr;</b> appears in the energy calculations (e.g. <b>cyclopentadienyl</b> system). However, real coefficients eventually emerge by combining complex conjugate pairs using <b>Euler's</b> famous formula, which maps them to real <b>sine</b> and <b>cosine</b> functions. This is demonstrated below for the <b>cyclopentadienyl</b> system, where taking the normal <b>secular determinant</b> approach proves difficult.  



<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------ FIG 28 - HMOT Frost Circles ------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<a id="Fig28"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/HMO_Frost_Circles.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 28</u>: Frost Circles / Polygon Method.</b> This graphical tool draws a regular polygon (# sides = # carbons) within a circle. Points of contact between the polygon and circle represent the energy levels for the $\large \pi$-electron system. Each polygon is positioned such that one of its vertices comes in contact with the lowest point of the circle. Since the radius of the circle is $2\beta$ the corresponding ground state energy of the system will be $\alpha + 2 \beta$ (i.e. bottom energy level). The actual energy values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are empirically determined. The horizontal $\alpha$ line running through the centre of circle marks the boundary (i.e. non-bonding level) between <b>bonding</b> and <b>non-bonding</b> [MO]{#Blk}. Simple trigonometric ratios produced by the geometric shapes allow for easy calculations of the [MO]{#Blk} energy levels. The three molecules illustrated above highlight some of the important <b>aromatic</b> (<b>Huckle's rule: 4n + 2</b> $\large \pi$-electrons) features that make cyclic <b>polyenes</b> energetically stable. For example, the closed-shell character of the ground state wave function of <b>aromatic</b> molecules (e.g. cyclopentadienyl anion, benzene) results in a relatively wide energy gap between the <u>highest occupied</u> [MO]{#Blk} and the <u>lowest unoccupied</u> [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. [HOMO–LUMO gap]{#Blk}). This means valence electrons found in the [HOMO]{#Blk} have to interact with a more energetic photons in order to enter an excited state (i.e. &ldquo;<i>jump up</i>&rdquo; to the next highest energy level, which would be the [LUMO]{#Blk}). Conversely, the instability of an <b>anti-aromatic</b> state (<b>4n</b> = $\large \pi$-electrons</b>), as exemplified by <b>cyclobutadiene</b>, is due to its partially filled non-bonding orbitals. The unstable open-shell configuration, along with its notable structural strain causes **cyclobutadiene** to spontaneously distorts its own geometry resulting in bond-length alternations (i.e. takes on a rectangular geometry).<b>[@dewar_self-consistent_1965; @reeves_possible_1969; @borden_potential_1978; @wu_is_2012]</b>  

</div>

<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


To really appreciate the **Polygon** method consider the following **secular determinant** calculation for the **cyclopentadienyl** $\large \pi$-electron system, which is similar to the **Allyl** system in that it has three different chemical &ldquo;<i>species</i>&rdquo;, including: (i) a <b>cation</b> ($4 \large \pi$-electrons: [[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>]<sup>+</sup>), (ii) a <b>radical</b> ($5 \large \pi$-electrons: [[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>]<sup>&sdot;</sup>), and an <b>anion</b> ($6 \large \pi$-electrons: [[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>]<sup>-</sup>). The actual <b>cyclopentadiene</b> molecule itself has five conjugated [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals, with four of them bearing only a single electron, which is typically depicted in **Lewis** structures. The variable number of electrons that occupy the remaining [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital essentially defines the &ldquo;<i>species</i>&rdquo; of this five carbon system. Although it is only one more carbon atom than <b>cyclobutadiene</b>, its <b>secular determinant</b> is a bit more laborious to solve (i.e. five roots).  

<br>

$$\\
\begin{align*}
0 \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{ \left| \begin{array}
\\
x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1
\\
1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1
\\
1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x
\\
\end{array} \right| }^{\large |det|} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} x
\overbrace{ \left| \begin{array}
\\
x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x
\\
\end{array} \right|}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^*} \; - \; 1 \overbrace{ \left| \begin{array}
\\
1 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1
\\
1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x
\\
\end{array} \right|}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\dagger}} \; + \; 1 \overbrace{ \left| \begin{array}
\\
1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x & \phantom{.} 1
\\
0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1 & \phantom{.} x
\\
1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 1
\\
\end{array} \right|}^{\large \text M_{(1,5)}^{\ddagger}}
\\
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.}
x \left[ \, x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
x & 1 & 0 \\
1 & x & 1 \\
0 & 1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{**}} \; - \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
1 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & x & 1 \\
0 & 1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{**}} \; \right] \; - \; 1 \left[ \, 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|ccc|}
x & 1 & 0 \\
1 & x & 1 \\
0 & 1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{\dagger \dagger}} \; - \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & x & 1 \\
1 & 1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\Large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\dagger \dagger}} \; \right]
\\
& \phantom{...} + \; 1 \left[ \, 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
1 & x & 1 \\
0 & 1 & x \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{\ddagger \ddagger}} \; - \; x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & x & 1 \\
0 & 1 & x \\
1 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\ddagger \ddagger}}
\; + \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & x \\
1 & 0 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,3)}^{\ddagger \ddagger}} 
\; \right]
\\
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} x \left[ \, x \cdot \Bigg[ x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
x & 1 \\
1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{***}} \; - \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
1 & 1 \\
0 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{***}} \; \Bigg] \; - \; 1 \cdot \Bigg[ 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
x & 1 \\
1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{***}} \; - \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 \\
0 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{***}} \; \Bigg] \; \right]
\\
& \phantom{...} - \; 1 \left[ \, 1 \cdot \Bigg[ x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
x & 1 \\
1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{\dagger \dagger \dagger}} \; - \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
1 & 1 \\
0 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\dagger \dagger \dagger}} \; \Bigg] \; - \; 1 \cdot \Bigg[ -1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 \\
1 & x \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\dagger \dagger \dagger}} \; \Bigg] \; \right]
\\
& \phantom{...} + \; 1 \left[ \, 1 \cdot \Bigg[ 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
1 & x \\
0 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,1)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; - \; x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & x \\
0 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; + \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,3)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; \Bigg] \right.
\\
& \phantom{...} - \; x \, \left. \Bigg[ - x \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & x \\
1 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; + \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,3)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; \Bigg] \; + \; 1 \; \Bigg[ - 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & x \\
1 & 1 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,2)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \; + \; 1 \cdot \overbrace{\begin{array}{|c|}
0 & 0 \\
1 & 0 \\
\end{array}}^{\large \text M_{(1,3)}^{\ddagger \ddagger \ddagger}} \Bigg] \; \right]
\\
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} x \Bigg[ x \bigg[ x(x^2 \; - \; 1) \; - \; 1(x) \bigg] \; - \; 1 \bigg[ x^2 \; - \; 1 \bigg] \Bigg] \; - \; 1 \Bigg[ 1 \bigg[ x(x^2 \; - \; 1) \; - \; 1 (x) \; - \; 1 \bigg] \Bigg] 
\\
& \phantom{..} + \; 1 \Bigg[ 1 \bigg[ 1 \bigg] \; - \; x \bigg[ x^2 \; - \; 1 \bigg] \; + \; 1 \bigg[ x \bigg] \Bigg]
\\[10px]
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} (x^5 \; - \; 3x^3 \; + \; x) \; - \; ( x^3 \; + \; 2x \; + \; 1) \; + \; (1 \; - \; x^3 \; + \; 2x)
\\[10px]
0 \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} x^5 \; - \; 5x^3 \; + \; 5x \; + \; 2
\\
\end{align*}$$

<br>

A **secular determinant** described by a fifth-degree polynomial has five <u>roots</u>, each corresponding to a specific energy level. One approach to finding these multiple roots is to carry out <b><a class="one" href="https://www.wtamu.edu/academic/anns/mps/math/mathlab/col_algebra/col_alg_tut37_syndiv.htm" target="_blank" title="Go to Virtual Math Lab">synthetic division</a></b> on the polynomial. This method is similar to long division, but far more simpler to carry out. According to the <b><a class="one" href="https://matterofmath.com/algebra/rational-root-theorem/" target="_blank" title="Go to MatterOfMath">Rational Root Theorem</a></b>, a logical candidate to start the division process would be the positive or negative value of the actual remainder (i.e. $x = \pm \frac{p}{q} = \pm 2$, where $p$ = remainder constant, and $q$ = coefficient of highest order term).  

<br>

$$\\
\large \text{Synthetic Division of}
\\
\large \text{Cyclopentadiene Secular Determinant}
\\[15px]
x^5 \normalsize \; - \; 5x^3 \; + \; 5x \; + \; 2 \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \overbrace{x^5 \; + \; 0x^4 \; - \; 5x^3 \; + \; 0x^2 \; + \; 5x \; + \; 2}^{\large \underline{6 \, term} \; \text{Polynomial}}
\\[20px]
\begin{align*}
& \phantom{...........................} \overbrace{5^{th} \; \phantom{..} 4^{th} \; \phantom{...} 3^{rd} \; \phantom{..} 2^{nd} \; \phantom{.} \, 1^{st} \; \phantom{..} rem.}^{\large \text{coefficients of} \; \underline{6 \, term} \; \text{Polynomial}}
\\
& \left.
\begin{array}
\\
\text{Potential Root} \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} - 2
\\
\end{array} \right.
\left. \begin{array}{|c}
\\
1 & \phantom{.} 0 & \, - 5 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{..} 5 & \phantom{...} 2
\\
1 & \; - 2 & \phantom{..} \; 4 & \phantom{.} \, 2 & - 4 & \phantom{.} -2
\\ \hline
\end{array}
\right.
\\
& \phantom{..........................} \, \underbrace{1 \phantom{..} \, - 2 \phantom{..} \, - 1 \phantom{...} \, 2 \phantom{...} \; \; 1}_{\text{coefficients for 5 term Polynomial}} \phantom{.} \; \underbrace{0}_{^* \text{remainder}}
\end{align*}
\\
\overbrace{(x \; + \; 2)}^{ \; \, \Huge \checkmark \\ \; \text{root}} \, \overbrace{(x^4 \; - \; 2x^3 \; - \; x^2 \; + \; 2x \; + \; 1)}^{new \; \underline{5 \, term} \; \text{Polynomial}} \; = \; 0
\\$$


Unfortunately the above calculation leaves us with a 4<sup>th</sup> degree polynomial that is not readily amenable to the same mathematical treatment (Note: there are <b><a class="one" href="https://www.emathhelp.net/calculators/algebra-2/polynomial-roots-calculator/" target="_blank" title="Go to eMathHelp">polynomial calculators</a></b> available on line). Nevertheless the new polynomial can be re-written as the <u>square</u> of a <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/quadratic-equation.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">quadratic equation</a></b>, with the latter being easily dealt with using the familiar <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/completing-square.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">completing the squares</a></b> technique.  


$$\\
\large \text{Complete the Square}
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
x^4 \; - \; 2x^3 \; - \; x^2 \; + \; 2x \; + \; 1 \; = &
\phantom{..} (x^2 \; + \; k \, x \; + \; \ell) (x^2 \; + \; m \, x \; + \; n)
\\
\; = & \phantom{..} (x^2 \; + \; k \, x \; + \; \ell)^2 \phantom{...} \Longleftarrow \text{where} \; k = m \; \text{and} \; \ell = n
\\[10px]
\large \text{Expand} & \; \large \text{Squared Polynomial:}
\\
(x^2 \; + \; kx \; + \; \ell)^2 \; = &
\; x^4 \; + \; 2 k x^3 \; + \; k^2 x^2 \; + \; 2 \ell x^2 \; + \; 2 k \ell x \; + \; \ell^2
\\
= & \; x^4 \; + \; 2 k x^3 \; + \; ( k^2 \; + \; 2 \ell ) x^2 \; + \; 2 k \ell x \; + \; \ell^2
\end{align*}
\\[15px]
x^4 \; - \; \overbrace{2x^3}^{\large *} \; - \; x^2 \; + \; \overbrace{2x}^{\large **} \; + \; 1 \phantom{..} = \phantom{..} x^4 \; + \; \overbrace{2 k x^3}^{\large *} \; + \; ( k^2 \; + \; 2 \ell ) x^2 \; + \; \overbrace{2 k \ell x}^{\large **} \; + \; \ell^2
\\[5px]
\require{enclose} \enclose{circle}{1} \phantom{..} 2 k x^3 \; = \; - 2 x^3 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} 2 k \; = \; - 2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} k \; = \; - 1^{\large ^\dagger}
\\
\require{enclose} \enclose{circle}{2} \phantom{..} 2 \overbrace{ k }^{\dagger} \ell x \; = \; 2 x \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} 2(-1) \ell \; = \; 2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \ell \; = \; - 1
\\[10px]
(x^2 \; + \; kx \; + \; \ell)^2 \; = \; \overbrace{(x^2 \; - \; x \; -\; 1)}^{\text{2}^{nd} \, \text{order = 2 roots}} \, ^{\large 2{^\ddagger}} \phantom{...} \Huge \checkmark \normalsize \; \Longleftarrow \phantom{..} \text{Total of 4 Roots}^{\ddagger}$$


$$\\
\large \text{Quadratic Equation:} \normalsize \phantom{...} x \; = \; \frac{-b \; \pm \; \sqrt{b^2 \; - \; 4ac}}{2a}
\\
a \; = \; 1 , \phantom{...} b \; = \; -1 , \phantom{...} c \; = \; -1
\\[5px]
\left. \begin{array}
& \large x \; = \; \frac{1 \, \pm \, \sqrt{( - 1)^2 \; - \; 4 (1)( - 1)}}{2(1)} \; = \; \frac{ 1 \, \pm \, \sqrt{5}}{2}
\\
\end{array} \right] \; \text{Two pair}
\\[5px]
\begin{align*}
& x \; = \; \overbrace{ \frac{\alpha - \text E_{\large \pi}}{\beta}}^{\text{Huckel's} \\ \, x \, \text{value}} \; = \; - 2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_1} \; = \; \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta
\\
& x \; = \; \frac{1 \, - \, \sqrt{5}}{2} \; = \; \frac{\alpha - \text E_{\large \pi}}{\beta} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_2} \; = \; \text E_{\large \pi_3} \; = \; \alpha \; + \; 0.61803 \, \beta
\\
& x \; = \; \frac{1 \, + \, \sqrt{5}}{2} \; = \; \frac{\alpha - \text E_{\large \pi}}{\beta} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_4} \; = \; \text E_{\large \pi_5} \; = \; \alpha \; - \; 1.618 \, \beta
\end{align*}
\\$$


When the **Polygon** method is applied to the same problem it quickly becomes apparent why this geometric tool is so useful for calculating [MO]{#Blk} energy levels.  


$$\\
\large \text{Frost Circles / Polygon Method}
\\
\Big[ \, \text{Note:} \phantom{.} sin \, (18^{\circ}) \; = \; 0.30902, \phantom{..} sin \, (30^{\circ}) \; = \; 0.5, \phantom{..} sin \, (54^{\circ}) \; = \; 0.80902, \phantom{..} sin \, (90^{\circ}) \; = \; 1 \, \Big]
\\
\large \text{Let} \normalsize \; z_{\pi} \; = \; \text{unknown} \; \beta \; \text{value (Fig. 26)} 
\\[15px]
\begin{align*}
\large 1. \phantom{.} \text{Cyclopentadiene} \phantom{..} &
\\
z_{\large \pi_2} \; = \; z_{\large \pi_3} \; = &
\phantom{..} 2 \beta \, (0.30902) \; = \; 0.618 \, \beta
\\
z_{\large \pi_4}^* \; = \; z_{\large \pi_5}^* \; = &
\; - 2 \beta \, (0.80902) \normalsize \; = \; - 1.618 \, \beta
\\[5px]
\text E_{\large \pi_1} \; = & \phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta
\\
\text E_{\large \pi_2} \; = \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_3} \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta
\\
\text E_{\large \pi_4}^* \; = \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_5}^* \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; - \; 1.618 \beta
\\[5px]
\large 2. \phantom{.} \text{Benzene} \; (\text C_6 \text H_6) \phantom{..} \; &
\\
z_{\large \pi_2} \; = \; z_{\large \pi_3} \; = &
\phantom{..} 2 \beta \, (0.5) \; = \; \beta
\\
z_{\large \pi_4}^* \; = \; z_{\large \pi_5}^* \; = &
\; - \beta
\\
z_{\large \pi_6}^* \; = \; - 2 \beta \phantom{..} &
\\[5px]
\text E_{\large \pi_1} \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta
\\
\text E_{\large \pi_2} \; = \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_3} \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; + \; \beta
\\
\text E_{\large \pi_4}^* \; = \phantom{..} \text E_{\large \pi_5}^* \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; - \; \beta
\\
\text E_{\large \pi_6}^* \; = &
\phantom{..} \alpha \; - \; 2 \beta
\end{align*}
\\$$


Having calculated the energy levels for three cyclic hydrocarbons (**Fig. 28**) one can now determine the relative <u>stability</u> conferred by their respective conjugated $\large \pi$-electron systems (i.e. <b>Delocalization Energy</b>, or <b>DE</b>). As shown below the <b>DE</b> calculation is made using a hypothetical <u>localized</u> $\large \pi$-bond system as a control. For example, <b>cyclobutadiene</b>, which according to its **Lewis** structure has two localized $\large \pi$ bonds, shows <u>no increase</u> in energy stability when compared to a localized $\large \pi$-bonding system (i.e. 2 ethylene molecules serves as <u>reference</u>). This is readily apparent from its [MO]{#Blk} energy diagram (**Fig. 28**), which shows two degenerate non-bonding [MO]{#Blk} each containing a single electron (i.e. forming a di-radical). The lone electron pair occupies a single bonding [MO]{#Blk}. <b>Huckel</b> classified cyclic hydrocarbons, like <b>cyclobutadiene</b>, that contain <b>4n</b> $\large \pi$-electrons as <b>anti-aromatic</b>, and those with <b>4n + 2</b> $\large \pi$-electrons <b>aromatic</b> (i.e. <b>Huckel's rule</b>).<b>[@huckel_quantentheoretische_1931; @huckel_quanstentheoretische_1931; @huckel_quantentheoretische_1932]</b> **Benzene**, the prototypical **aromatic** molecule, is more chemically stable than its saturated counterparts (e.g. resists typical **alkene** addition reactions) due to the increased stability conferred by its electronic structure. Its [MO]{#Blk} energy diagram clearly shows three electron pairs occupying three <u>low energy</u> bonding [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. below the &alpha; line), while its high energy anti-bonding orbitals remain empty. Similar to <b>benzene</b> the <b>cyclopentadienyl anion</b> is also <b>aromatic</b>, and as a result quite chemically stable when compared to other carbo-anions. Overall each ring system shown in **Fig. 28** has at least one pair of <u>degenerate</u> [MO]{#Blk}, which is a consequence of their high order rotational <u>symmetry</u>. As mentioned previously the concept of orbital symmetry has important consequences for the reactivity of chemical groups. For example the degeneracy of <b>benzene</b> is a product of its molecular symmetry because the energy of one electron [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals are a product of their spatial environment. The high degree of rotational symmetry of <b>benzene</b> (i.e. six fold rotational axis passing perpendicular through the centre of the ring generates rotations of 60&deg;) allows each [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital to occupy different orientations within the same spatial environment (i.e. rotate it 60&deg; within the plane of the molecule produces an identical molecule). This means electrons are subjected to the same potential energy (i.e. degenerate) when occupying these different positions. Having no preferential rotational orientation means the six $\large \pi$-electron orbitals are delocalized across <u>equivalent</u> atoms and thus share the <u>same</u> energy at each of these positions.  


$$\\
\large \text{Delocalization Energy (DE)}
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
& \large 1. \; \text{Cyclobutadiene:}  \; ( \text C_4 \text H_4) \normalsize \phantom{..} (4 \; \large \pi \normalsize \, e^- \; \text{system} )
\\[5px]
& \text E_{(\text C_4 \text H_4)} \; = \phantom{..} 2(\alpha \; + \; 2 \beta) \; + \; 2 \alpha \; = \; 4 \alpha \; + \; 4 \beta
\\
& \text E_{(ref)} \; = \phantom{.} \text E_{2 [ \text C \; = \; \text C \large]} \; = \; 2(2 \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta) \; = \; 4 \alpha \; + \; 4 \beta
\\[5px]
& \text{DE}_{\large \pi} \; = \phantom{.} (4 \alpha \; + \; 4 \beta) \; - \; (4 \alpha \; + \; 4 \beta) \; = \; 0
\\[10px]
& \large \text{2.1 Cyclopentadiene Cation:} \; \big[ \text C_5 \text H_5 \big]^{\, +} \normalsize \phantom{..} (4 \, \large \pi \normalsize \; e^- \; \text{system})
\\[5px]
& \text E_{ (\text C_5^{\phantom{.}} \text H_5^{\, +})} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{ 2(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_2}} \, + \, \overbrace{2(\alpha \; + \; 2 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_1}} \; = \; 4 \alpha \; + \; 5.236 \beta
\\
& \text E_{(ref.)} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{2 \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta}^{\large \text{Ethylene} \\ \; \; \text{(C=C)}} \; + \; \overbrace{2(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large \text {2 E}_{\large \pi_2}} \; = \; 4 \alpha \; + \; 3.236 \beta
\\[5px]
& \text{DE} \; = \phantom{.} (4 \alpha \; + \; 5.236 \beta) \; - \; (4 \alpha \; + \; 3.236 \beta) \; = \; 2 \beta
\\[10px]
& \large \text{2.2 Cyclopentadiene Radical:} \; \big[ \text C_5 \text H_5 \big]^{\, \Large \cdot} \normalsize \phantom{..} (5 \, \large \pi \normalsize \; e^- \; \text{system})
\\
& \text E_{(\text C_5^{\phantom{.}} \text H_6^{\,})} \normalsize \; = \phantom{..} \overbrace{3(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_2} \; + \; 1 \text E_{\pi_3}} \, + \, \overbrace{2(\alpha \; + \; 2 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_1}} \; = \; 5 \alpha \; + \; 5.854 \beta
\\
& \text E_{(ref.)} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{2 \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta}^{\large \text{Ethylene} \\ \; \; \text{(C=C)}} \; + \; \overbrace{3(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large \text{3 E}_{\large \pi_2}} \; = \; 5 \alpha \; + \; 3.854 \beta
\\[5px]
& \text{DE} \; = \phantom{.} (5 \alpha \; + \; 5.854 \beta) \; - \; (5 \alpha \; + \; 3.854 \beta) \; = \; 2 \beta
\\[10px]
& \large \text{2.3 Cyclopentadiene Anion:} \; \big[ \text C_5^{\phantom{.}} \text H_5^{\,} \big]^- \normalsize \phantom{..} (6 \, \large \pi \normalsize \; e^- \; \text{system})
\\
& \text E_{(\text C_5^{\phantom{.}} \text H_5^-)} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{ 4(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_2} \; + \; 2 \text E_{\large \pi_3}} \, + \, \overbrace{2(\alpha \; + \; 2 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_1}} \; = \; 6 \alpha \; + \; 6.472 \beta
\\
& \text E_{(ref.)} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{2 \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta}^{\large \text{Ethylene} \\ \; \; \text{(C=C)}} \; + \; \overbrace{4(\alpha \; + \; 0.618 \beta)}^{\large \text {4 E}_{\large \pi_2}} \; = \; 6 \alpha \; + \; 4.472 \beta
\\[5px]
& \text{DE} \; = \phantom{.} (6 \alpha \; + \; 6.472 \beta) \; - \; (6 \alpha \; + \; 4.472 \beta) \; = \; 2 \beta
\\[10px]
& \large 3. \; \text{Benzene:} \, (\text C_6 \text H_6) \normalsize \phantom{..} (6 \, \large \pi \normalsize \; e^- \; \text{system})
\\[5px]
& \text E_{(\text C_6^{\phantom{.}} \text H_6^{\phantom{.}})} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{4(\alpha \; + \; \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_2} \; + \; 2 \text E_{\large \pi_3}} \, + \, \overbrace{2(\alpha \; + \; 2 \beta)}^{\large 2 \text E_{\large \pi_1}} \; = \; 6 \alpha \; + \; 8 \beta
\\
& \text E_{(ref.)} \; = \phantom{.} \overbrace{3( 2 \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta)}^{\large 3 \, \text{Ethylene} \\ \; \; \; \text{(C=C)}} \; = \; 6 \alpha \; + \; 6 \beta
\\[5px]
& \text{DE} \; = \phantom{.} (6 \alpha \; + \; 8 \beta) \; - \; (6 \alpha \; + \; 6 \beta) \; = \; 2 \beta
\end{align*}
\\$$


**Coulson** (1940) <b>[@coulson_calculation_1940]</b> also introduced a formula for calculating $\large \pi$-electron energy levels and coefficients for unbranched cyclic <b>polyenes</b>. As shown below the energy formula is easy to implement for both odd and even numbered cyclic <b>polyenes</b> (e.g. <b>cyclopentadienyl</b> and <b>benzene</b>).  


$$\\
\large \text{1. Coulson's Energy Formula for Cyclic Polyenes}
\\[10px]
k^{th} \normalsize \; = \, \large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \, \text{MO index}, \phantom{..} j^{th} \, = \, \text{atomic index}, \phantom{..} \alpha \, = \, \text{Coulomb Integral}
\\
\beta \, = \, \text{Resonance Integral}, \phantom{..} N \, = \, \# \, \text{C atoms}
\\[10px]
\large \text E_{\large \pi_k} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \beta \; cos \Bigg(\frac{2 \large \pi \; k}{N} \Bigg)
\\[10px]
k = 0, \; \pm 1, \; \pm 2 \phantom{..} ....\frac{N}{2} \phantom{.} \text{for even #} \; N \phantom{..} ....\frac{N-1}{2} \phantom{.} \text{for odd #} \; N
\\$$


$$\\
\big[ \, \text{Note: Molecular Orbitals} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{anti-bonding = MO*, bonding = MO} \, \big]
\\
\begin{align*}
& \text{e.g. Cyclopentadienyl System} \; \big[ \text C_5 \text H_5 \big]
\\
& \large N \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 5 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0, \; \pm 1, \; \pm 2 \, \Big] \; \text{Note: two degenerate pairs}
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; 0 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..}
\large \text E_{\text o} \normalsize  \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot 0}{5} \bigg)}^{\large cos(0) \; = \; 1} \; = \; \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{MO}
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; \pm 1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text E_{\pm 1} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot (\pm 1)}{5} \bigg)}^{ \large cos(\pm 72^{\circ}) \; = \; 0.309} \; = \; \alpha \; + \; 0.618 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{pair of MO} 
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; \pm 2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text E_{\pm 2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot (\pm 2)}{5} \bigg)}^{ \large cos(\pm 144^{\circ}) \; = \; -0.809} \; = \; \alpha \; - \; 1.618 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{pair of MO*} 
\\[10px]
& \text{e.g. Benzene} \; \big[ \text C_6 \text H_6 \big]
\\
& \large N \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 6 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0, \; \pm 1, \; \pm 2 \; +3 \, \Big] \; \text{Note: two degenerate pairs}
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; 0 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..}
\large \text E_{\text o} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot 0}{6} \bigg)}^{\large cos(0) \; = \; 1} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{MO}
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; \pm 1 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text E_{(\pm 1)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot (\pm 1)}{6} \bigg)}^{ \large cos(\pm 60^{\circ}) \; = \; 0.5} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 1 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{pair of MO} 
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; \pm 2 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text E_{(\pm 2)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot (\pm 2)}{6} \bigg)}^{ \large cos(\pm 120^{\circ}) \; = \; -0.5} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; - \; 1 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{pair of MO*} 
\\
& \large k \normalsize \; = \; + 3 \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \large \text E_{(+3)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \; + \; 2 \, \beta \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \pi \cdot (3)}{6} \bigg)}^{ \large cos(\pm 180^{\text o}) \; = \; -1} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \alpha \normalsize \; - \; 2 \, \beta \; \Bigg] \; \text{MO*} 
\\
\end{align*}$$


**Coulson's** coefficient formula is based on the **Bloch function** (i.e. wave function subjected to periodic modulation). According to **Felix Bloch's** theorem (1929)<b>[@bloch_uber_1929]</b> a wave function that experiences <u>periodic</u> changes in <u>potential energy</u> (e.g. electron moving within a periodic crystal lattice) takes the form of a <u>plane wave</u> (i.e. represented by the exponential function) and a periodic amplitude function. This periodic change in the electron's potential satisfies the inherent translational symmetry of cyclic **polyenes** (i.e. electrons moving between repeating carbon atoms within a well defined ring structure). As a consequence the complicated $N \times N$ **secular determinant** can be <u>replaced</u> by a single one dimensional equation, which takes the following mathematical form:  


$$\\
\large \text{Bloch Function}
\\
\Big [ \, \phantom{.} \text C \normalsize \; = \; \text{constant} , \phantom{.} \large a \normalsize  \; = \; \text{lattice vector} , \phantom{.} \large k \normalsize \; = \; \text{wave vector}, \phantom{.} \large e \normalsize \; = \; \text{base of the natural log} \, \Big]
\\
\large \text C \cdot \large \overbrace{\psi \normalsize (x)}^{ \phantom{..} \text{wave} \\ \text{function}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \psi \normalsize ( x \; + \; s \, a ) \; \bigg\} \; \text{where} \; s \; = \; 0 , \, 1 , \, 2 \; .... \phantom{.} s \in \mathbb Z
\\
\large \psi \normalsize ( x \; + \; s \, a ) \; = \; \overbrace{\large e^{ika}}^{\large \text{ phase} \\ \large \text{ factor}} \, \large \psi \normalsize (x)$$


The exponential function in the above expression is the phase factor, which accounts for each translational event of the electron (i.e. moving between $j^{th}$ atomic sites), be it clockwise or counter-clockwise. The <b>lattice vector</b> variable is a vector that joins any two lattice <u>points</u>. For a crystal lattice, which is a super-structure of periodically arranged atoms, the so called **primitive lattice vector** is a set of distance vectors that characterize the three dimensional crystal medium. Similarly we can make the assumption that the periodically arranged carbon atoms within a **polyene** structure approximates a simple lattice with a characteristic translational symmetry (i.e. shifting between atoms by a defined amount, or **lattice constant**). The **wave vector**, or **k**-vector in the above formula, is a vector that characterizes the spatial periodicity and direction of the wave-like electron as it moves through its medium.  


$$\\
\large \text{2. Coulson's Coefficient Formula for Cyclic Polyenes}
\\
k^{th} \; = \, \large \psi_{\pi} \normalsize \, \text{MO index} , \phantom{.} j^{th} \, = \, \text{atomic index} , \phantom{.} N \, = \, \text{# C atoms}
\\
\large i \normalsize \; = \; \text{imaginary #} , \phantom{.} \large e \normalsize \, = \, \text{base of natural log}
\\[15px]
\overbrace{\large e^{ix} \normalsize \; = \; cos (x) \; + \; \large i \normalsize \, sin(x) \phantom{...} \large | \normalsize \phantom{...} \large e^{ - ix} \normalsize \; = \; cos (x) \; - \; \large i \normalsize \, sin(x)}^{\large \text{Euler's Formula}}$$


$$\\
\large \text C_{j \, k} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt N}}^{\large \text{Norm.} \\ \large \, \text{factor}} \; \overbrace{e^{\large i \normalsize \Big( \large \frac{2 \pi \normalsize j \, k}{N} \Big)}}^{\large \, \text{phase} \\ \large \, \text{factor}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt N} \Bigg[ \, \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize j \, k }{N} \bigg)}^{\large \text{Coefficient #1}} \; + \; \large i \normalsize \, \overbrace{sin \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize j \, k }{N}\bigg)}^{\large \text{Coefficient #2}} \, \Bigg]
\\[10px]
\large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0 , \; \pm 1 , \; \pm 2 , \phantom{..} ....\frac{N}{2} \phantom{.} \text{for even #} \; N \phantom{..} ....\frac{N-1}{2} \phantom{.} \text{for odd #} \; N
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
& \large \text{when:} \normalsize \phantom{.} k \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{ 0 , \, 1 , \, 2 , \, ...}^{\large \text{single energy} \\ \large \phantom{......} \text{states}} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{Normalization factor} \; = \; \frac{1}{\sqrt N}
\\
& \large \text{when:} \normalsize \phantom{.} k \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\pm 1 , \, \pm 2 , \, ...}^{\large \text{degenerate} \\ \large \phantom{....} \, \text{pairs}} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text{Normalization factor} \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{N}}
\end{align*}
\\$$


The exponential term in **Coulson's** coefficient formula is the corresponding **phase factor** from **Bloch's function**. It governs the phase changes in the $\large \pi$-electron wave function as it moves around the ring of atoms. Part of the **phase factor** is the **wave vector** <b><i>k</i></b>. This quantum number denotes the <u>bonding</u> (i.e. positive integer) or <u>anti-bonding</u> (i.e. negative integer) character of the [MO]{#Blk}. Of course the exponential wave function is properly normalized (i.e. $N^{-1/2}$) across all $N$ carbon sites. Also the periodicity of the electron's movement within the molecule provides the necessary boundary conditions that convert the continuous standing wave function into a discrete quantized value. This periodicity is defined by the $L$ength of the ring structure (i.e. $\psi_{(x)} = \psi_{(x + L)}$), which restricts the <b>wave vector</b> ($k$) to discrete integer values. Fortunately the <b>&iscr;</b>maginary component of the formula (<b>&iscr;</b>) only defines the <u>phase shift</u> and <u>does not</u> affect the <u>magnitude</u> of the orbital coefficients. This means the formula provides us with <u>two coefficient values for each degenerate energy level</u> (i.e. opposite signs for opposite phase shifts) and only one coefficient for non-degenerate energy levels (i.e. where: $sin(2 \large \pi \normalsize) = 0$). For example, the <u>aromatic</u> $6 \large \pi \normalsize e^-$ <b>cyclopentadienyl anion</b> &ldquo;<i>species</i>&rdquo; (i.e. $\text{Huckel's rule:} \; 4n + 2 = 6$ where $n = 1$) would have the following coefficient values for each of its bonding and anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk}:  


$$\\
\large \text{Coulson's Coefficient: Cyclopentadienyl anion} \; \big[ \text C_5 \text H_5 \big]^- 
\\[5px]
k^{th} \; = \, \large \psi_{\large \pi} \normalsize \, \text{MO index} , \phantom{..} j^{th} \, = \, \text{atomic index} , \phantom{..} N \, = \, \text{# carbon atoms}
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
\large 1. \normalsize \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(k \, = \, 0)} & \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi_{\large \pi_1} \normalsize \; (\text{lowest energy bonding MO})
\\
\text C_{1} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \text C_{2} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text C_{3} \phantom{.} = \text C_{4} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text C_{5} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt 5} \overbrace{cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot j \cdot 0 }{5}}^{\large cos(0) \, = \, 1} \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt 5}
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large 2. \normalsize \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(k \, = \, +1)} & \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi_{\large \pi_2} \normalsize \; (\text{degenerate bonding MO})
\\[5px]
\text C_{1} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} \; cos \bigg(\frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot 1 \cdot 1}{5} \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (72^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.1954
\\
\text C_{2} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, \overbrace{cos \, (144^{\circ})}^{\large \text{multiples} \\ \phantom{...} \text{of} \; 72^{\circ}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.5117
\phantom{.....} \text C_{3} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (216^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.5117
\\
\text C_{4} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (288^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.1954 \phantom{.......} \; \text C_{5} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (360^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.6325
\end{align*}$$


$$\begin{align*}
\large 3. \normalsize \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(k \, = \, -1)} & \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi_{\large \pi_3} \normalsize \; (\text{degenerate bonding MO})
\\[5px]
\text C_{1} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (72^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.6015 \phantom{........} \text C_{2} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (144^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.3717 
\\
\text C_{3} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (216^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.3717 \phantom{....} \; \text C_{4} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (288^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.6015
\\
\text C_{5} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (360^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large 4. \normalsize \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(k \, = \, +2)} & \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi^*_{\large \pi_4} \normalsize \; (\text{degenerate anti-bonding MO})
\\[5px]
\large \text C_{1} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} \; cos \bigg( \frac{2 \large \pi \normalsize \cdot 1 \cdot 2 }{5} \bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (144^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.512
\\
\large \text C_{2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, \overbrace{cos \, (288^{\circ})}^{\large \text{multiples} \\ \phantom{...} \text{of} \; 144^{\circ}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.1954 \phantom{......} \large \text C_{3} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (432^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.1954
\\
\large \text C_{4} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (576^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.5117 \phantom{....} \large \text C_{5} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, cos \, (720^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.6325
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large 5. \phantom{.} \large \psi_{(k \, = \, -2)} & \normalsize \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \large \psi^*_{\large \pi_5} \normalsize \; (\text{degenerate anti-bonding MO})
\\
\large \text C_{1} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (144^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.3717 \phantom{......} \large \text C_{2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (288^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.6015
\\
\large \text C_{3} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (432^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.6015 \phantom{......} \large \text C_{4} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (576^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.3717
\\
\large \text C_{5} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} 0.632 \, sin \, (720^{\circ}) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0
\end{align*}$$


$$\\
\large \text{Set of coefficient weighted MO wave functions:}
\\
\begin{align*}
& \large \psi_{\large \pi_1} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{1}{\sqrt 5} \Big[ \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; + \; \large \phi_2 \normalsize \; + \; \large \phi_3 \normalsize \; + \; \large \phi_4 \normalsize \; + \; \large \phi_5 \normalsize \Big]
\\[5px]
& \large \psi_{\large \pi_2} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.1954 \, \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; - \; 0.5117 \, \large \phi_2 \normalsize \; - \; 0.5117 \, \large \phi_3 \normalsize \; + \; 0.1954 \, \large \phi_4 \normalsize \; + \; 0.6325 \, \large \phi_5
\\[5px]
& \large \psi_{\large \pi_3} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.6015 \, \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; + \; 0.3717 \, \large \phi_2 \normalsize \; - \; 0.3717 \, \large \phi_3 \normalsize \; - \; 0.6015 \, \large \phi_4
\\[5px]
& \large \psi_{\large \pi_4} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 0.5117 \, \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; + \; 0.1954 \, \large \phi_2 \normalsize \; + \; 0.1954 \, \large \phi_3 \normalsize \; - \; 0.5117 \, \large \phi_4 \normalsize \; + \; 0.6325 \, \large \phi_5
\\[5px]
& \large \psi_{\large \pi_5} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 0.3717 \, \large \phi_1 \normalsize \; - \; 0.6015 \, \large \phi_2 \normalsize \; + \; 0.6015 \, \large \phi_3 \normalsize \; - \; 0.3717 \, \large \phi_4
\end{align*}$$

<b><u>Figure 29</u>: Cyclopentadienyl System.</b> The relative size of each [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbital are shown proportional to the magnitudes of their coefficients. Only a select number of coefficients are shown while those not specified can be easily deduced by virtue of the molecule's symmetry. The [AO]{#Blk} phases are <u>symbolized</u> by either shading (e.g. black = + phase) or the sign ($\pm$) attached to the coefficient. The total $\large \pi$-bonding energy of the cyclic <b>anion</b> &ldquo;<i>species</i>&rdquo; is $6 \alpha + 6.472 \, \beta$, which has three pairs of $\large \pi$-electrons filling three bonding orbitals. The <b>aromatic</b> (<b>Huckel's Rule: 4n + 2 = 6</b>, with <b>n = 1</b>) closed shell configuration of [[C]{#Blk}<b><sub>5</sub></b>[H]{#Blue}<b><sub>5</sub></b>]<sup>-</sup> results in an increase in energy stability when compared to its open chain counterpart the <b>pentadienyl anion</b> (i.e. $6 \alpha + 5.464 \, \beta$). The <b>aromatic</b> property of this molecule widens the energy gap between the highest occupied [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. <b>HOMO</b>) and the lowest unoccupied [MO]{#Blk} (i.e. <b>LUMO</b>). This means more energetic photons are needed to excite valence electrons in order for them to make the quantum &ldquo;<i>leap</i>&rdquo; from <b>HOMO</b> to <b>LUMO</b>. Theoretically an infinitely large cyclic or open chain conjugated <b>polyene</b> would reduce the <b>HOMO-LUMO</b> gap to zero. Such a theoretical <b>polyene</b> would be analogous to a one dimensional metallic conductor. The alternating single and double bonds would essentially become equal in length creating a continuum of overlapping $\large \pi$-orbitals that would allow &ldquo;<i>free</i>&rdquo; flowing electrons. However, such a large <b>polyene</b> lattice is structurally unstable (i.e. <b>Peierls</b>—<b>Nabarro</b> stress or distortion).<b>[@peierls_size_1940; @nabarro_dislocations_1947; @lu_peierlsnabarro_2005]</b> Spontaneous periodic oscillations of the atomic positions break the uniformity of such an idealized $\large \pi$-electron medium. So in reality it would act more like a semiconductor (i.e. narrow band gap). Fortunately <b>doping</b> (i.e. introducing charge carriers) <b>polyenes</b> can create highly conductive materials.<b>[@shirakawa_synthesis_1977; @chiang_electrical_1977; @chiang_synthesis_1978]</b> In fact there is a considerable amount of research focused on creating new types of electronics (e.g. sensors, organic LEDs, PV cells) that exploit the semi-conducting properties of polymers that have large delocalized electron networks (e.g. films of polyacetylene).<b>[@swager_50th_2017; @miao_cyclic_2021]</b>  

</div>

<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>
<!------------------------------------------------------>


<a id="LCAOpi2"></a>
**[IV - 2. LCAO & Conjugated &pi; Bonds in Heteroatomic Systems]{#Blk}:** Most biomolecules that contain conjugated $\large \pi$-bonds are made up of [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}arbon as well as other elements, particularly [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}itrogen (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://www.rcsb.org/ligand/HEM" target="_blank" title="Go to RCSB-PDB">Heme</a></b> group of <b><a class="one" href="https://pdb101.rcsb.org/motm/41" target="_blank" title="Go to PDB-101">hemoglobin</a></b>)<b>[@perutz_structure_1960]</b> and [[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}xygen (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chebi/CHEBI:177831" target="_blank" title="Go to ChEBI">Furan fatty acids (FuFA)</a></b>).<b>[@okada_antioxidant_1990; @okada_hydroxyl_1996; @lemke_synthesis_2014; @chang_emerging_2025]</b> Wave equations that describe orbitals belonging to different elements must therefore account for the differences in the electron affinity (i.e. **electronegativity**) of these different elements. Fortunately this can be accomplished using existing **Huckel** [MO]{#Blk} treatments by simply adjusting the **Coulombic** ($\alpha$) and **Resonance** ($\beta$) integrals using dimensionless empirical parameters (i.e. scalar coefficients). As shown below the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are adjusted for a hetero-atom (**X**) with respect to the corresponding carbon (reference) values.  


$$\\
\large \alpha_{X} \; = \; \alpha_{\text C} \; + \; h_{X} \beta \phantom{......} \beta_{(\text C-X)} \; = \; k_X \beta_{(\text C - \text C)}
\\[5px]
\Big[ \, \text{Note:} \phantom{.} h_{\text X} \; \text{and} \phantom{.} k_X \; \text{are dimensionless empirical parameters} \, \Big]
\\[15px]
\left. \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline
\large \; \text{Atom} \; & \large \; h_X^{\dagger} \; & \large \; \text{Bond} \; & \large \; k_X^{\dagger} \;
\\[10px]
\hline {\phantom{......} \, - \stackrel{\Large ..}{\text N} \, = \\ \phantom{....} \, (\text{Pyridine})} & \large 0.5 & { \text C - \stackrel{\Large ..}{\text N} \, = \\ \text C = \stackrel{\Large ..}{\text N} - } & \large 1
\\[10px]
\hline {\phantom{......} \, -\stackrel{\Large ..}{\underset{\text{|}}{\text N}}- \\ \phantom{.....} (\text{Pyrrole})} & \large 1.5 & \text C \, - \stackrel{\Large ..}{\underset{\text{|}}{\text N}}- & \large 0.8
\\[10px]
\hline {\phantom{.....} \, -\overset{\Large ..}{\underset{\Huge ^{..}}{\text O}}- \\ \phantom{.....} (\text{Furan}) } & \large 2 & \text C - \overset{\Large ..}{\underset{\Huge ^{..}}{\text O}} \, - & \large 0.8
\\[10px]
\hline {\, = \overset{\Large ..}{\underset{\Huge ^{..}}{\text O}}} & \large 1 & \text C = \overset{\Large ..}{\underset{\Huge ^{..}}{\text O}} & \large 1
\\[10px]
\hline {\phantom{.....} -\text{CH}_3 \\ \phantom{.} (\text{Methyl Group})} & \large 2 & \text C \, - \text{CH}_3 & \large 0.7
\\ \hline \end{array} \right.
\\$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<b><sup>&dagger;</sup>Ref:[@streitwieser_molecular_1961; @streitwieser_molecular_1962]</b>

<!---- FIG 30 - HMO Heterocyclic Systems ----->
<!-------------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig30"></a>

<figure id="FRight350b">
![](images/HMO_Heterocyclic_molecules.jpg){width=275px}
<figcaption>
<b>Figure 30: Heterocyclic Molecules</b>
</figcaption>

<!-------------------------------------------->

The number of electrons a hetero-atom donates to a $\large \pi$ system depends on the nature of its bonding. For example, the [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} atom of **pyrrole** ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>4</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}, **Fig. 30**) has three of its five valence electron taking part in $\large \sigma$ covalent bonding (i.e. two [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and one [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}), and a lone pair of electrons occupying an unhybridized [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital that is perpendicular to the plane of the ring. Because of this geometry the lone pair of electrons interacts with the [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue} orbitals of the four carbon atoms resulting in an <b>aromatic</b> $\large \pi$-bonding system (i.e. delocalization energy stabilizes the structure). Chemically this means the lone pair is less likely to bond with [[H]{#SBlue}]{#strokeB}, which makes it a weak base (i.e. its <b><a class="one" href="https://chem.libretexts.org/Courses/Brevard_College/CHE_104%3A_Principles_of_Chemistry_II/07%3A_Acid_and_Base_Equilibria/7.12%3A_Relationship_between_Ka_Kb_pKa_and_pKb" target="_blank" title="Go to LibreTexts">conjugate acid</a></b> has a <i>pK</i><sub>a</sub> &approx; 0.4). However, in the case of the 6-member ring <b>pyridine</b> ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>5</sub>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}), the lone pair of electrons held by [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} do not interact with the $\large \pi$-bonding system, since they occupy a [[sp2]{#SBlue}]{#strokeB} hybridized orbital that lies within the plane of the ring (i.e. orthogonal to the $\large \pi$-bonding system). As a result there is only one electron residing within an unhybridized [2]{#Blk}[&pscr;]{#Blue} orbital that can take part in $\large \pi$-bonding. Although its an <b>aromatic</b> $\large \pi$-electron system like <b>pyrrole</b>, unlike the latter the lone pair of electrons of [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} can interact &ldquo;<i>freely</i>&rdquo; with other electron &ldquo;<i>loving</i>&rdquo; molecules (i.e. <b>electrophiles</b>). As a result <b>pyridine</b> is more basic than <b>pyrrole</b> (i.e. its <b><a class="one" href="https://chem.libretexts.org/Courses/Brevard_College/CHE_104%3A_Principles_of_Chemistry_II/07%3A_Acid_and_Base_Equilibria/7.12%3A_Relationship_between_Ka_Kb_pKa_and_pKb" target="_blank" title="Go to LibreTexts">conjugate acid</a></b> <i>pK</i><sub>a</sub> &approx; 5.25).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; To find the [MO]{#Blk} energies of a hetero-cyclic system the adjusted integrals need to be incorporated into the <b>secular equation</b>. For the <b>Coulomb integral</b> ($\alpha_X = \int \phi_X \, \hat H \, \phi_X d \text v$), which measures the electron-attracting ability of an atom, this means its value must be related to the <b><a class="one" href="#VBTen" target="_blank" title="Go to Valence Bond Theory Section">electronegativity</a></b> of the atom ($\chi_{_X}$). Specifically we would compare the two bonded atoms within a conjugated $\large \pi$-system (e.g. [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} and [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}) based on their differences in electronegativity (i.e. $\alpha_{_X} - \alpha_{_B} = c \, [\chi_{_X} - \chi_{_B}]$). This, in turn, would be incorporated into the energy equation using a dimensionless constant (i.e. $h_{_X}$) of $\beta$, with $\alpha_{_B}$ representing the reference carbon value (i.e. $\alpha_{_\text{C}}$).  


$$\\
\Big[ \large \text{Note:} \; \alpha_{_X} \normalsize \; = \; \text{hetero-atom coulomb integral}, \; \large \alpha_{_C} \normalsize \; = \; \text{reference carbon coulomb integral} \normalsize \Big]
\\
\large \alpha_{_\text X} \normalsize \; - \; \large \alpha_{_\text C} \normalsize \; = \; \large h_{_\text X} \large \beta_{_\text{C}} \normalsize \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \large \alpha_{_\text X} \normalsize \; = \; \large \alpha_{_\text C} \normalsize \; + \; \large h_{_\text X} \large \beta_{_\text{C}}
\\$$


Clearly the **Coulombic integral** is dependent on the <b><a class="one" href="#VBTen" target="_blank" title="Go to Valence Bond Theory Section">electronegativity</a></b> of the hetero-atom. As for the **Resonance integral**, which measures the attraction of a bond for valence electrons, the value of $\beta_{_\text{X-C}}$ is an empirical variable. Mathematically this relationship can be expressed as:  


$$\\
\large \beta_{_\text{(X-C)}} \normalsize \; = \; \large k_X \, \beta_{\text C}
\\$$


The tabulated $k_X$ values shown above represent some of the most common types of bonds found in biomolecules.<b>[@streitwieser_molecular_1961; @streitwieser_molecular_1962]</b> Of course the only way to see how hetero-atoms are accommodated by [Huckel's MO]{#Blk} theory is by example. Once again we can take a closer look at **pyrrole**.  


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\\
& \large 1. \; \text{Pyrrole:} \phantom{..} \alpha_{_{\text N}} \normalsize \; = \; \large \alpha \normalsize \; + \; \large 1.5 \, \beta , \phantom{..} \beta_{_{\text N}} \normalsize \; = \; \large 0.8 \, \beta
\\[5px]
\large |det| \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \large \left| \begin{array}
\\
\alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}}
\\
\phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
\phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \phantom{.} 0
\\
\phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}}
\\
\phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \phantom{.} 0
\\
\phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta_{_{\text N}} & \alpha_{_{\text N}} - \text E
\end{array} \right| \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large 0
\end{align*}$$


$$\begin{align*}
& \phantom{.........................} \Large \Big \Downarrow
\\[5px]
\large 0 \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \large \left| \begin{array}
\\
\alpha + 1.5 \beta - \text E & \phantom{.} 0.8 \beta & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0.8 \beta
\\
\phantom{.} 0.8 \beta & \alpha - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0
\\
\phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta & \alpha - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta & \phantom{.} 0
\\
\phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta & \alpha - \text E & \phantom{.} \beta
\\
\phantom{.} 0.8 \beta & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} 0 & \phantom{.} \beta & \alpha - \text E
\\
\end{array} \right| \end{align*}$$


$$\begin{align*}
& \phantom{.........................} \Large \Big \Downarrow
\\[5px]
& {\large \text{Recall: express energies relative to} \; \alpha \; \text{in units of} \; \beta}
\\
& \phantom{..................} \large x \normalsize \; = \; \large \frac{\alpha - \text E}{\beta}
\\[5px]
& \phantom{.........................} \Large \Big \Downarrow
\\[5px]
\large 0 \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \large \overbrace{\left| \begin{array}
\\
\phantom{..} x + 1.5 & \phantom{...} 0.8 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 0.8 \phantom{..}
\\
\phantom{..} 0.8 & \phantom{...} x & \phantom{...} 1 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 0 \phantom{..}
\\
\phantom{..} 0 & \phantom{...} 1 & \phantom{...} x & \phantom{...} 1 & \phantom{...} 0 \phantom{..}
\\
\phantom{..} 0 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 1 & \phantom{...} x & \phantom{...} 1 \phantom{..}
\\
\phantom{..} 0.8 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 0 & \phantom{...} 1 & \phantom{...} x \phantom{..}
\\
\end{array}
\right|}^{\Large \text{Hamiltonian Matrix}}
\\
\end{align*}
\\$$


The above **Hamiltonian matrix** can be algebraically expanded to produce the 5<sup>th</sup> order polynomial for **pyrrole** (Note: for brevity the detailed algebra derivation is not shown).  


$$\\
\large x^5 \normalsize \, + \, \large 1.5x^4 \normalsize \,- \, \large 4x^3 \normalsize \,- \, \large 4.5x^2 \normalsize \, + \, \large 3x \normalsize \, + \, \large 1.5 \normalsize \; = \; \large 0
\\$$


Finding the five roots to this characteristic polynomial, which represents the energies of the corresponding five [MO]{#Blk}, is not possible using general algebraic formulas. Instead chemists use symmetry arguments (i.e. **Group theory**) to generate new sets of wave functions known as **S**ymmetry **A**dapted **L**inear **C**ombinations, or **SALCs**.<b>[@streitwieser_molecular_1962]</b> Although this ingenious method greatly simplifies the problem (i.e. generates two matrix blocks: 3&times;3 and 2&times;2) we can instead turn to a computer program called <b><a class="one" href="https://ctom-ism2.github.io/hulis/index.shtml" target="_blank" title="Go to HuLis">HuLis</a></b> to carry out the calculations for **pyrrole**.<b>[@humbel_getting_2007; @hagebaum-reignier_huckel_2007; @HuLis_2008; @carissan_huckel-lewis_2008]</b> This free Java based program (Note: abbreviation of <b>Hu</b>ckel-<b>L</b>ew<b>is</b>) evaluates <b>Lewis resonance</b> structures using <b>Huckel</b> wave functions (**Fig. 31**).  


<!------------------------------------->
<!---- FIG 31 - HMO Pyrrole HuLis ----->
<!------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig31"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/Pyrrole_HuLis.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>
<b><u>Figure 31</u>: HuLis (Huckel-Lewis) analysis of Pyrrole.</b> Shown above is the detailed <b>Huckel</b> [MO]{#Blk} analysis of <b>pyrrole</b> using the free <b><a class="one" href="https://ctom-ism2.github.io/hulis/index.shtml" target="_blank" title="Go to HuLis">HuLis</a></b> program.<b>[@humbel_getting_2007; @hagebaum-reignier_huckel_2007; @HuLis_2008; @carissan_huckel-lewis_2008]</b>  The results are displayed in tabular form, including (among others): <b>(i)</b> the energies of each [MO]{#Blk} wave function; <b>(ii)</b> the total energy of the $6 \large \pi$-electron <b>pyrrole</b> system (i.e. $6 \alpha + 8.25 \beta$); <b>(iii)</b> orbital coefficients for each bonding and anti-bonding [MO]{#Blk} wave function; and <b>(iv)</b> the formal net charges associated with each atom of the lowest energy bonding [MO]{#Blk} ($\psi_{\pi_1}$). The analysis was carried out using well known <b>h<sub>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}</sub></b> and <b>k<sub>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}</sub></b> values.<b>[@streitwieser_molecular_1961; @streitwieser_molecular_1962]</b>  A localized **Lewis** resonance structure of **pyrrole** is also shown (bottom right). One of the interesting findings is the positive charge assigned to [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} and the negative charges assigned to the [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} atoms (i.e. creates a dipole moment). A high electron density value was also assigned to [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}, which makes sense given its relatively high electronegativity value (i.e. pulls electrons away from neighbouring atoms such as the $\large \sigma$ bonded [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom). So it would seem that the high electron density of [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} is off-set by its electron donating activity (i.e. lone pair donated to the delocalized $\large \pi$-electron system). The latter is of course responsible for the aromatic status of the molecule, which confers increased molecular stability. The theoretical <u>localized</u> valence charge assigned to [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} must simply represent the net electron activity of this molecule. The relatively electron &ldquo;rich&rdquo; carbon atoms can potentially act as nucleophiles during a chemical reaction (e.g. <u>substitution</u> of [[Cl]{#Olive}]{#strokeB} for [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}). Conversely the electron &ldquo;<i>poor</i>&rdquo; [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} can potentially act as a relatively weak proton acceptor (i.e. weak base).  

</div>


<a id="MOTah"></a>
<b>[&thinsp; 4.3.1 Approximating the Ground State Energy Level of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}ydrogen &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}:</b> Generating <u>exact</u> analytical solutions for the ground-state energy ([[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>o</sub></b>) of atoms and molecules with multiple electron-electron interactions is not possible (i.e. three body problem). Fortunately there are a number of <u>approximation methods</u> that are capable of estimating the ground state energy of a quantum system (e.g. Variational method, Perturbation theory). The **Variational Method** is particularly satisfying since it's a relatively straight forward way of estimating the ground state (i.e. upper bound) using wave functions.<b>[@griffiths_introduction_1994; @mcquarrie_physical_1997]</b> For example we known from previous discussions that [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>o</sub></b> can be expressed using the <b>Hamiltonian</b> operator:  


$$\tag{52}$$


$$\\
\large \hat H \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} = \text E_{\text o} \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o}
\\
\text{Integrate Density Function and Solve for} \; \text E_{\text o} 
\\
\int \psi^*_{\text o} \, \hat H \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} \, d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int \psi^*_{\text o} \, \text E_{\text o} \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} \, d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text E_{\text o} \int \psi^*_{\text o} \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} \, d \text v
\\
\large \text E_{\text o} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\int \psi^*_{\text o} \, \hat H \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} \, d \text v}{\int \psi^*_{\text o} \, \psi^{\phantom{.}}_{\text o} \, d \text v}$$


To approximate $\psi_{\text o}$ we can start with a relatively simple <u>trial</u> wave function, arbitrarily called $\xi$, which also can be expressed using a **Hamiltonian** operator:  


$$\tag{53}$$


$$\large \text E_{\xi} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\int \xi^* \, \hat H \, \xi^{\phantom{.}} \, d \text v}{\int \xi^* \, \xi^{\phantom{.}} \, d \text v} \phantom{...} \Longrightarrow \phantom{...} \text{Where:} \phantom{..} \overbrace{\text E_{\xi} \; \ge \; \text E_{\text o}}^{\large \text{Variational} \\ \phantom{....} \text{Principle}}
\\[25px]
\large \text E_{\xi} \, \normalsize (\alpha, \beta, \gamma ...) \phantom{.} \ge \phantom{.} \large \text E_{\text o}$$


Although $\xi$ is not equal to $\psi_{\text o}$ we can <u>minimize</u> [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>&xi;</sub></b> with respect to its <u>variational</u> parameter $\alpha$ (**Eqn. 54**) to generate the best possible estimate of [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>o</sub></b>, albeit a slightly higher one (i.e. upper bound).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; For example, what if the ground state energy of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} was not known. To approximate it we could use a <u>trial</u> function like: $\xi_{(r)} = e^{- \alpha r^2}$. This **Gaussian function** is a logical choice since it closely approximates the potential energy of an electron as it changes with distance (i.e. [V]{#Blk} decays exponentially with increasing distance from the nucleus).<b>[@griffiths_introduction_1994; @mcquarrie_physical_1997]</b> As discussed in later sections the use of multiple **Gaussian functions** turns out to be a very effective way of modelling electron orbitals (see **Information Box 4**).  


$$\tag{54}
\\
\large \text{Trial Wave Function:}
\\
\Big[ \, \text{Note:} \phantom{..} e \; = \; \text{base of natural log}, \phantom{.} r \; = \; \text{distance vector}, \phantom{.} \alpha \; = \; \text{variational parameter}\, \Big]
\\
\large \xi_{(r)} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large e^{- \alpha r^2}
\\$$


To calculate [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>&xi;</sub></b> obviously requires solutions to both the numerator and denominator of **Eqn. 53**. However, before carrying our the calculus lets first review what we do know about the problem, namely the **Hamiltonian** and the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#3DSE" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">wave equation</a></b>:  


$$\tag{55}$$


$$\text{Recall: } \text{Hamiltonian} \phantom{.} \text{Energy} \phantom{.} \text{relation}
\\
\big[ \text{Note:} \; \mu \; = \; \text{reduced mass} \; \text{of p}^+ \, e^- \; \text{system} \big]
\\
\\
\large \hat H \cdot \xi \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text E \cdot \xi \normalsize
\\
\large \hat H \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 \mu r^2} \overbrace{\Bigg[ \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg( r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg) \; + \; \frac{1}{sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \bigg( sin \theta \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg) \; + \; \frac{1}{sin^2 \theta} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \phi^2} \Bigg]}^{\large \text{Laplacian Operator } (\nabla^2) \text{ Spherical coordinates}} \; + \; \overbrace{\text V}^{\large \text{PE}}
\\
\phantom{.}
\\
\text{Potential Energy (V) of } e^- \text{ interacting with } Z \text{e nuclear charge, with } Z \text{ = atomic #}
\\
\large \text V \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} -\frac{(Z \text e)^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\text o} r}
\\ \phantom{.}
\\
\text{Combined Hamiltonian and Trial Wave Function } \large \xi \normalsize
\\
\big[ \, \text{Note:} \; \large \xi \; \normalsize \text{has only a} \; \large r \normalsize \text{adial variable since we are only dealing with a} \; 1s \; \text{orbital} \big]
\\
\large \hat H \normalsize \cdot \large \xi \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \Bigg( - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 \mu r^2} \bigg[ \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg( r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg) \bigg] \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{\text e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\text o} r} \Bigg) \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}$$


In order to calculate the numerator of **Eqn. 53** we first need to calculate $\hat H \cdot \large \xi$. Fortunately the [1&sscr;]{#Blk} orbital of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} is only dependent on the $\large r$adial component (i.e. independent of $\theta$ or $\phi$), which makes the calculation relatively straight forward.  


$$\large \hat H \cdot \xi \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 \mu r^2} \phantom{.} \overbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial r} \bigg( r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \bigg)}^{\large Partial \phantom{.} Differentials} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{(Z\text e)^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\text o} r}  \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}
\\[25px]
\large \text{Note Calculus Product Rule:}
\\
\text{Product Rule: } \frac{\partial}{\partial x} x e^{-ax^2} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} x \Big( \frac{\partial}{\partial x}e^{-ax^2} \Big) \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} e^{-ax^2} \Big( \frac{\partial}{\partial x} x \Big)
\\[25px]
\large \text{Recall: Calculus of exponential functions}
\\
\text{Exponential Functions: } \frac{\partial}{\partial x} e^{-ax^2} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \Big( -2ax \Big) e^{-ax^2}
\\[35px]
\boxed{\text{Step #1}} \, - \, \text{Calculate Partial Differentials:}
\\
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial r} \Bigg( r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \Bigg) \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \Bigg( r^2 \phantom{.} \bigg[ -2 \alpha r \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \bigg] \Bigg) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} -2 \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \Bigg( r^3 \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \Bigg)
\\
= &
-2 \alpha \Bigg[r^3 \big( -2 \alpha r \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}\big) \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \big( 3r^2 \big) \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}  \Bigg]
\\
= &
\phantom{.} 4 \alpha^2 r^4 \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} 6 \alpha r^2 \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}
\\
\end{align*}$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #2}} \, - \, \text{Combine Hamiltonian with Trial Function and simplify expression:}
\\
\begin{align*}
\large \hat H \cdot \xi \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 \mu r^2} \phantom{.} \bigg( 4 \alpha^2 r^4 \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} 6 \alpha r^2 \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \bigg) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{\text e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\text o} r}  \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}
\\\\
= &
\phantom{.} - \frac{2 \alpha^2 \hbar^2 r^2}{\mu} \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \frac{3 \alpha \hbar^2}{\mu} \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{\text e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_{\text o} r}  \phantom{.} e^{- \alpha r^2}
\\
\end{align*}$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #3}} \, - \, \text{Integrate the Numerator over all 3 (spherical) dimensions:}
\\
\Big[\text{Note Spherical Volume elements:} \phantom{..} d \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{r^2 \phantom{.} dr}^{1} \phantom{.} \overbrace{sin \theta  \phantom{.} d \theta}^{2} \phantom{.} \overbrace{d \phi}^{3} \Big]
\\
