For example, pairing **sine** with **cosine** is well suited for <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/calculus/integration-by-substitution.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">integration by substitution</a></b>. It's also worth reiterating that <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/numbers/e-eulers-number.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">exponential functions</a></b> are relatively easy to work with using differential and integral calculus (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://www.mathsisfun.com/calculus/integration-by-parts.html" target="_blank" title="Go to MathIsFun">integration by parts</a></b>).  


$$\boxed{\text{Step #3}} \; \text{Integration by Substitution for} \; \theta \; \text{variable dimension}
\\
\text{Let:} \; y \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{r^2 \; + \; \text R^2 \; - \; 2r \text R \, cos \theta}
\\
\frac{d(y^2)}{dy} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 2y \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} d(y^2) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 2y \cdot dy
\\
\text{and} 
\\
\frac{d(y^2)}{d\theta} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 2r \text R \cdot sin \theta \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} d(y^2) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 2r \text R \cdot sin \theta \cdot d\theta
\\
2y \phantom{.} dy \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 2r \text R \, sin \theta \, d\theta \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} d \theta \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}y \, dy}{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}r \text R \, sin \theta} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{y \, dy}{r \text R \, sin \theta}
\\
\begin{align*}
\large \langle \text X \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{2}{a_{\text o}^2} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \, \require{cancel} \cancel{r} \Bigg [ \int_0^{\pi} e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, \require{cancel} \cancel{sin \theta} \, \frac{y \, dy}{\require{cancel} \cancel{r} \text R \, \require{cancel} \cancel{sin \theta} } \Bigg ] \, dr
\\
\large \langle \text X \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{\frac{2}{a_{\text o}^2 \; \text R}}^{\text{constants}} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \Bigg [ \int_0^{\pi} y \, e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy \Bigg ] \, dr
\\
\end{align*}$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #4}} \; \text{Integration by Part for} \; \theta \; \text{variable}
\\ 
\text{general formula} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \int u \phantom{.} \frac{d \text v}{dx} \, du \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} (u) (\text v) \; - \; \int \text v \, \frac{du}{d \text x} \, dx
\\
\text{Let:} \phantom{..} u \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} y \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \frac{du}{dy} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\frac{dy}{dy}}^{\large 1} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} du \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} dy
\\
\text{Let:} \phantom{..} \frac{d \text v}{dy} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int \frac{d \text v}{dy} \, dy \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - a_\text{o} e^{-y/a_{\text o}}
\\ \;
\\
\text{Now Solve:} \phantom{..} \int_0^{\large \pi} y \phantom{.} e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy \phantom{...} \text{using general formula above}
\\
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\large \pi} y e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} (y) \, (-a_{\text o} \, e^{-y/a_{\text o}}) \; - \; \int_0^{\large \pi} - a_\text{o} \, e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy
\\
= & \phantom{.} -y \, a_{\text o} \, e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \; - \; a_{\text o}^2 \, e^{-y/a_{\text o}}
\\
= & \phantom{.} - a_{\text o} e^{-y/a_{\text o}}(y \; + \; a_{\text o})
\\
\end{align*}$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #5}} \; \text{Plug in values from step 4 and Integrate over new} \; \theta \; \text{boundary} 
\\[5px]
\text{Range values:} \phantom{...} cos(\pi) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} -1 \phantom{...} \text{and} \phantom{...} cos(0) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\begin{align*}
y(\pi) \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \sqrt{r^2 \; + \; \text R^2 \; - \; 2r \text R \, (-1)} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{r^2 \; + \; \text R^2 \; + \; 2r \text R} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{(r \; + \; \text R)^2}
\\
= & \phantom{.} r \; + \; \text R
\\
y(0) \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \sqrt{r^2 \; + \; \text R^2 \; - \; 2r \text R \, (1)} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{r^2 \; + \; \text R^2 \; - \; 2r \text R} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sqrt{(r \; - \; \text R)^2}
\\
= & \phantom{.} | r \; - \; \text R |
\\
\large \langle \text X \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{2}{a_{\text o}^2 \text R} \large \int \normalsize e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \Bigg [ \large \int_{|r \; - \; \text R|}^{r \; + \; \text R} \normalsize y \phantom{.} e^{-y/a_{\text o}} \, dy \phantom{.} \Bigg ] dr
\\
= & \phantom{.} \frac{-2 \require{cancel} \cancel{a_{\text o}}}{a_{\text o}^{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}} \text R} \large \int \normalsize e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \Bigg [ \bigg[ e^{-y/a_{\text o}}(y \; + \; a_{\text o}) \bigg]_{|r \; - \; \text R|}^{r \; + \; \text R} \Bigg] \, dr
\\
\large \langle \text X \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \text R} \large \int \normalsize e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \bigg[ e^{-(r \; + \; \text R)/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; + \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} e^{-(|r \; - \; \text R|)/a_{\text o}} \Big( |r \; - \; \text R | \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \bigg] \, dr
\\
\end{align*}$$


To complete the integration operation in step 5 new boundary conditions need to be calculated by plugging the $\theta$ values into $y$. Fortunately the values of <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer2_atom/#DFunc" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer2">cosine</a></b> functions are well known. Integrating the wave function using the new upper and lower limits produces a slightly simpler equation (i.e. two variables remaining: $\vec r$ and $\text R$). Unfortunately the lower limit of the integral is an absolute value (i.e. $|r - \text R|$). This treatment is necessary since the scalar distance has to be positive (i.e. need <u>real</u> distance). Considering that the proton occupies a central position within the <b>1&sscr;</b> orbital it is only logical that the electron be some real positive distance from this central reference point. Fortunately integrating using this unusual lower limit can be dealt with by simply dividing the integral into two parts, which produces three separate integral operations that need to be performed (step 6).  


$$\boxed{\text{Step #6}} \; \text{Note:} \; \text{distance} \; | r - \text R | \; \text{has to be a real positive value}
\\
\text{Need to perform two step Integration:} \phantom{..} 0 \rightarrow \text{R} \phantom{..} \text{and} \phantom{..} \text{R} \rightarrow \infty
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \text R} \Bigg[ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-r/a_{\text o}} \bigg[ e^{-(r \; + \; \text R)/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; + \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \; - \; e^{-(|r \; - \; \text R|)/a_{\text o}} \Big( |r \; - \; \text R | \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \bigg] \Bigg] \, dr
\\
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \text R} \Bigg[ e^{- \text R / a_{\text o}} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; + \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \; - \; \int_0^{\text R} e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \cdot e^{(-r \; + \; r)/a_{\text o}} \Big( \overbrace{\text R \; - \; r}^{\large \text R \; > \; r} \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr 
\\
& - \int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{\text R/a_{\text o}} \cdot e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( \overbrace{r \; - \; \text R}^{\large r \; > \; \text R} \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \, \Bigg]
\\
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \text R} \Bigg[ e^{- \text R / a_{\text o}} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; + \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \; - \; e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \int_0^{\text R} \, \overbrace{e^{(0)/a_{\text o}}}^{1} \Big( \text R \; - \; r \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr 
\\
& - \phantom{.} e^{\text R/a_{\text o}} \int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; - \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \; \Bigg]
\\
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \text R} \Bigg[ e^{- \text R / a_{\text o}} \overbrace{\int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r + \text R + a_{\text o} \Big) dr}^{\text{Int1}} \phantom{..} - \phantom{..} e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \overbrace{\int_0^{\text R} \Big( \text R - r + a_{\text o} \Big)dr}^{\text{Int2}} \phantom{.} 
\\
& - \phantom{.} e^{\text R/a_{\text o}} \overbrace{\int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r - \text R + a_{\text o} \Big)dr}^{\text{Int3}} \phantom{.} \Bigg]
\\
\end{align*}$$

<br>

$$\\
\boxed{\text{Step #7}} \; \text{Solve Integral #1 using Integration by Parts}
\\
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r + \text R + a_{\text o} \Big) dr \phantom{..} = \phantom{.} \int_0^{\infty} r e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \Big(\text R + a_{\text o} \Big) \int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr
\\
\boxed{\text{Step #7.1}} \; \text{Integration by Part (see Part 4 for General Formula)}
\\
\text{Let:} \phantom{.} u = r \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \frac{du}{dr} = \frac{dr}{dr}= 1 \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} du = dr
\\
\text{Let:} \phantom{.} \frac{d \text v}{dr} = e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \phantom{.} \Longrightarrow \phantom{.} \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int \frac{d \text v}{dr} dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{a_\text{o}}{2} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}}
\\
\int r e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} (r) \Big( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \int - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{a_{\text o} \phantom{.} r}{2} \phantom{.} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \phantom{.} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}}
\\
\int r \cdot e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}r \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg)
\\
\boxed{\text{Step #7.2}} \; \text{Complete integration across boundaries} \; (\text{when:} \; r \rightarrow \infty \phantom{..} e^{-r} = 0)
\\
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r + \text R + a_{\text o} \Big) dr \phantom{..} = &
\phantom{..} \Bigg[ e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}r \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \Bigg]_{0}^{\infty} + \phantom{.} \Big(\text R + a_{\text o} \Big) \Bigg[ - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Bigg]_{0}^{\infty}
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \Bigg[ 0 \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}(\infty) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} e^0 \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}(0) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \Bigg]
\\
& + \phantom{.} \Big(\text R + a_{\text o} \Big) \Bigg[ - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}(0) \phantom{.} - \phantom{.} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} e^0 \bigg) \Bigg]
\\
= &
\phantom{..} \Bigg[ 0 + 0 + \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \Bigg] + \Big(\text R + a_{\text o} \Big) \Bigg[ \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} \Bigg]
\\
\end{align*}
\\
\boxed{\; \text{Integral  #1  Solution} \phantom{..} = \phantom{..} \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \phantom{.} + \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o} \phantom{.} \text R}{2} \;}
\\$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #8}} \; \text{Solve Integral #2}
\\
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\text R} \Big( \text R \; - \; r \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \Bigg[ \text R \, r \; - \; \frac{r^2}{2} \; + \; a_{\text o}r \Bigg]_{0}^{\text R}
\\
= & \phantom{.} \Bigg[ \bigg( \text R^2 \; - \; \frac{\text R^2}{2} \; + \; a_{\text o} \, \text R \bigg) \; - \; \bigg( 0 \; - \; 0 \; + \; 0 \bigg) \Bigg]
\\
\end{align*}
\\
\boxed{\; \text{Integral #2 Solution} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\text R^2}{2} \; + \; a_{\text o} \, \text R \;}
\\$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #9}} \; \text{Solve Integral #3}
\\[5px]
\int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; - \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \int_{\text R}^{\infty} r \cdot e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \, dr \; + \; \Big( a_{\text o} \; - \; \text R \Big) \int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \, dr
\\[5px]
\boxed{\text{Step #9.1}} \; \text{Integration by Parts (formula from step 4) - repeat of step 7}
\\
\text{Let} \phantom{.} u \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} r \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \frac{du}{dr} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} 1
\\
\text{Let} \phantom{.} \frac{d \text v}{dr} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \phantom{..} \Longrightarrow \phantom{..} \text v \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - \frac{a_\text{o}}{2} \, e^{-2r/a_{\text o}}
\\[5px]
\begin{align*}
\int_{\text R}^{\infty} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Big( r \; - \; \text R \; + \; a_{\text o} \Big) \, dr \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \Bigg[ e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}r \; - \; \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \Bigg]_{\text R}^{\infty} \; + \; \Big( a_{\text o} \; - \; \text R \Big)\Bigg[ - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2} e^{-2r/a_{\text o}} \Bigg]_{\text R}^{\infty}
\\
= &
\phantom{.} \Bigg[ 0 \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}(\infty) \; - \; \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \; - \; e^{-2 \text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o}}{2}(\text R) \; - \; \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg) \Bigg] 
\\
& +
\phantom{.} \Big( a_{\text o} \; - \; \text R \Big)\Bigg[ - \frac{a_\text{o}}{2} (0) \; + \; \frac{a_\text{o}}{2} \, e^{-2 \text{R}/a_{\text o}} \Bigg]
\\
= &
\phantom{.} \require{cancel} \cancel{\frac{\text R \; a_{\text o}}{2} \; e^{-2 \text R/a_{\text o}}} \; + \; \frac{a_{\text o}^2}{4} \, e^{-2 \text R/a_{\text o}} \; + \; \frac{a_\text{o}^2}{2} \, e^{-2 \text{R}/a_{\text o}} \; - \; \require{cancel} \cancel{\frac{\text R \, a_\text{o}}{2} \, e^{-2 \text{R}/a_{\text o}}}
\\
\end{align*}
\\
\boxed{ \; \text{Integral #3 Solution} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \, e^{-2R/a_{\text o}} \; }
\\$$


$$\boxed{\text{Step #10}} \; \text{Plug in solutions to integrals #1-3 to finalize Exchange Integral}
\\
\begin{align*}
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \; \text R} \Bigg[ \; e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \; + \; \frac{a_{\text o} \; \text R}{2} \bigg) \; - \; e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{\text R^2}{2} \; + \; a_{\text o} \phantom{.} \text R \bigg) \; - \; e^{\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \; e^{-2R/a_{\text o}} \bigg) \Bigg]
\\
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-2}{a_{\text o} \; \text R} \Bigg[ \; \require{cancel} \cancel{e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg)} \; + \; e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \; \frac{a_{\text o} \phantom{.} \text R}{2} \; - \; \frac{\text R^2}{2} \; - \; a_{\text o} \phantom{.} \text R \bigg) \; - \; \require{cancel} \cancel{e^{- \text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{3 a_{\text o}^2}{4} \bigg)} \Bigg]
\\
\langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{-\require{cancel} \cancel{2}}{a_{\text o} \; \require{cancel} \cancel{\text R}} \Bigg[ \; e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( - \frac{a_{\text o} \; \require{cancel} \cancel{\text R}}{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}} \; - \; \frac{\text R^{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}}}{\require{cancel} \cancel{2}} \; \bigg) \Bigg] \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}}}{a_{\text o}} \bigg( a_{\text o} \; + \; \text R \bigg)
\\
\end{align*}
\\
\boxed{ \; \langle \text X \rangle \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( 1 \; + \; \frac{\text R}{a_{\text o}} \bigg) \; }
\\$$


As shown above the solution to the **Exchange Integral** is long and mathematically complex, but certainly doable using introductory level calculus. Nevertheless, plugging all of the integral solutions back into the $\langle \text E \rangle$ equation for [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b><sup>+</sup> provides us with a final equation (**Eqn. 73**) that can be plotted (**Fig. 34**) as a function of the inter-nuclear distance (i.e. **Bohr** radius normalized distance = $\text R/a_{\text o}$). The plot clearly shows that the <u>bonding</u> [MO]{#Blk} of [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b><sup>+</sup> does indeed have an energy <u>minimum</u> (i.e. $\text R/a_{\text o} \approx 2.5$). Therefore it is safe to say that [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b><sup>+</sup> does represent a &ldquo;<i>true</i>&rdquo; **bound state**.  


$$\tag{73}$$


$$\begin{align*}
\text{Final Exchange (X) Integral:} &
\phantom{..} \text X \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{-\text R/a_{\text o}} \bigg( 1 \; + \; \frac{\text R}{a_{\text o}} \bigg)
\\[5px]
\text{Final Overlap (S) Integral:} &
\phantom{..} \text S \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} e^{- \text R/a_{\text o}} \Bigg[ \, 1 \; + \; \frac{\text R}{a_{\text o}} \; + \; \frac{1}{3} \bigg( \frac{\text R}{a_{\text o}} \bigg)^2 \, \Bigg]
\\[5px]
\text{Final Direct (D) Integral:} &
\phantom{..} \text D \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{a_{\text o}}{\text R} \Bigg[ \, 1 \; - \; e^{-2\text R /a_{\text o}} \bigg( \frac{\text R}{a_{\text o}} \; + \; 1 \bigg) \Bigg]
\\[5px] 
\text{Energy Expectation Value:} &
\phantom{.} \text{Bonding} \; (+) \; \text{and anti-Bonding} \; (-) \; \text{Orbitals}
\\[5px]
\large \langle E \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \large \langle \hat H \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \frac{\int \psi^* \, \big( \hat H \big) \, \psi^{\phantom{.}} \, d^3r}{\int \psi^* \, \psi^{\phantom{.}} \, d^3r} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \text{E}_{\text{1s}} \normalsize \Bigg[ \, 1 \; + \; 2\frac{\big( \text D \pm \text X \big)}{\big( 1 \pm \text S \big)} \, \Bigg]
\\[10px]
\text{Average Total Energy of System} & \, \text{includes Potential Energy term for 2 Protons}
\\[5px]
\large \langle \hat H \rangle \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \large \text{E}_{\text{1s}} \normalsize \Bigg[ \phantom{.} 1 \; + \; 2\frac{\big( \text D \pm \text X \big)}{\big( 1 \, \pm \, \text S \big)} \; - \; \frac{2 \, a_{\text o}}{\text R} \, \Bigg]
\\[5px]
\large \text{Let:} \phantom{..} \text F(x) \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \large \frac{\langle \hat H \rangle}{\text{E}_{\text{1s}}} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \Bigg[ \, 1 \; + \; 2 \frac{\big( \text D \phantom{.} \pm \phantom{.} \text X \big)}{\big( 1 \phantom{.} \pm \phantom{.} \text S \big)} \; - \; \frac{2 \, a_{\text o}}{\text R} \, \Bigg]
\\
\end{align*}$$


```{r echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
### Hamiltonian for simplest molecule ==> H2+ ion
### Range of rA = R/a0 values
rA <- seq(0.1, 6, by = 0.02)

### H2+ ion 
DirInt <- 1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA)
XInt <- exp(-rA)*(1 + rA)
OvInt <- exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3)

### Total Hamiltonian with PE of 2 protons added / E bonding Function for H2+ ion
HamFuncB <- function(rA){
  out <- -(1 + 2*((1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA) + (1 + rA)*exp(-rA))/(1 + exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3))) - 2/rA)
  return(out)
  }

### Total Hamiltonian ... / E anti-bonding Function for H2+ ion
HamFuncAB <- function(rA){
  out <- -(1 + 2*((1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA) - (1 + rA)*exp(-rA))/(1 - exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3))) - 2/rA)
  return(out)
  }

### Energy of H2+ ion relative to dissociated species = H+ + H
DeltaE <- function(rA){
  out <- ((1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA) + (1 + rA)*exp(-rA))/(1 + exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3)))
  return(out)
  }

### Energy of H2+ ion relative to dissociated species = H+ + H
DeltaEd <- function(rA){
  out <- ((1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA))/(1 + exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3)))
  return(out)
  }

### Energy of H2+ ion relative to dissociated species = H+ + H
DeltaEx <- function(rA){
  out <- (((1 + rA)*exp(-rA))/(1 + exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + (rA^2)/3)))
  return(out)
  }

### Calculate values for H2+ ion - Bonding MO
HamFuncB <- sapply(rA, HamFuncB)
HamFuncB_df <- data.frame(rA = rA, Value = HamFuncB)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
HamFuncB_df <- rename(HamFuncB_df, HamFuncBvalue = Value)

### Calculate values for H2+ ion - Anti-bonding MO
HamFuncAB <- sapply(rA, HamFuncAB)
HamFuncAB_df <- data.frame(rA = rA, Value = HamFuncAB)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
```

```{r echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
DI <- function(rA){
  out <- 1/rA - (1 + 1/rA)*exp(-2*rA)
  return(out)
  }

XI <- function(rA){
  out <- exp(-rA)*(1 + rA)
  return(out)
  }

OI <- function(rA){
  out <- exp(-rA)*(1 + rA + rA^2/3)
  return(out)
  }

DI2 <- sapply(rA, DI)
DI2_df <- data.frame(rA = rA, Value = DI2)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
DI2_df <- rename(DI2_df, DIvalue = Value)

XI2 <- sapply(rA, XI)
XI2_df <- data.frame(rA = rA, Value = XI2)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
XI2_df <- rename(XI2_df, XIvalue = Value)

OI2 <- sapply(rA, OI)
OI2_df <- data.frame(rA = rA, Value = OI2)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
OI2_df <- rename(OI2_df, OIvalue = Value)

### Merge Value columns from data frames
DOX_df <- left_join(DI2_df, XI2_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, OI2_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, DeltaE_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, DeltaEx_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, DeltaEd_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, HamFuncB_df)
DOX_df <- left_join(DOX_df, HamFuncAB_df)
DOX_df2 <- slice(DOX_df, 21:296)
```

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


<a id="MOTchem"></a>
**[&thinsp; 4.4 Frontier Molecular Orbitals and Chemical Reactivity &thinsp;]{style="border: 2px solid black;"}:** A typical chemical reactions involves molecular interactions (i.e. between **reactants**) that give rise to new molecules (i.e. **products**). In order for these molecular collisions to be productive the **reactants** must not only be properly oriented, but also have sufficient energy. The energy driving the reaction forward is primarily used to <u>activate</u> the **reactants**, via the breaking of existing bonds and the formation of new ones. This is why chemical reactions are not spontaneous. Even though a given reaction may be thermodynamically favourable, such as in the case of **exothermic** reactions (i.e. **products** are much lower in energy than the **reactants**), it still requires a &ldquo;<i>spark</i>&rdquo; of energy to start the reaction. If, on the other hand, chemical reactions were spontaneous than life itself would have likely not evolve on this planet. Under this scenario any organic molecule that comes in contact with atmospheric oxygen would quickly undergone combustion. Obviously there is more to a chemical reaction than just its **reactants** and **products**. Indeed, every chemical reaction where chemical bonds are broken will have a relatively high energy intermediate known as the **transition state** ([[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}).<b>[@eyring_activated_1935; @evans_applications_1935]</b> The specific energy required to form the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} complex is called the **energy of activation** ([[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b>). Based on the collision theory ($\text{rx. rate} \propto \text{# collisions/time}$) if [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> is much higher than the average kinetic energy of the molecules then the reaction will proceed very slowly. The corresponding <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer1_atomists/#BarFormula" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer1">Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of the molecular velocities</a></b> would show few fast-moving molecules that could overcome such a high energy barrier. Conversely, if [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> is much smaller than the average kinetic energy of the molecules, then a significant fraction of the molecules would have enough kinetic energy to overcome this energy barrier. One way of calculating [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> is to use the <b><a class="one" href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1903/arrhenius/facts/" target="_blank" title="Go to NoblePrize.org">Arrhenius</a></b> (1889) equation, which quantifies the relationship between the rates of chemical reactions and temperature (<b>Eqn. 75</b>).<b>[@arrhenius_uber_1889; @arrhenius_uber_1889-1]</b>  


$$\tag{74}$$


$$\\
\large \text{Collision Model - Gas Chemical Kinetics:}
\\
\large \text{Arrhenius Equation}^{\dagger}
\\
\text{Note:} \phantom{..} A \; = \; \text{collision frequency constant}, \; k \; = \; \text{rate constant}
\\
R \; = \; \text{universal gas constant}, \; \text T \; = \; \text{temperature (Kelvin)}
\\
\large e \normalsize \; = \; \text{base of the natural logarithm scale}
\\[5px]
\Large ^{\dagger} \, \left. \begin{array}{|c|}
\hline
\large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.}  A \cdot \large e^{\frac{- \text E_a \, }{\, \text{RT} \,}}
\\[10px]
\hline \end{array} \right.
\\[10px]
\large ln(k) \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large ln \normalsize \big( A \big) \; + \; \frac{- \text E_a}{\text{R}} \, \bigg[\frac{1}{\, \text{T}} \bigg]
\\[10px]
\overbrace{\large ln(k)}^{\large y} \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{\frac{- \text E_a \, }{\, \text{R}}}^{\large m} \, \overbrace{\bigg[\frac{1}{\, \text{T}} \bigg]}^{\large x} \; + \; \overbrace{\large ln \normalsize \big( A \big)}^{\large b}
\\$$


<!-------------------------------------->
<!---- FIG 35 - Arrhenius function ----->
<!-------------------------------------->
<a id="Fig35"></a>

<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/ArrhEqn_ExpFunc_plot.jpg){width=600px}

<b>Figure 35: Arrhenius Equation</b>
</figure>
</div>
</div>
<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->

The variable $k$ (i.e. # collisions that yield <b>product</b> per second) in <b>Eqn. 74</b> is equal to the frequency factor $A$ (i.e. total # of collisions per second) times the <u>probability</u> (i.e. $e^{-\text{E}_a/\text{RT}}$) that a given collision yields **product**. When this equation is log (natural) transformed it creates a <u>linear</u> equation that can be easily plotted. If the kinetic data is fitted to the **Arrhenius** equation and graphed the slope of the line of best fit would be equal to [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub>/R</b>, and its y-intercept would be equal to the collision frequency $A$ (**Fig. 36**). Simply looking at the non-transformed **Arrhenius** equation (**Fig. 35**) one can see that the rate constant ($k$) is dependent on both [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> and temperature (<b>T</b>). It is also clear to see that the rate constant ($k$) is directly proportional to the collision frequency ($A$), which you may recall from earlier discussions about the <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/opcchemprimer1_atomists/#MBDh2" target="_blank" title="Go to ChemPrimer1">Maxwell-Boltzmann</a></b> molecular speed distributions in <b>ChemPrimer1</b> is temperature dependent. Notably the changes in [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> will have a significant affect on the rate constant $k$ since a chemical reaction will proceed very slowly if [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> is prohibitively high. Nevertheless, even a reaction rate with a relatively large [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> will increase quite rapidly with increasing temperature. This effect will be modified by the collision frequency ($A$) since it also increases with temperature (i.e. increase kinetic energy of molecules increases collision frequency). To illustrate the importance of the **Arrhenius equation** consider the following chemical reaction involving the hydroxyl radical and methane:  


$$\\
^{\Large \cdot}\text{OH} \; + \; \text{CH}_4 \phantom{.} \longrightarrow \phantom{.} \text H_2 \text{O} \; + \; ^{\Large \cdot}\text{CH}_3
\\$$


The chemistry of free radicals is a fascinating one. Besides playing a major role in health and chronic diseases,<b>[@Harman_aging_1956; @beckman_free_1998; @wang_superoxide_2018; @chandimali_free_2025]</b> some like $^{\Large \cdot}\text{OH}$ also play an important role in regulating the atmosphere (i.e. major tropospheric oxidant of volatile organic compounds).<b>[@lelieveld_role_2004; @monks_gas-phase_2005; @lelieveld_global_2016; @chen_sources_2019; @berg_temperature-dependent_2024; @hoover_measurements_2026]</b> For example **Florian Berg** and colleagues (2024) studied the temperature dependent reaction rates of the hydroxyl radical with several alkanes, including the major greenhouse gas methane.<b>[@berg_temperature-dependent_2024]</b> The results of one of their experiments, tabulated below, was fitted to the <b>Arrhenius equation</b> and plotted (**Fig. 36**).  


$$\\
\text{Temperature-dependent Hydroxyl radical reaction rates of methane}
\\
\left. \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline {\phantom{.} \\ \text{Temperature} \\ \phantom{.....} \text{(K)}} & {\phantom{.} \\ \phantom{...} \large \frac{\Large 1}{\Large \text K}} & {\phantom{.} \\ \phantom{........} \large k \\ (10^{-14} \, \text{cm}^3 \, \text{sec}^{-1})} & {\phantom{.} \\ \phantom{..} \large \ln(k)} 
\\[10px]
\hline 340.3 & 0.00294 & 1.40 & 0.33647
\\[10px]
\hline  331.1 & 0.00302 & 1.12 & 0.11333
\\[10px]
\hline  321.7	& 0.00311	& 0.99 & -0.01005
\\[10px]
\hline  312.4 & 0.00320 & 0.83 & -0.18633
\\[10px]
\hline  303.1 & 0.00330 & 0.73 & -0.31471
\\[10px]
\hline  293.8 & 0.00340 & 0.62 & -0.47804
\\[10px]	
\hline  286.0 & 0.00350 & 0.50 & -0.69315
\\[10px]
\hline \end{array} \right.
\\$$

The equation to the line of &ldquo;best fit&rdquo; and the adjusted <b>R<sup>2</sup></b> statistic, which assesses the how well the model fits the data, is also included. The value of [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> for the experimental temperature range of 280-340 <b>K</b> under standard pressure conditions (i.e. 1 **bar**) was calculated using the slope: [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> = $1735 \, \text K \times (8.314 \; \text J \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text K^{-1}) \; \approx \; 14.4 \; \text{kJ} \, \text{mol}^{-1}$.

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


Another more convenient way of determining [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> involves measuring the rate constant using only two temperature data points. This can be done by simply rearranging the **Arrhenius equation** so that it takes the following form:  


$$\tag{75}$$


$$\\
\large \text{Temperature Data Points:}
\\
\large ln \, k_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large ln \normalsize \big( A \big) \; + \; \frac{- \text E_a}{\text{R}} \, \Bigg[ \frac{1}{\, \text{T}_1} \Bigg]
\phantom{.......}
\large ln \, k_2 \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large ln \normalsize \big( A \big) \; + \; \frac{- \text E_a}{\text{R}} \, \Bigg[ \frac{1}{\, \text{T}_2} \Bigg]
\\
\large ln \, k_2 \normalsize \; - \; \large ln \, k_1 \normalsize \phantom{.} = 
\phantom{.} \frac{- \text E_a}{\text{R}} \, \Bigg[ \frac{1}{\, \text{T}_2} \; - \; \frac{1}{\, \text{T}_1}\Bigg]
\\
\large \text E_a \normalsize \phantom{.} = 
\phantom{.} - \text R \normalsize \left( \frac{ln \, k_2 \; - \; ln \, k_1}{ \, \Big[ \large \frac{1}{\text T_2} \; - \; \frac{1}{\text T_1} \, \Big]} \right)
\\
\begin{align*}
\\
\text{e.g.} \phantom{..} \text T_1 \; = & \; 286, \phantom{.} ln \, k_1 \; = \; -0.69315
\phantom{....} \text T_2 \; = \; 340.3, \phantom{.} ln \, k_2 \; = \; 0.33647
\\
\large \text E_a \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} - \text 8.314 \; \text J \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text K^{-1} \normalsize \cdot \left( \frac{\Big(0.33647 \; - \; (-0.69315) \Big) \, \text K}{ \, \Big[ \large \frac{1}{340.3 \, \text K} \; - \; \frac{1}{286 \, \text K} \, \Big]} \right)
\\
\large \text E_a \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} - \text 8.314 \; \text J \, \text{mol}^{-1} \, \text K^{-1} \normalsize \cdot \left( \frac{1.02962}{ \, -0.00055792} \, \text K \right)
\\
\large \text E_a \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} 15.343 \; \text{kJ} \, \text{mol}^{-1}
\end{align*}
\\$$


Although the two-point (n = 2) version of the equation is more convenient to use it's not as accurate as graphing the entire data set (n = 7). Regardless of what form you use the **Arrhenius** equation can only be used for gas-phase kinetics. Fortunately **Henry Eyring** and **Michael Polanyi** (1935) developed a new equation (i.e. **Eyring-Polanyi** or equation) as part of their novel **transition state** ([[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}) <b>theory</b>.<b>[@eyring_activated_1931, @eyring_activated_1935; @evans_applications_1935]</b> Although the **Eyring-Polanyi** equation is like the **Arrhenius equation**, in that it describes the relationship between chemical reaction rates and temperature, it's also unique in a number of ways. Firstly, the **Eyring-Polanyi** equation is based on a [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} mechanism as apposed to the more simplier collision theory. Secondly, it can be used to study not only gases, but also liquids and solids. Thirdly, it links reaction rates with the thermodynamic properties of the chemical system, including <b>Gibb's free energy of activation</b> ($\Delta \text G^{\ddagger}$). Unlike the more familiar <b>Gibb's free energy</b> ($\Delta \text G$), which measures how &ldquo;favourable&rdquo; a chemical reaction is under constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta{\text G}^{\ddagger}$ is a measure of the energy barrier (i.e. position of [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} along reaction coordinate path) that <b>reactants</b> must overcome to form a **product**.  


$$\\
\large ^{\ddagger} \text{Eyring-Polanyi Equation}
\\
\text{Note:} \phantom{..} k \; = \; \text{rate constant}, \; k_{\text B} \; = \; \text{Boltzmann's constant}, \; h \; = \; \text{Planck's constant},
\\
\text T \; = \; \text{absolute Temperature}, \; \Delta{\text G}^{^\ddagger} \; = \; \text{Gibb's free energy of activation},
\\
\text R \; = \; \text{Universal Gas constant}, \; \Delta \text H \; = \; \text{Enthalpy}, \; \Delta \text S \; = \; \text{Entropy}
\\[5px]
\Large ^{\ddagger} \, \left. \begin{array}{|c|}
\hline
\large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \frac{k_{\text B} \, \text T}{h} \, e^{\frac{- \, \Large \Delta \text G^{^{\large \ddagger}}}{\text{RT}}}
\\[10px]
\hline \end{array} \right.
\\[10px]
\begin{align*}
\text{Given:} \phantom{..} \Delta \text G^{^{\large \ddagger}} \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \Delta \text H^{^{\large \ddagger}} \; - \; \text T \, \Delta \text S^{^{\large \ddagger}}
\\
\large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \frac{k_{\text B} \, \text T}{h} \cdot \large e^{\frac{- \, \Large (\Delta \text H^{^{\large \ddagger}} \; - \; \text T \, \Delta \text S^{^{\large \ddagger}})}{\Large \text{RT}}}
\\
\large k \normalsize \phantom{.} = & \phantom{.} \frac{k_{\text B} \, \text T}{h} \cdot \large e^{^\frac{\, \Large \Delta \text S^{^{\large \ddagger}}}{\Large \text{R}}} \cdot e^{^\frac{- \Large \Delta \text H^{^{\large \ddagger}}}{\Large \text{RT}}}
\end{align*}
\\$$


$$\text{Rearrange equation then log (natural) transform it:}
\\
\begin{align*}
\frac{k}{\text T} \normalsize \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \frac{k_{\text B}}{h} \cdot \large e^{^\frac{\, \Large \Delta \text S^{^{\large \ddagger}}}{\Large \text{R}}} \cdot e^{^\frac{- \Large \Delta \text H^{^{\large \ddagger}}}{\Large \text{RT}}}
\\[5px]
\overbrace{ln \bigg( \frac{k}{\text T} \bigg)}^{\large \text y} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.}  - \overbrace{\frac{\Delta \text H^{\ddagger}}{\text{R}}}^{\large \text m} \, \overbrace{\bigg[ \frac{1}{\text T} \bigg]}^{\large \text x} \; + \; \overbrace{ln \bigg( \frac{k_{\text B}}{h} \bigg) \; + \; \frac{\Delta \text S^{\ddagger}}{\text R}}^{\large \text b}
\\[15px]
^{\dagger}\text{Alternate} \, & \, \text{linearized (y = mx + b) form:}
\\
\overbrace{\text T \cdot ln \bigg( \frac{k}{\text T} \bigg)}^{\large \text y} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{\Bigg[ ln \bigg( \frac{k_{\text B}}{h} \bigg) \; + \; \frac{\Delta \text S^{\ddagger}}{\text R} \Bigg] \, \text T}^{\large \text{mx}} \; - \; \overbrace{\frac{\Delta \text H^{\ddagger}}{\text{R}}}^{\large \text b}
\\ \end{align*} 
\\$$

<sup>&dagger;</sup><b>Ref:[@lente_common_2005]</b>

<a id="Fig37"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">

![](images/plotEE.jpg){width=600px}

<b><u>Figure 37</u>: Eyring-Polanyi (EP) plot of the temperature-dependent rate coefficients for Hydroxyl radical reaction with Methane.</b> The above plot was generated using reaction rate data from **Florian Berg** et. al (2024) (Note: downloaded data from <b><a class="one" href="https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/24/13715/2024/" target="_blank" title="Go to ACP">supplemental material</a></b> file). A line of &ldquo;best fit&rdquo; (dashed line) was generated using a linear regression model of the log (natural) transformed reaction rates versus (inverse) temperature (Note: shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval). The equation of the line of &ldquo;best fit&rdquo; and the adjusted **R<sup>2</sup>** statistic, which assesses the model's fit to the data, is shown in the top right corner of the plot. The apparent <b>enthalpy of activation</b> (<b>&Delta;H<sup>&Dagger;</sup></b>) for the chemical reaction can be calculated by multiplying the absolute value of the slope by the ideal gas constant **R**: <b>&Delta;H<sup>&Dagger;</sup></b> = 8.314 J/(mol&sdot;K) &times; 1424 K = 11.84 kJ/mol. The **enthalpy of activation** can now be used to calculate [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> via the following mathematical relationship: <b>&Delta;H<sup>&Dagger;</sup> = [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<sub>a</sub> - RT</b>. Solving for [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> (i.e. **T** = 313 K) generates a value of 14.44 kJ/mol, which closely matches the [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> generated using the **Arrhenius** equation (14.425 kJ/mol). However, calculating the apparent <b>entropy of activation</b> (<b>&Delta;S<sup>&Dagger;</sup></b>) is a little more complicated since corrections have to be implemented (i.e. volume units require standard-state adjustment factor). Nevertheless, using a known pre-exponential factor (<b>A = 1.13 &times; 10<sup>6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>/(mol&sdot;sec)</b>) the value of <b>&Delta;S<sup>&Dagger;</sup></b> can be calculated using the following standard formula (standard conditions: 1 bar pressure):  


$$\Delta \text S^{\ddagger} \; = \; \text R \times ln \Bigg[ \frac{A \, h}{e^2 \, k_{_{\text B}} \, \text T} \Bigg] \; \approx \; - 145.5 \; \text J \, \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}$$

where the physical constants and variables are: (i) <b>R</b> = gas constant = 8.31446 J/(mol-K); (ii) <b>k<sub>B</sub></b> = Boltzmann constant = 1.38065 &times; 10<sup>-23</sup> J/K; (iii) <b>&planckh;</b> = Planck's constant = 6.626072 &times; 10<sup>-34</sup>&sdot;J&sdot;sec; (iv) <b>T</b> = absolute temperature = 293.15 K; and (v) <b><i>e</i></b> = base of natural logarithm.  

</div>

<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------------------------------->


The thermodynamic properties of the hydroxyl radical reaction reveals some interesting aspects about its mechanism. Firstly, the energy barrier separating the **reactants** from the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (i.e. [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> ~14.4 kJ/mol) is not typical of most chemical reactions (i.e. > 50 kJ/mol). However, according to **George Hammond's Postulate** (1955):


>"In highly exothermic steps it will be expected that the transition states will resemble reactants closely and in endothermic steps the products will provide the best models for the transition states ....the postulate applies to fast, exothermic reactions and, by the principle of microscopic reversibility, to any reactions which have a finite rate in the reverse direction."<b>[@hammond_correlation_1955]</b>


So this highly **exothermic** chemical reaction (see calculations below), which is largely driven by the highly reactive hydroxyl radical, has (according to **Hammond's Postulate**) a [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} that closely resembles the **reactants** both energetically and structurally.  


$$\\
\text{According to Hess's Law} \; \Delta H^\circ \; (\text{enthalpy of a reaction) is equal to:}
\\
\text{(Note:  BDE = bond dissociation energy)}
\\[10px]
\Delta H_{rxn}^\circ \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \sum \text{BDE}_{\small \text{broken}} - \sum \text{BDE}_{\small \text{formed}}
\\
\Delta H_{rxn}^\circ \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \overbrace{439 \, \text{kJ/mol}}^{\text{methane: C-H}} \; - \; \overbrace{497 \, \text{kJ/mol}}^{\text{water: O-H}} \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} - 58 \, \text{kJ/mol}
\\$$
 

Presumably the similarities between the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and **reactants** means that relatively little energy is needed to alter the structure of the **reactants** before bond breaking events occur, which lowers the energy barrier in the process. It's also worth noting that the <u>empirically</u> generated [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> for our hydroxyl radical reaction is an average energy value across varying temperature conditions. More accurate [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> values for this important reaction have been generated (i.e. 14.7 kJ/mol) using more extensive computational based methods (e.g. Density Functional Theory) that take into consideration the molecule's fundamental vibrational properties (i.e. zero-point vibrational energies),<b>[@korchowiec_hydrogen_1999]</b> but this is beyond the scope of this discussion. This bi-molecular reaction also has a relatively low $\Delta \text S^{\ddagger}$ (i.e. -145.5 J/mol&sdot;K), which suggests that the **reactants** require a specific spatial/angular orientation in order to successfully produce a **product** (i.e. **reactants** lose some translational and rotational freedoms, which decreases the randomness or **entropy** of the system). Of course, [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> can vary considerably depending upon the type of chemical reaction and the reaction conditions (e.g. required bond-breaking energies, temperature, pressure, etc.). For example, the famous **Haber-Bosch process** is a highly **endothermic** reaction (i.e. [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> + 3 [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> &rarr; 2 [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b>) that has an [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> of approximately 460 kJ/mol. Because of the high energy barrier (Note: reaction requires the breaking of a triple bond within [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>) this important chemical process, which is responsible for global fertilizer production,<b>[@erisman_how_2008]</b> requires metal catalysts in addition to high pressures and temperatures.<b>[@Haber_nobel_1920]</b> It's estimated that this one chemical process is responsible for consuming ~2% of the global energy supplies, and producing ~3% of global [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b> emissions.<b>[@IEA_ammonia_2021; @fao_greenhouse_2024; @mingolla_low-carbon_2025]</b>

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
### Define coordinate grids for bond distances (C-H and O-H)
r_CH <- seq(0.8, 2.5, length.out = 100) 
r_OH <- seq(0.8, 2.5, length.out = 100) 
pes_grid <- expand.grid(r_CH = r_CH, r_OH = r_OH)

### PES function of C-H and O-H distances incorporates 1D stretching potential for each bond:
### Energy as a Morse function bond distances: V(rCH, rOH) = D_e(CH) x (1 - exp[-beta_CH(rCH - r_eq(CH))])^2
### Typical r_eq = 1.09 for C-H, and r_eq = 0.96 for O-H
### Exact value of beta (De) depends on hybridization state of Carbon (sp3 C-H => beta ~1.8 - 2.0 A)
### Smaller beta parameter => broader & shallower potential well. For O-H radical bond beta = 2.2 A
### Model (C-H bond breaking + OH bond forming) beta value with coupled Morse potential, which is
### Gaussian with a pre-exponential constant corresponding to height of energy barrier
### Energy Barrier = Ea + deltaH = 11.84 + 14.4 = ~26 kJ/mol
### Averaged De values = 468 kJ/mol (De{CH} ~439 kJ/mol, De{OH} ~497 kJ/mol)
### Exponential term reduces to e^0 = 1, so pre-exponential constant A represents the peak amplitude
### at the saddle point, with De controlling the width and decay as you move away from it

pes_function <- function(r_CH, r_OH) {
  reactants <- 47 * (1 - exp(-1.9 * (r_CH - 1.09)))^2
  products <- 47 * (1 - exp(-2.2 * (r_OH - 0.96)))^2
  TS <- 10 * exp(-47 * (r_CH - 1.33)^2 - 47 * (r_OH - 1.2)^2) ### coupling
  return(reactants + products + TS)
}

### Calculate energy for each grid point
pes_grid$Energy <- pes_function(pes_grid$r_CH, pes_grid$r_OH)

```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
### Create sequences for the bond lengths (in Angstroms)
r_CH_vals <- seq(0.8, 2.5, length.out = 100)
r_OH_vals <- seq(0.8, 2.5, length.out = 100)

### Calculate the energy grid using outer()
### outer() applies the function to every combination of the two vectors
### outer() = evaluates pes_function across every combination of X and Y
### arrays to generate a 100 x 100 matrix of energy values (Z)
z_energy <- outer(r_CH_vals, r_OH_vals, pes_function)

```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
  ylab = expression(r[OH] ~ "Bond Length (\u00C5)"), ### y-axis label + subscript

)
```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
### Coupled Morse Potential: CH4 + OH --> CH3 + H2O
library(ggplot2)

### Define Constants and Parameters
De_CH <- 459.3  # kJ/mol (Dissociation energy = C-H methane)
De_OH <- 517.6  # kJ/mol (Dissociation energy = O-H water)
re_CH <- 1.087  # Angstroms (Equ. distance = C-H)
re_OH <- 0.957  # Angstroms (Equ. distance = O-H)
beta_CH <- 1.88 # 1/Angstrom (Morse parameter for C-H stiffness)
beta_OH <- 2.25 # 1/Angstrom (Morse parameter for O-H stiffness)

### Coupled Morse Potential Function = vector of bond orders 'n'
### from 1 (reactants) to 0 (products)
coupled_morse <- function(n) {
  # Pauling's bond length relationship for fractional bonds
  # r = re - 0.26 * ln(n)
  # ifelse = if r_OH > 0 then compute, but if r_OH < 0 then default value is 5
  r_CH <- ifelse(n > 0, re_CH - 0.26 * log(n), 5.0) 
  r_OH <- ifelse((1 - n) > 0, re_OH - 0.26 * log(1 - n), 5.0)
### Standard Morse potentials
V_CH <- De_CH * (1 - exp(-beta_CH * (r_CH - re_CH)))^2
V_OH <- De_OH * (1 - exp(-beta_OH * (r_OH - re_OH)))^2

### Coupled system PE profile relative to separated reactants
### Energy tracked as the penalty = (breaking C-H) - (gain of forming O-H)
V_total <- V_CH + (V_OH - De_OH)

return(data.frame(BO_CH = n, r_CH = r_CH, r_OH = r_OH, Energy = V_total))
}

### Generate Reaction Profile
bond_orders <- seq(1, 0, length.out = 200)
profile_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(bond_orders, coupled_morse))

### Find TS (max. energy along the path)
ts_index <- which.max(profile_data$Energy)
ts_state <- profile_data[ts_index, ]

print(paste("TS Target Energy Barrier:", round(ts_state$Energy, 2), "kJ/mol"))
print(paste("TS C-H Bond Length:", round(ts_state$r_CH, 3), "\u00C5"))
print(paste("TS O-H Bond Length:", round(ts_state$r_OH, 3), "\u00C5"))
```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}

ggplot(profile_data, aes(x = 1 - BO_CH, y = Energy)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c3e50", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = ts_state, aes(x = 1 - BO_CH, y = Energy), color = "#e74c3c", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Coupled Morse Potential: CH4 + OH Reaction Profile",
       x = "Reaction Coordinate (Progress: 0 = Reactants, 1 = Products)",
       y = "Relative Potential Energy (kJ/mol)") +
  theme_minimal()

```

<a id="Fig38"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/PESplot.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 38</u>: Potential Energy Surface (PES) model of Hydroxyl Radical reaction with Methane.</b> **(A)** The well known **Morse function** (see below) was used to simulate the **potential energy** (**V<sub>(r)</sub>**) of the simultaneous bond-breaking ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}) and bond-forming ([[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}) events of this reaction via the intermediate [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} complex (<b>&#9417;</b>).<b>[@morse_diatomic_1929; @Ball_physical_2014]</b> The total **V<sub>(r)</sub>** of the system was then plotted (gradient style) on a two-dimensional grid (**B**). Bond distances are often modelled like classical **harmonic oscillators**. Stretching a bond beyond its equilibrium position is resisted due to attractive Coulombic forces. However, as the inter-nuclear distance continues to increase (i.e. more energy input) the attractive forces slowly dissipate leading to the bond's dissociation (i.e. bond breaks). Conversely, when the bond distance contracts its **V(r)** rapidly increases due to repulsive Coulombic forces. This type of behaviour, which is not perfectly **harmonic**, can be conveniently modelled using **Morse functions**. The specific equilibrium bond length and potential well widths used in the calculations were: (i) for the [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} of methane, 1.09 &Aring; and 1.9 &Aring; and (ii) for the [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} of water, 0.96 &Aring; and 2.2 &Aring;, respectively. A **Gaussian** like function was used for the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}, with bond distances of 1.33 &Aring; (i.e. ~22% stretch of methane [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} bond) and 1.2 &Aring; (~25% stretch of [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} bond) being used for the calculation. For illustrative purposes a reduced value (i.e. 47 kJ/mol) of the averaged $\text D_e$ value (i.e. ~470 kJ/mol) of the reactant (~439 kJ/mol) and product (~497 kJ/mol) was used in this simulation to more clearly define the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (&ldquo;saddle&rdquo; point) along the reaction path. For the **Gaussian** like function of the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} the pre-exponential constant (i.e. $A$ = 10 kJ/mol) representing the peak amplitude of the reaction path (i.e. [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}, where $A \cdot e^0 = A$) was also reduced for illustrative purposes (i.e. $A$ = [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> + <b>&Delta;H<sup>&Dagger;</sup></b> = 11.84 + 14.4 = 26.24 kJ/mol). These altered values accentuate the height, width and decay of the energy contours moving away from the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}. Altogether the plot shows: (i) the reactant &ldquo;valley&rdquo; - located where $r_{\text{C-H}}$ is close to equilibrium (1.09 &Aring;) and $r_{\text{O-H}}$ is large (<b>&#9415;</b>); (ii) the product &ldquo;valley&rdquo; - where $r_{\text{O-H}}$ is close to equilibrium (0.96 &Aring;) and $r_{\text{C-H}}$ is large (<b>&#9413;</b>); and (iii) the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}, which is a <u>maximum</u> in <u>one</u> direction (i.e. only along the reaction coordinate path) and a <u>minimum</u> in all other directions within the energy landscape. This makes it a first-order <b>&ldquo;saddle&rdquo;</b> point (<b>&#9417;</b>).<b>[@schlegel_geometry_2011]</b>  


$$\\
^{\large \dagger}\text{Morse Potenital Energy Function:} \phantom{..} \text V(r) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \text D_e \Big(1 \; - \; e^{-a \, \Delta r} \Big)^2
\\[10px]
\text{TS Gaussian Function:} \phantom{..} \text V(r) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} A \cdot e^{\big(\large - \text D_e \, (r_{\text{CH}} \; - \; 1.33)^2 \; - \; \text D_e \, (r_{\text{OH}} \; - \; 1.2)^2 \normalsize \big)}
\\$$


Note that the physical constants and variables for the above functions are: (i) $\text D_e$ = potential energy well depth, which represents the bond dissociation energy; (ii) $e$ = **Euler's** number, which is the base of natural logarithms; (iii) $a$ = width of the potential energy well is related to the force constant $k_e$ by $a = \sqrt{k_e / 2 \text D_e}$. This force constant is directly related to the stiffness of a bond (i.e. $k_e$ is the same as restoring force of a spring as described in <b><a class="one" href="https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/hookes-law/latest/hookes-law_all.html" target="_blank" title="Go to PhET">Hooke's Law</a></b>). Like a stiff spring, a stiff bond has a strong restoring force even when it is subjected to small stretches; (iv) $\Delta r \; = \; r \, - \, r_{equ.}$ = difference between a given inter-nuclear distance, or $r$, and the <u>equilibrium</u> bond length (i.e $r_{equ.}$ = distance at minimum energy); (v) $A$ is the corresponding amplitude of the **Gaussian** like function.  

</div>
