<b>Figure 39: Reaction Coordinate</b>
</figcaption>

</figure>
<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->

The above plots crudely simulate the potential energy landscape of the bond-forming and bond-breaking events of the hydroxyl radical reaction. However, it may be more intuitive to describe these molecular events in terms of the **electrophilic** and **nucleophilic** nature of the **reactants**. In this way we can view the entire reaction through the &ldquo;lens&rdquo; of Coulombic interactions (e.g. **electrophile** attacking a **nucleophile**). But what part of a molecule serves as the source of the **electrophilic** or **nucleophilic** activity? To answer this question requires a more thorough understanding of the electron density distribution of the molecules, something that was previously discussed in the context of **Huckel's** [MO]{#Blk} theory. Despite the algebraic complexity one could calculate and visualize, courtesy **HuLis**, the electron density distribution of a conjugated $\large \pi$-bonding system, which helped to explain why some positions within these types of molecules are more likely to be the site of a chemical reaction. Using the electron density of molecules to explain chemical reactions, including the exact position of the atoms and the kinetics of the reaction (i.e. rate constants, activation energy, number of transition states, etc.) would be ideal. However, such mechanistic details are rather rare for most chemical reactions. Often times we only have a **reaction co-ordinate**, which is a relatively simple graphical representation of the energetics of a chemical reaction over time (**Fig. 39**). These graphs highlight the energy levels of the **reactants**, [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} and **products**, as well as the energy differences between **reactant** and **product** (i.e. **enthalpy**, or <b>&Delta; H</b>) and **reactant** and [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (i.e. energy of activation, or [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b>). With this information one can quickly determine whether a chemical reaction is **exothermic** (i.e. heat energy released, <b>&Delta; H</b> < 0) or **endothermic** (i.e. heat energy consumed, <b>&Delta; H</b> > 0).  
&nbsp; &nbsp; [MO]{#Blk} theory does offer some insight into the reactivity of molecules via so called **frontier orbitals**, namely: (i) the **H**ighest **O**ccupied **M**olecular **O**rbital, or **HOMO**; (ii) the **L**owest **U**noccupied **M**olecular **O**rbital, or **LUMO**; and (iii) the **S**ingle **O**ccupied **M**olecular **O**rbital or **SOMO**. According to the **F**rontier **M**olecular **O**rbital (**FMO**) theory, which was developed by <b><a class="one" href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1981/fukui/facts/" target="_blank" title="Go to Noble Prize">Kenichi Fukui</a></b> (1952), electrons within the **HOMO** of one molecule interacts with the empty **LUMO** of another molecule.<b>[@fukui_molecular_1952; @fukui_molecular_1954; @Fukui_simple_1964; @fukui_formulation_1970]</b> As mentioned previously **HOMO** holds the highest energy valence electrons, while **LUMO** represents the lowest energy empty orbital. When the chemical reaction involves free radicals then **LUMO** is replaced by **SOMO** (**S**ingly **O**ccupied **M**olecular **O**rbital), due to the presence of an unpaired electron. For our reaction the **HOMO** of methane acts as a **nucleophile**, while the **SOMO** of the hydroxyl radical acts as the **electrophile** (**Fig. 40**). The **nucleophilic** methane donates an electron from its **HOMO** $\large \sigma$-bond to the **SOMO** of the **electrophilic** hydroxyl radical. Overall we can say the frontier **SOMO** of the hydroxyl radical functions as an electron acceptor, which increases its electron density via the breaking of a [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>-</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} $\large \sigma$-bond in methane. However, one of the most important factors that determines the success of the reaction is the size of the **HOMO-SOMO** energy gap, which must be relatively small to ensure strong orbital &ldquo;mixing&rdquo;. Another key aspect of the theory is **orbital symmetry**, specifically the phase of the overlapping orbitals (i.e. matching signs = constructive interference). This latter point is not surprising given the wave-like properties of electrons as discussed at length above. Lastly, one must also consider the **spatial** or **steric** constraints of the chemical system. Specifically the spatial orientation, or angles, the **reactants** must assume in order to successfully interact with one another (i.e. provide maximize orbital overlap).  


<!------------------------------------>
<!------ Fig. 40 HOMO-SOMO Rx. ------->
<!------------------------------------>
<a id="Fig40"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/SOMO_HOMO.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 40</u>: SOMO-HOMO interaction of Hydroxyl radical reaction with Methane.</b> The **SOMO** of the hydroxyl radical is made up of a [2]{#Blk}[p]{#Blue} non-bonding orbital of [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}, which is nearly perpendicular to the central $\large \sigma$-bond between [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB} and [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}. The **SOMO-HOMO** energy gap is relatively small (Note: approximate ionization energy values: &#9312;, &#9313;, &#9314;),<b>[@collin_ionization_1967; @ruscic_enthalpy_2002; @dodson_vacuum_2018]</b> which allows for good orbital &ldquo;mixing&rdquo;. Lastly, the high electronegativity of [[O]{#Red}]{#strokeB}xygen coupled with its half-filled [2]{#Blk}[p]{#Blue} orbital makes the radical highly reactive (i.e. very favourable thermodynamically given the relatively low [[E]{#Red}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>a</sub></b> of the reaction). 

</div>

<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->
<!-------------------------------------------->


Unfortunately our current knowledge of most chemical reactions is largely macroscopic in nature. Often times the tools we use to study them are limited (e.g. exact quantum solutions are only possible for the simplest two atom system, and approximation methods rely on multiple simplifying assumptions). Although thermodynamic methods do provide very meaningful insights, they too are limited in what they can tell us (e.g. average energies). The most intuitive pedagogical tool for studying chemical reactions is perhaps electron (arrow) &ldquo;pushing&rdquo; diagrams. Anyone who studied organic chemistry as a student learned how arrows are used to track or map electron movements between **nucleophiles** and **electrophiles** (e.g. see: <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Fig_SerProt" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP">serine proteases</a></b>). These types of diagrams are somewhat similar in function to <b><a class="one" href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1965/feynman/facts/" target="_blank" title="Go to NobelPrize.org">Feynman</a></b> diagrams, since they both convert abstract rules into simple elegant drawings. For free radical chemical reactions such diagrams largely map the movements of single electrons (Note: <b><a class="one" href="https://opc-project.netlify.app/project/pnps/#Fig_VitCE" target="_blank" title="Go to PNP">lipid peroxidation</a></b> example). However, these simple drawings do not tell the whole story of a chemical reaction, since other important factors are often left out (e.g. many proteins like enzymes are flexible and undergo changes in shape, which usually requires X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy or Cryo-EM techniques to observe).<b>[@henzler-wildman_dynamic_2007; @kovermann_structural_2015; @riziotis_conformational_2022]</b> The recent use of machine learning (**ML**) algorithms for protein and biomolecular structure predictions (i.e. <b><a class="one" href="https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/" target="_blank" title="Go to AFDB">AlphaFold2 Protein Structure Database</a></b>, and <b><a class="one" href="https://alphafoldserver.com/welcome" target="_blank" title="Go to AFS">AlphaFold3 Server</a></b>),<b>[@jumper_highly_2021; @bertoni_alphafold_2026; @abramson_accurate_2024]</b> is an exciting new way of studying molecules. However, using **ML** algorithms to make chemistry predictions (e.g. synthesis, bio-activity and energetics studies),<b>[@behler_generalized_2007; @meuwly_machine_2021; @kaser_neural_2023; @tu_predictive_2023]</b> is greatly hampered by the enormous diversity and unstructured nature of chemical &ldquo;space&rdquo;.<b>[@mitchell_machine_2014; @reymond_chemical_2015]</b> Current publicly available chemical databases (e.g. <b><a class="one" href="https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/" target="_blank" title="Go to PubChem">PubChem</a></b>, <b><a class="one" href="https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/" target="_blank" title="Go to ChEMBL">ChEMBL</a></b> and <b><a class="one" href="https://commonchemistry.cas.org/" target="_blank" title="Go to CAS Common Chemistry">CAS</a></b>)<b>[@nicola_public_2012; @gonzalez-medina_open_2017; @jacobs_cas_2022]</b> are not standardized (e.g. differing file types for molecular structures), nor do they share the same information. Most were designed to document the biological activity of small molecules (e.g. drug screening). Other promising technologies that can be applied to chemistry problems (e.g. molecular modelling for medical and materials science) is quantum computing. Although it holds great promise, particularly in terms of its computational speed when compared to conventional computing,<b>[@feynman_quantum_1985; @aspuru-guzik_simulated_2005; @whitfield_simulation_2011; @reiher_elucidating_2017]</b> its prohibitively expensive (i.e. hardware and infrastructure) for most scientists. There are cheaper options, such as &ldquo;cloud&rdquo; access to quantum computing service providers. For example, **IBM** offers access to their quantum computing systems via a <b><a class="one" href="https://www.ibm.com/quantum/products" target="_blank" title="Go to IBM">Pay-as-you-Go-Plan</a></b> that starts at 96 USD/minute. For large biotech companies that spend many years and millions of dollars on drug discovery such spending is well justified. However, quantum computing hardware is not only expensive (i.e. > 1 million USD for entry level systems), it also requires dedicated resources and infrastructure.<b>[@krasnok_QuComp_2026]</b> It's also subject to other limitations (e.g. fragile nature of **Qubits**), which makes it inferior (certainly on a practical scale) to classical computation methods (e.g. **D**ensity **F**unctional **T**heory, or **DFT**). This is rather disappointing since quantum computing should, by its very nature, be able to map and quantifying multiple quantum states with great ease.<b>[@feynman_quantum_1985; @lloyd_universal_1996]</b> Hopefully, in the not so distant future, quantum computing will become a routine and practical modelling tool for basic scientists.  


<a id="Box4"></a>
<!------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------  Info Box4 ------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------->

<div style="border: 2px solid black; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<span id="strokeB"><span id="DB">&thinsp; INFORMATION BOX 4 - Computational (<i>ab initio</i>) Chemistry &thinsp;</span></span>
</div>
<div style="position: relative;">

Computational methods used to model molecules are largely based on **G**aussian **F**unctions (**GF**), which form the basic units of <b><a class="one" href="https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Quantum_Mechanics/17%3A_Quantum_Calculations/ab_initio_Basis_Sets" target="_blank" title="Go to Chemistry LibreText">basis functions</a></b> used by **D**ensity **F**unction **T**heory (**DFT**) methods.<b>[@hohenberg_inhomogeneous_1964; @kohn_self-consistent_1965; @huzinaga_GaussianMO_1965; @hehre_GaussianMO_1969; @huzinaga_approxAO_WaveFunc_1971; @ditchfield_GaussianMO_1971; @hehre_GaussianMO_1972]</b> The use of computational friendly **Gaussian** functions (i.e. $e^{\large \alpha r^2}$), which was pioneered by **Samuel F. Boys** (1950),<b>[@boys_GaussianMO_1950]</b> to approximate electronic wave functions have largely replaced **Slater Type Orbital** (**STO**) functions (i.e. $e^{\large \zeta r}$).<b>[@slater_atomic_1930; @slater_directed_1931; @hartree_self-consistent_1939]</b> Although **STO** functions accurately model the characteristic exponential radial decay of an atom's electronic charges, the integral calculus used to calculate them is computationally &ldquo;expensive&rdquo;. Fortunately multiple **Gaussian functions** (**GF**) can be used to approximate a **STO**. Replacing one **STO** function with more than one **GF** seems counter intuitive, but computers can handle **Gaussian** type integrals far more easily than **STO** type integrals. This is largely due to the fact that <b><a class="one" href="https://www.3blue1brown.com/?topic=probability&lesson=gaussian-convolution" target="_blank" title="Go to 3Blue1Brown">multiplying two (or more) GF produces one new GF</a></b>. Obviously the main point here is that multi-electron integral calculations, which can number in the millions, are efficiently computed using **GF**. For example, a simple 10 atom organic molecule like **pyrrole** ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>4</sub></b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>5</sub></b>[[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB}) modelled using a **basis set** like **STO-3G** carries out out over 100,000 two-electron integral calculations, while a slightly more modern and accurate **basis set** like **6-31G** (**N** = 55 **basis functions**) would require over 1.1 million two-electron calculations (Note: # calculations &asymp; **N**<sup>4</sup>/8). For a **pyrrole** molecule the number of primitive **GF** used by **STO-3G** is 90 (<b><u>Note</u>:</b> **N** = # **basis functions** = # atoms &times; [orbitals/atom] &times; [**basis functions**/orbital] = [4 [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} &times; 5 &times; 1] + [1 [[N]{#FGr}]{#strokeB} &times; 5 &times; 1] + [5 [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} &times; 1 &times; 1] = 30 **basis functions**. Each **basis function** is a contraction of 3 primitive **GF**, which means there are a total of 90 primitive **GF** per molecule). As shown below plotting a single **GF** (**Fig. 42A**) clearly fails to accurately replicate the exponential radial decay of a spherical [1s]{#Blk} [AO]{#Blk} (i.e. lacks a &ldquo;cusp&rdquo; at its centre, and it decays faster due to its squared exponent). However, a linear combination of three (or more) **GF**, as exemplified by **G3** (**Fig. 42A**, and mathematically expressed below), can clearly overcome these limitations. Unfortunately using **basis sets** to model the electronic structure of large molecules is not trivial since the shape of electron density clouds can vary (e.g. spherical [1s]{#Blk} versus a dumbbell shaped [2p]{#Blue} orbital), particularly in response to its environment (e.g. water can distort the shape of electron density clouds). As a result many different types of <b><a class="one" href="https://www.basissetexchange.org/" target="_blank" title="Go to Basis Set Exchange">basis sets</a></b> have been developed to account for these different electronic behaviours (e.g. geometries, energies, bond polarization, etc.).<b>[@teale_dft_2022; @bursch_best-practice_2022]</b>  


$$\\
\text{Slater Type Orbitals (STO), Gaussian Type Orbitals (GTO)},
\\
\text{and Gaussian Functions (GF)}
\\
\Big[ \text{Note:} \phantom{.} N = \text{normalization factor}, \; r = \text{radial distance} \Big]
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize i}^{\normalsize \text{STO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large N \normalsize e^{- \large \zeta \, r}
\phantom{........} \large \psi_{\normalsize i}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize (r, \, \alpha) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large N \normalsize e^{- \large \alpha \, r^2}
\\
\large \psi_i^{\normalsize \text{STO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} \approx \phantom{.} \large \psi_i^{\normalsize \text{GTO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} = \phantom{.} \large \sum_{i \, = \, 1}^{n} \normalsize \; c_i \; \large \psi_{\normalsize i}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize (r, \, \alpha_i)
\\$$


For each basic **GF** the exponential factor $\alpha$ determines its lateral spread (e.g. small value produces a more diffuse or wide **Gaussian**), while the position ($r$) of the function is purposely centred on an atom. The height or amplitude of the **GF** is determined by the pre-exponential coefficient ($c_i$). For example, [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB} has four valence atomic orbitals (i.e. [2s]{#Blk}, [2p<sub>x</sub>]{#Blue}, [2p<sub>y</sub>]{#Blue}, [2p<sub>z</sub>]{#Blue}) and one inner or **core** [1s]{#Blk} orbital (i.e. 5 orbitals in total). Therefore we would need one **basis function** for each of these five [AO]{#Blk}. Since there are 3 contracted **GF** per **basis function** that would give us 15 primitive **GF** per carbon atom. Differences in the behaviour of the core and valence orbitals (i.e. core orbitals have a relatively stable radius, while the shape of valence orbitals are often distorted by neighbouring atoms) have resulted in the design of &ldquo;split&rdquo; **basis sets**. For example, the split-valence **basis set** known as **3-21G**, which was designed by <b><a class="one" href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1998/summary/" target="_blank" title="Go to Nobel.com">John Pople's</a></b> group (1980), accurately models the geometries and electronic properties of small organic molecules. Although it has been largely superseded by more accurate **basis sets** it's still used today (e.g. quick geometry optimizations).<b>[@Binkley_Pople_1980; @ahlrichs_GaussianMO_1981]</b>

<a id="Fig41"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/BasisSetExchange.jpg){width=700px}
</figure>
</div>

<b><u>Figure 41</u>: Basis Set Exchange</b>
</div>

The first number in the **3-21G basis set** refers to the three <u>primitive</u> **GF** (e.g. $g_1, g_2, g_3$) that are combined (i.e. &ldquo;contracted&rdquo;) to form a single **basis function** for the inner/core orbital (i.e. $\text{AO}_{1 \text s} = \large \text c_{\normalsize 1 \text s} \normalsize (f_1 g_1 \, + \, f_2 g_2 \, + \, f_3 g_3)$ ). The next two numbers after the hyphen indicate a split-valence configuration (Note: **sp** = [s]{#Blk} and [p]{#Blue} orbitals share the same double **basis function**, $\text{AO}_{\text{sp}} = \large \text c_{\normalsize 2} \normalsize (f_4 g_4 \, + \, f_5 g_5) + \large \text c_3 \normalsize (f_6 g_6)$). The so called &ldquo;inner&rdquo; valence **basis function** is a contraction of 2 <u>primitive</u> **GF** (i.e. $g_4, g_5$), while the &ldquo;outer&rdquo; valence **basis function** is made up of a single (i.e. non-contracted) <u>primitive</u> **GF** whose <u>fixed</u> coefficient is equal to unity (i.e. $f_6 = 1$). Splitting the valence shell into two **basis functions** allows the electron structure to expand or stretch in order to more accurately model chemical bonding. It's worth noting that the term &ldquo;contraction&rdquo; refers to a <u>fixed</u> linear combination of primitive **GF**. This means the coefficients of the primitives are optimized, fixed values or constants ($f_i$). This leaves the <u>group</u> coefficient ($c_i$) as a variable, which serves as a weighting factor for the contracted **basis function**. This latter coefficient does not appear in the output of the **basis set** shown above since it is a variable (i.e. changes depending on the unique geometry and electronic state of the molecule). To illustrated the usefulness of **GF** three **basis functions** (i.e. **G1**, **G2** and **G3**) are plotted below (**Fig. 42A**).<b>[@mcquarrie_physical_1997]</b>  


$$\\
\begin{align*}
\large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{STO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} \approx \overbrace{\large \sum_{\large i \, = \, 1}^{n \, = \, 1} \; c_{\normalsize (\text{1s}_{\Large i})} \; \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, \alpha_{_{\large \text{1s}_{\Large i}}})}^{\text{G1}} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.4166)
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{STO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} \approx \overbrace{\large \sum_{\large i \, = \, 1}^{n \, = \, 3} \; c_{\normalsize (\text{1s}_{\Large i})} \; \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, \alpha_{_{\large \text{1s}_{\Large i}}})}^{\text{G3}} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{0.446}^{f_1} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.1688)
\\
+ \; \overbrace{0.5353}^{f_2} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.6239) \; + &
\; \overbrace{0.1543}^{f_3} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 3.425)
\\
\large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{STO}} \normalsize (r, \zeta) \phantom{.} \approx \overbrace{\large \sum_{\large i \, = \, 1}^{n \, = \, 6} \; c_{\normalsize (\text{1s}_{\Large i})} \; \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, \alpha_{_{\large \text{1s}_{\Large i}}})}^{\text{G6}} \phantom{.} = &
\phantom{.} \overbrace{0.1303}^{f_1} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.10)
\\
+ \; \overbrace{0.4165}^{f_2} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.2431) \; + &
\; \overbrace{0.3706}^{f_3} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 0.626)
\\
+ \; \overbrace{0.1685}^{f_4} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 1.8222) \; + &
\; \overbrace{0.0494}^{f_5} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 6.5131)
\\
+ \; \overbrace{0.0092}^{f_6} \, \large \psi_{\normalsize \text{1s}}^{\normalsize \text{GF}} \normalsize ( r, \, 35.5231) \; \; &
\end{align*}
\\$$


Using **basis sets** to model the chemical properties of molecules is of course a major goal of computational quantum chemistry. So we can re-visit the hydroxyl radical reaction with methane (i.e. abstraction of a [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom) and analyze it in more detail. For example, in order to model the **transition state** ([[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}) of this chemical reaction we need a **basis set** that accounts for loosely bound electrons (i.e. diffuse functions) and potentially distorted or bent electron densities (i.e. polarization functions).  


$$\text{CH}_4 \, + \, \cdot\text{OH} \; \rightarrow \; \cdot\text{CH}_3 \, + \, \text{H}_2\text O$$


Polarization functions are particularly important due to the distorted electron density along the reaction coordinate of the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (i.e. bond stretching and compression events affect the activation energy). The analysis can be carried out using two popular and free (academic use only) chemistry computer programs known as <b><a class="one" href="https://avogadro.cc/index.html" target="_blank" title="Go to Avogadro">Avogadro (v2.0)</a></b> and <b><a class="one" href="https://www.faccts.de/orca/" target="_blank" title="Go to ORCA">ORCA (v6.1.0)</a></b>.<b>[@hanwell_avogadro_2012; @Neese_ORCA_program_2012; @Neese_ORCA_pkg_2020; @Neese_Orca6_2025]</b> **Avogadro** is a molecular visualization program capable of generating input files for several advanced quantum chemistry software packages such as **ORCA**. Although **ORCA** is only run via command line **Avogadro** is capable of visualizing various **ORCA** output files. **ORCA** has many useful functions for analyzing chemical reactions, including the **N**udged **E**lastic **B**and (<b><a class="one" href="https://www.faccts.de/docs/orca/6.1/manual/contents/structurereactivity/neb.html" target="_blank" title="Go to ORCA">NEB</a></b>) method.<b>[@asgeirsson_nudged_2021]</b> The nice thing about the **NEB** method is that it approximates the geometry of a [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} based solely on the known geometries of the **reactants** and **products**. It essentially finds a **M**inimum **E**nergy **P**ath (**MEP**) that connects these two defined energy <u>minimized</u> states. Somewhere along this path one or more potential energy **maxima** may be found (i.e. **saddle points** representing one or more [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} along the **reaction co-ordinate**). Before running **NEB** the geometry of the **reactants** and **products** must be configured using the basic build and editing tools of **Avogadro**, and then subjected to **ORCA** geometry optimization scans (i.e. used a **DFT method** known as an Unrestricted Kohn-Sham, or **UKS**, version of **B3LYP**, and a **basis set** known as **def2-TZVP**). The **UKS** method is required for any open shell (i.e. unpaired electrons) systems like our hydroxyl radical, while **B3LYP** is a standard density function used in geometry optimization calculations.<b>[@kohn_self-consistent_1965; @pople_spin-unrestricted_1995; @lee_B3LYP_1988; @becke_B3LYP_1993]</b> The **basis set** known as **def2-SVP** is often used for small molecules,<b>[@weigend_balanced_2005]</b> while the auxiliary basis set **def2/J** helped optimize the electronic structure calculations.<b>[@eichkorn_auxiliary_1997; @weigend_accurate_2006]</b> Chain-of-Spheres Exchange (**COSX**) and **Shark** algorithms, as well as the sequential Image-Dependent Pair Potential (**S-IDPP**) method were also used (&ldquo;under-the-hood&rdquo;) by **ORCA** to speed up various calculations (i.e. **DFT** method, molecular integrals, Minimum Energy Path).<b>[@Neese_HF_DFT_COSalg_2009; @Izsak_COSalg_LPCC_2012; @helmich-paris_improved_2021; @Neese_Shark_Integral_2022; @smidstrup_improved_2014; @schmerwitz_improved_2024]</b> The time it takes to complete an **ORCA** geometry optimization scan depends on the size of the molecule, as well as your choice of **basis sets**. Fortunately this quantum system only has 7 atoms, which reduces the time it takes to complete the computations (**Run Times:** reactant file = 9 minutes 4 seconds 452 msec, product file = 24 minutes 33 seconds 518 msec). A simple <u>input</u> text file (&ldquo;.inp&rdquo;) was then generated via **Avogadro's** main &ldquo;input&rdquo; feature. This small file contains: (i) the names of the specific **ORCA** jobs (**NEB-TS** and **Freq**) to be performed; (ii) the names of the electronic structure method (**UKS B3LYP** calculation) and **basis sets** (**def2-SVP**) used in the main calculations; (iii) the maximum number of optimization cycles to be performed (optional); (iv) the names of the **reactant** and **product** input .xyz files; and (v) the charge state (i.e. 0) and **M**ultiplicity (**M**) of the chemical system (i.e. **M** = **S** &times; (1/2) + 1 = **2** &times; (1/2) + 1 = 2). **M** is a calculation based on the number of unpaired electrons (**n** = 1), which determines the electronic spin (**S**) state of the chemical system (i.e. **S** = 2**n** = 2 &times; 1 = 2). Since we are dealing with a <u>neutral</u> hydroxyl radical: **M** = 2 and the charge is zero. The **NEB-TS** method carries out an additional [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} geometry optimization calculation (**OptTS**) once a likely [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} geometry has been found, which makes this version of **NEB** more computationally demanding (**Run Time:** 3 hours 37 minutes 57 seconds 353 msec). Once the **NEB-TS** calculations are completed several different file types are generated in your designated **ORCA** job folder, including: (i) &ldquo;.interp&rdquo;, (ii) &ldquo;.output&rdquo;, (iii) &ldquo;NEB-TS_converged.xyz&rdquo; and (iv) &ldquo;trj.xyz&rdquo;. The &ldquo;.interp&rdquo; file contains a path summary of the **NEB-TS** calculations. It's in the form of two simple tables, each listing the reaction coordinate (column 1), Bohr radii (column 2), and energy of the reaction (column 3). The first table is a truncated version (i.e. 10 of the 81 steps for my reaction), while the second table lists all 81 steps. Graphing the energy values versus the reaction coordinates (pathway) reveals a clear peak, which presumably is the most likely [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} structure (**Fig. 42B**). Opening either the &ldquo;NEB-TS_converged.xyz&rdquo; file (i.e. single converged structure) or the &ldquo;trj.xyz&rdquo; file (i.e. multiple stacked pics that can be played as an animation) in **Avogadro** shows the candidate [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} structure. **Avogadro** provides a number of viewing options, such as a simple ball-and-stick model (**Fig. 42C**). You can also add surface layers to your ball-and-stick model. For example the **Van der Waals** surface (i.e. physical space a molecule occupies) in combination with the **E**lectrostatic **P**otential (**EP**) surface provides a view of the molecule's charge distribution. Various molecular properties can also be retrieved using the &ldquo;Analyze&rdquo; feature, such as the partial charges assigned to each atom, or the various bond angles. The calculated geometry of the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} for our hydroxyl radical reaction shows a nearly linear array of the three key atoms: [[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} (i.e. $\measuredangle 169^{\circ}$ bond angle). The breaking bond length ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}<b>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}) is stretched approximately 14% (1.24 &Aring;) when compared to methane (1.09 &Aring;), while the developing [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} bond is ~1.29 &Aring;. The latter bond length is considerably larger (~34%) than the normal 0.96 &Aring; bond length found in water. Lastly the methyl group ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub></b>), which will become a radical on the **product** side of the reaction, is taking on a more planar geometry (i.e. [[sp2]{#SBlue}]{#strokeB} hybrid orbital geometry).

<b><u>Figure 42</u>: Gaussian Functions (GF) & ORCA Computer analysis of [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} complex for Hydroxyl radical reaction with Methane.</b>

<a id="Fig43"></a>
<div style="border: 2px solid gray; padding: 5px;">
<div align="center">
<figure>
![](images/TS_Bond_freq_animation.gif){width=600px}
</figure>
</div>
<b><u>Figure 43</u>: Transition State Vibrational Mode</b>. Opening the <b>NEB</b> output file in <b>Avogadro</b> displays the geometry optimized transition state along with a table of computed vibrational frequencies. The program allows you to visualize any vibrating frequency of the candidate [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} molecule in animation mode. The [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} atom at the centre of the [[TS]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} ([[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>3</sub>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b>&sdot;&sdot;&sdot;</b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}) is shown moving in a periodic-like fashion similar to a classical harmonic oscillator. As [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB} moves closer to the hydroxyl radical (i.e. abstraction process), which will eventually form a [[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<b><sub>2</sub></b>[[O]{#OrR}]{#strokeB} molecule, the remainder of the methane molecule begins to take on a more planar geometry (i.e. eventual methyl radical product: <b>&sdot;</b>[[C]{#Blk}]{#strokeB}[[H]{#Blue}]{#strokeB}<sub>3</sub>).  

</div>

### Define paths to all PNG files
png_files <- list.files(path = "images", pattern = "*.png", full.names = TRUE)

### Sort files numerically (animate in correct order) and Read images into R object
png_files <- mixedsort(png_files)
animation_frames <- image_read(png_files)

### Animate the frames (fps)
TS_Bond_freq_animated_gif <- image_animate(animation_frames, fps = 5)

### Write gif animation to file
image_write(TS_Bond_freq_animated_gif, "images/TS_Bond_freq_animation.gif")

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
z1 = 1.24
a1 = 0.4166

rSTO <- seq(0, 5, by = 0.02)
rGTO <- seq(0, 5, by = 0.02)

N1 <- (2*a1/pi)^(3/4)

STO <- function(rSTO) {
  out <- (z1^3/pi)^(1/2) * exp(- z1*rSTO)
  return(out)
  }

GTO <- function(rGTO) {
  out <- N1*exp(- a1*rGTO^2)
  return(out)
  }

a4a = 0.12217
a4b = 0.453757
a4c = 2.0133
a4d = 13.3615
N4a <- (2*a4a/pi)^(3/4)
N4b <- (2*a4b/pi)^(3/4)
N4c <- (2*a4c/pi)^(3/4)
N4d <- (2*a4d/pi)^(3/4)

a3a = 0.1688
a3b = 0.6239
a3c = 3.425
N3a <- (2*a3a/pi)^(3/4)
N3b <- (2*a3b/pi)^(3/4)
N3c <- (2*a3c/pi)^(3/4)

G3 <- function(rGTO) {
  out <- (0.4446)*N3a*exp(- a3a*rGTO^2) + (0.5353)*N3b*exp(- a3b*rGTO^2) + (0.1543)*N3c*exp(- a3c*rGTO^2)
  return(out)
  }

G4 <- function(rGTO) {
  out <- (0.50907)*N4a*exp(- a4a*rGTO^2) + (0.47449)*N4b*exp(- a4b*rGTO^2) + (0.13424)*N4c*exp(- a4c*rGTO^2) + (0.01906)*N4d*exp(- a4d*rGTO^2)
  return(out)
  } 

a6a = 0.1
a6b = 0.2431
a6c = 0.626
a6d = 1.8222
a6e = 6.5131
a6f = 35.5231
N6a <- (2*a6a/pi)^(3/4)
N6b <- (2*a6b/pi)^(3/4)
N6c <- (2*a6c/pi)^(3/4)
N6d <- (2*a6d/pi)^(3/4)
N6e <- (2*a6e/pi)^(3/4)
N6f <- (2*a6f/pi)^(3/4)

G6 <- function(rGTO) {
  out <- (0.1303)*N6a*exp(- a6a*rGTO^2) + (0.4165)*N6b*exp(- a6b*rGTO^2) + (0.3706)*N6c*exp(- a6c*rGTO^2) + (0.1685)*N6d*exp(- a6d*rGTO^2) + (0.0494)*N6e*exp(- a6e*rGTO^2) + (0.0092)*N6f*exp(- a6f*rGTO^2)
  return(out)
  }


STO1 <- sapply(rSTO, STO)
STO1_df <- data.frame(rSTO = rSTO, Value = STO1)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
lookup <- c(STO1value = "Value", x = "rSTO")
STO1_df <- rename(STO1_df, all_of(lookup))

GTO1 <- sapply(rGTO, GTO)
GTO1_df <- data.frame(rGTO = rGTO, Value = GTO1)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
lookup2 <- c(GTO1value = "Value", x = "rGTO")
GTO1_df <- rename(GTO1_df, all_of(lookup2))

GTO3 <- sapply(rGTO, G3)
GTO3_df <- data.frame(rGTO = rGTO, Value = GTO3)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
lookup2 <- c(GTO3value = "Value", x = "rGTO")
GTO3_df <- rename(GTO3_df, all_of(lookup2))

GTO4 <- sapply(rGTO, G4)
GTO4_df <- data.frame(rGTO = rGTO, Value = GTO4)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
lookup2 <- c(GTO4value = "Value", x = "rGTO")
GTO4_df <- rename(GTO4_df, all_of(lookup2))

GTO6 <- sapply(rGTO, G6)
GTO6_df <- data.frame(rGTO = rGTO, Value = GTO6)
### Change Column Names using **rename** function of "dplyr" package
lookup2 <- c(GTO6value = "Value", x = "rGTO")
GTO6_df <- rename(GTO6_df, all_of(lookup2))

### Merge Value columns from data frames
SGTO1_df <- left_join(STO1_df, GTO1_df)
SGTO1_df <- left_join(SGTO1_df, GTO3_df)
SGTO1_df <- left_join(SGTO1_df, GTO4_df)
SGTO1_df <- left_join(SGTO1_df, GTO6_df)

```


```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
### Generate STO and GTO plots
SGTOplot <- ggplot(SGTO1_df, aes(x = x, y = STO1value)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = STO1value, color = "STO"), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  geom_line(aes(y = GTO1value, color = "G1"), linetype = 3, linewidth = 1, lineend = "round") +
  geom_line(aes(y = GTO3value, color = "G3"), linetype = 3, linewidth = 1, lineend = "round") +
  geom_line(aes(y = GTO6value, color = "G6"), linetype = 3, linewidth = 1, lineend = "round") +
  scale_colour_manual("",
       breaks = c("STO", "G1", "G3", "G6"),
       values = c("STO" = "black", "G1" = "blue3", "G3" = "red3", "G6" = "tan2"),
       labels = c("STO", "G1", "G3", "G6")) +
  labs(x = expression(Distance~(r/a[o])), y = expression(psi[~"1s"(r)])) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        # top, right, bottom, left margins
        plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 5, b = 5, l = 10, unit = "pt"),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(color = "black", size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.8, 0.7),
        legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "black", fill = "white",
                                             linetype = 1, linewidth = 1))

ggsave("SGTO.jpg", width = 7, height = 5)
print(SGTOplot)

```
